Empirical evaluations across computer vision and natural language processing benchmarks demonstrate that FedFit significantly narrows the sparse-to-dense accuracy gap, outperforming state-of-the-art methods while maintaining high communication efficiency. Our code is available at .

title: Minari: Infrastructure for Collaborative Reinforcement Learning Datasets
summary: Minari: Infrastructure for Collaborative Reinforcement Learning Datasets Offline reinforcement learning (RL) depends on shared datasets, but sharing them is still hard. Each benchmark ships its own format, documentation is thin, and most datasets cannot be regenerated once the environment code moves on. We introduce Minari, an open-source Python library for creating, sharing, and loading RL datasets. Its API follows Gymnasium, so recording a dataset means wrapping an environment and stepping through it as usual. From there, users can attach metadata, filter, combine, and shuffle datasets, and publish or download them with one command through the HuggingFace Hub. Every dataset stores the environment specification, seeds, applied wrappers, and pinned package requirements needed to rebuild the environment and regenerate the data. TorchRL, AgileRL, and d3rlpy already load Minari datasets natively, so switching datasets in those libraries takes one line of code. Minari also hosts 338 reproducible datasets (350K trajectories, 55M steps) covering robotic locomotion and manipulation, maze and grid navigation, language-conditioned instruction following, Atari, and web navigation, including a full regeneration of D4RL with public generation scripts. We report baseline scores for six offline RL algorithms on the regenerated D4RL and MuJoCo datasets.

title: RSIMed: Scaling Medical Foundation Models beyond Limited Clinical Data via Retrieval-Grounded Self-Evolution
summary: RSIMed: Scaling Medical Foundation Models beyond Limited Clinical Data via Retrieval-Grounded Self-Evolution Rare diseases are hard to diagnose, and the labeled clinical records needed to train models for them are few, private, and slow to extend, since a specialist must read every case. A model that writes its own training tasks could learn beyond these records, but no program can check a model-written diagnosis, and a wrong answer key corrupts training. To tackle this dilemma between data scarcity and difficulty of data annotations, we introduce RSIMed, Recursive Self-Improvement in Medicine, one of the first self-evolving pipelines in which a task proposer co-evolves in context with a diagnostic solver on real clinical records. Seeded by training admissions, a frozen copy of the solver writes each clinical question from retrieved medical evidence, so its answer rests on a source, and steers topics and difficulty toward what the solver still gets wrong. On rare-disease diagnosis from MIMIC-IV admissions, the accuracy of RSIMed-27B grows linearly with training compute, while a static pool of generated tasks collapses. Without any external model, RSIMed-27B and RSIMed-9B reach 0.516 and 0.488 diagnostic accuracy, above every off-the-shelf GPT-5.6 setting, whose best reaches 0.399 at 38 times the inference cost of RSIMed-27B. Tasks written by four external teachers, including GPT-5.5, train a less accurate diagnostician than the solver's own. Trained only on diagnosis, RSIMed-RL-27B also improves on the physician-written tasks of HealthBench Professional, from 0.291 to 0.303 in adjusted score.

title: CARET: Clinical Assertion-Aware Residual Calibration for Medical Image-Text Alignment
summary: CARET: Clinical Assertion-Aware Residual Calibration for Medical Image-Text Alignment Medical vision--language models align radiographs with free-text reports, but radiology language distinguishes explicit findings, negation, uncertainty, and omission. Treating these report states as interchangeable during feature adaptation can change image predictions without supporting visual evidence. We introduce CARET, a parameter-efficient image-side adaptation method that retains pretrained image and text encoders and uses paired positive and negative clinical statements to define a low-dimensional semantic correction space. A bounded residual adjusts image features along these directions, while assertion-aware supervision distinguishes explicitly present and absent findings from uncertain or unmentioned ones. At inference, the adapter requires only an image; textual references remain fixed. In zero-shot classification, CARET achieves 67.80\% accuracy on CheXpert 5$\times$200 and 65.20\% on RSNA. These scores exceed the published CLEFT-LoRA results by 1.06 and 0.27 percentage points, respectively. Comparisons to literature baselines are informative but not controlled for differences in pretraining and evaluation protocols. Ablations across eight components identify the four-state distinction and assertion objective as major contributors, with task-dependent effects for nonmention preservation and pair alignment.

title: RescueVLM: Model-Agnostic Vision-Language Framework for Rescue Drone Imagery
summary: RescueVLM: Model-Agnostic Vision-Language Framework for Rescue Drone Imagery 7 pages, 6 figures A single unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) mission over an incident site produces hundreds of images, far more than a rescue commander can review under time pressure, and human screening of destruction imagery carries a documented psychological cost. The two obvious remedies both fail in search and rescue (SAR) practice: cloud vision-language model (VLM) services are excluded because the imagery must not leave the incident network under GDPR and German civil-protection (BOS) rules, and fine-tuned specialist detectors age quickly while retraining and re-certifying them exceeds most SAR organizations resources. We present RescueVLM, an open-source, training-free and model-agnostic triage tool built on SketchVLM: a general-purpose open-weight VLM runs fully on-premise and is swapped for a newer model through a simple dropdown selection, so triage quality grows with the underlying models because all task knowledge lives in prompts and an output contract rather than in trained weights. One natural-language query over a mission folder returns a ranked shortlist with per-image justifications, editable SVG overlay annotations, and a GPS map of the hits. In a qualitative evaluation on German fire-brigade field data from three real deployments and a live fire exercise, a single query condenses an entire survey mission into a handful of annotated frames that a commander can review at a glance.

title: LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.6 Technical Report
summary: LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.6 Technical Report Recent advances in audio-driven avatar video generation have enabled increasingly realistic synthesis, yet achieving precise lip-audio synchronization, natural, human-like motion, and visual consistency over long sequences remains challenging. We present LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.6, which builds on LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.5 to improve expressive naturalness and reduce error accumulation during extended generation, e.g., exaggerated lip movements and overly red, temporally unstable lip coloration, enhance the naturalness of facial expressions and coordinated head and body movements. These improvements are driven by a refined post-training pipeline that integrates reinforcement learning, improved classifier-free guidance strategies for DMD-based few-step distillation, long-video rollouts, and on-policy distillation. Together, these refinements improve expressive realism and enable the generation of videos exceeding 10 minutes while maintaining visual quality and temporal consistency. Arena evaluations show that LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.6 outperforms its predecessor and competing commercial audio-driven avatar models, demonstrating the effectiveness of the improved post-training pipeline.

title: Scaling Channel-Adaptive Self-Supervised Learning
summary: Scaling Channel-Adaptive Self-Supervised Learning Recent advances in self-supervised pre-training of foundation models for natural images have made them a popular choice for various visual systems and applications. Self-supervised strategies are also promising in non-RGB scientific imaging domains such as in biology, medical and satellite imagery, but their broader application is hampered by heterogeneity in channel composition and semantics between relevant datasets: two datasets may contain different numbers of channels, and these may reveal distinct aspects of an object or scene. Recent works on channel adaptive strategies report substantial advantages for those that account for variable channel compositions without sacrificing the ability to jointly encode channels; yet, how these strategies behave at scale remains unclear. We here show that, surprisingly, trained across large-scale datasets, independent-encoding of channels outperforms joint-encoding methods by a substantial margin. We validate this result along an extensive set of experiments on various datasets from cell microscopy to geospatial imagery. Our DINO BoC approach sets a new state-of-the-art across challenging benchmarks, including generalization to out-of-distribution tasks and unseen channel combinations. We open-source code and model weights for a new general-purpose feature extractor for fluorescent microscopy.

title: Guided Group Featurizers (GGF): Improving Block-Sparse Featurizers with Object-Guided Learning
summary: Guided Group Featurizers (GGF): Improving Block-Sparse Featurizers with Object-Guided Learning Block-sparse featurizers (BSFs) use groups of learned directions to capture the multidimensional structure of visual concepts. However, grouping alone does not ensure that information about a concept is consolidated within a single group. We introduce Guided Group Featurizers (GGF), a novel object-guided extension that uses object annotations for initialization and training while preserving the BSF architecture. We assess whether each group's strongest response regions share an object type, part or material across images. Blinded reviews give GGF groups an average semantic coherence score of $94.1\pm0.9$%, versus $83.0\pm1.9$% for SLiCS and $65.3\pm2.2$% for supervised Vanilla BSF. GGF's consolidation advantage extends to unguided categories: one selected group per category covers $65.6\pm2.4$% of target-containing crops, versus $58.2\pm2.2$% for supervised Vanilla BSF, at approximately 5% false-positive rates for both. Across COCO and VOC, GGF also improves single-group object Capture and localization over Vanilla BSFs, SLiCS and Concept-SAE. Its groups produce more focused and reproducible object responses while supporting recognition and retaining associations under rotation, scale and brightness changes. GGF also uses fewer learned parameters than Concept-SAE and shorter recorded VOC training loops than both supervised alternatives. These findings support object guidance for organizing more interpretable BSF groups and show that response concentration extends to categories excluded from guidance.

title: FiReIQ: Field-Level Confidence Estimation with Reasoning and Image Quality in Document Extraction
summary: FiReIQ: Field-Level Confidence Estimation with Reasoning and Image Quality in Document Extraction Work in Progress Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in structured document extraction, yet their deployment in high-stakes applications requires reliable confidence estimates for individual fields. Existing uncertainty estimators often aggregate signals across an entire generation, obscuring field-specific reasoning uncertainty while overlooking visual degradations that may lead to confident extraction errors. To address these limitations, we introduce FiReIQ, a field-level confidence estimation framework that combines field-aligned reasoning signals from a single VLM generation with local and global image-quality features through quality-conditioned visual fusion. To facilitate systematic evaluation, we further introduce FiReIQ-Bench, a benchmark spanning financial receipts and legal contracts. Experiments with two reasoning VLMs show that FiReIQ consistently improves confidence discrimination, selective prediction, and probabilistic accuracy over existing estimators. These gains extend to private financial service data, where FiReIQ improves AUROC by 6.8% and coverage at 95% precision by 10.6% over an existing baseline. Together, these results highlight the potential of FiReIQ to reduce manual review while enabling more reliable document automation.

title: UnSPAD: Uncertainty-aware Single Photon Burst Photography
comment: Accepted at The Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV) 2027
summary: UnSPAD: Uncertainty-aware Single Photon Burst Photography Accepted at The Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV) 2027 We introduce UnSPAD, an uncertainty-aware burst photography framework capable of fusing and denoising arbitrarily long sequences of binary single photon avalanche diode (SPAD) measurements. Unlike prior methods that require fixed burst lengths or rely on powerful generative priors, UnSPAD combines learned motion estimation with uncertainty-informed measurement fusion and denoising to produce temporally consistent, hallucination-free reconstructions. UnSPAD first forms an initial scene estimate by averaging flow-aligned binary frames. UnSPAD then uses per-pixel uncertainty maps to perform uncertainty-aware denoising; the denoiser is informed about which regions accumulated the fewest observations (and thus contain the most relative shot noise) due to motion, occlusion, or alignment errors. This two-step reconstruction pipeline helps mitigate hallucinations---outside of the structure implicitly introduced by the flow estimates, the initial scenes estimates are entirely prior-free. Experiments on real and simulated SPAD and quantum image sensor (QIS) benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art reconstruction quality, improved temporal consistency, and superior color fidelity relative to the state of the art.

title: RAVEN-Bench: A Paired EO-IR Video QA Benchmark for Aerial Multimodal Understanding
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Datasets and Benchmarks Track)
summary: RAVEN-Bench: A Paired EO-IR Video QA Benchmark for Aerial Multimodal Understanding Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Datasets and Benchmarks Track) Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have advanced rapidly in image and video understanding, yet their ability to reason over paired aerial electro-optical and infrared (EO-IR) videos remains poorly understood. Such video poses a harder test than standard RGB video QA: targets are often small, evidence may appear only briefly, viewpoints change with the platform, and useful cues may appear in only one stream. We introduce RAVEN-Bench (Reasoning over Aerial Videos with EO-IR aligNment), a paired EO-IR video QA benchmark for low-altitude aerial multimodal understanding. RAVEN-Bench contains 100 temporally aligned EO-IR video pairs and 1,200 human-authored four-way multiple-choice questions, each independently audited for answer keys, modality requirements, evidence intervals, and group validity. It supports EO-only, IR-only, and paired EO+IR evaluation, and uses hierarchical capability levels and structured question groups to diagnose paired-input gain beyond the stronger unimodal condition, unimodal reliance, target consistency, and evidence-chain coherence. We evaluate frontier, open-weight, and remote-sensing MLLMs, showing that aggregate accuracy can overstate evidence-supported EO-IR reasoning. RAVEN-Bench provides controlled modality conditions and group-level diagnostics for auditing whether progress on RGB video benchmarks transfers to aerial cross-spectral understanding. Code and data are available at and .

title: CISyn: Human Mesh Recovery in Close Interactions with Physics-Simulated Synthetic Data
summary: CISyn: Human Mesh Recovery in Close Interactions with Physics-Simulated Synthetic Data 3D human mesh recovery (HMR) in close-interaction scenarios is hindered by the lack of large-scale, accurately annotated training data: real capture is expensive, and existing synthetic datasets rarely include physical contact. We introduce CISyn, a large-scale synthetic dataset purpose-built for close human-human interactions, generated via physics simulation and Blender-based rendering. By simulating collision dynamics between SMPL-X-rigged humanoids, CISyn naturally produces the contact, mutual occlusion, and pose entanglement that characterize close-interaction scenes, with no manual annotation effort. The released set provides 25,000 sequences with accurate 3D annotations. We further propose an uncertainty-aware loss that allows models to learn more effectively from the heavily occluded examples in our data. Augmenting state-of-the-art HMR training with CISyn and replacing the regression loss with our uncertainty-aware variant yields consistent improvements on close-interaction benchmarks, validating CISyn as a scalable complement to real-world data. The dataset, generation pipeline, and code are available at .

title: Effects of Conventional, Adaptive, and AI-Powered Upscaling on the Legibility of License Plates
summary: Effects of Conventional, Adaptive, and AI-Powered Upscaling on the Legibility of License Plates Small details in digital images -- a face, a street sign, a license plate -- are routinely upscaled in hopes of making them interpretable. Upscaling options now range from conventional interpolation, whose operations are spatially invariant and fully explainable, to AI-powered methods that synthesize detail potentially absent from the source. Here, we ask which of these techniques most reliably helps human readers. In two online experiments, we measured legibility of 255 US license plates ranging in resolution from 128 to 8 pixels tall, as well as their legibility after upscaling by eight different methods. Legibility of the un-upscaled plates collapsed from ceiling to floor across a narrow band of plate heights (32 to 10 pixels). Conventional upscaling techniques (bilinear, bicubic, and Lanczos interpolation) gave modest gains of about 5-9 percentage points within this range. Nearest-neighbor interpolation, however, was harmful, rendering unreadable many plates that were readable without any upscaling. Advanced methods diverged: SwinIR, an open-source AI enhancer, raised performance by up to 38 points relative to no upscaling, while an adaptive denoiser-based image prior and commercial AI upscaler tended to impair legibility. We found no strong evidence of consistent character hallucinations across methods. Decomposing the task, conventional interpolators mainly helped readers count characters, whereas SwinIR alone made the characters themselves more identifiable.

title: Probing Where Surprise Happens: Localized Violation-of-Expectation Evaluation of Video World Models
summary: Probing Where Surprise Happens: Localized Violation-of-Expectation Evaluation of Video World Models 8 pages, 4 figures Violation-of-expectation (VOE) benchmarks evaluate intuitive physics in video world models by testing whether physically impossible events produce greater prediction errors than matched possible events. However, conventional VOE evaluations aggregate prediction errors across space and time, making it unclear whether successful discrimination reflects model's understanding of physical violations at the locations and time where they occur. To address this limitation, we introduce localized VOE evaluation, a framework that measures prediction error differences between possible and impossible events within spatial regions and temporal intervals associated with physical violations. We compare global, temporally localized, and spatiotemporally localized evaluations of V-JEPA models pretrained on developmental egocentric videos or large-scale natural video datasets. Our results reveal that global and localized judgments can diverge in both directions: global aggregation can either obscure correct localized discrimination or produce apparent discrimination without corresponding localized evidence. During continued pretraining on developmental egocentric videos, agreement between global and localized judgments changes non-monotonically, while confidence in localized judgments increases despite modest improvements in accuracy. Together, these findings establish localized VOE evaluation as a complementary diagnostic for assessing intuitive physics in video world models and demonstrate that global prediction errors do not necessarily reflect the spatiotemporal evidence of physical violations.

title: Role-Separated Diffusion Transformers: Global Rule Isolation and Deterministic Sampling Manifold Compression
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Github Repo: this https URL
summary: Role-Separated Diffusion Transformers: Global Rule Isolation and Deterministic Sampling Manifold Compression 10 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Github Repo: We present Role-Separated Diffusion Transformers (RoSeDiT), a new diffusion transformer architecture that isolates the global rule from the image tokens. RoSeViT showed in visual reasoning that a vanilla ViT spreads a shared rule over all $L$ tokens at an entropy of order $Ld$, whereas an enforced controller route reduces it to order $d$. In class-conditional DiT and SiT, the class and the noise level are explicitly conditioned by adaLN, so a RoSeViT-style controller channel on the ViT side is insufficient to establish the full role separation. By introducing the adaLN listening mechanism, which makes adaLN compute under the controller's command, RoSeDiT brings the entropy theorem and role separation into the latent diffusion domain. Under the same SiT training and evaluation protocol at the same level of parameter count, RoSeDiT surpasses SiT at all four model scales at 400K steps, and RoSeDiT-L/2 even surpasses SiT-XL/2's 17.2 FID with 15.34 and 32% fewer parameters. RoSeDiT-XL/2 surpasses SiT-XL/2's 7M-step FID of 8.3 at 1.4M steps with 7.98, using one-fifth as many training steps. We further observe that models with the same denoising loss can have a large FID gap, which indicates a misalignment between the denoising objective and the image manifold. We formalize this phenomenon into Deterministic Sampling Manifold Compression (DSMC), a two-stage training schedule with which RoSeDiT-XL/2 surpasses SiT + REPA's 4M-step FID of 5.9 at 2.4M steps with 5.84.

title: Hard or Mislabeled? Failure Screens Enrich Vision Benchmarks for Label Errors
summary: Hard or Mislabeled? Failure Screens Enrich Vision Benchmarks for Label Errors 28 pages, 5 figures, 16 tables Hard vision benchmarks often keep images that strong classifiers get wrong. Since a classifier is also marked wrong when the label is wrong, such failure screens may collect label errors. We measure this on ImageNet's twice-relabeled validation set with 103 classifiers. Among the 1,892 images that all 66 supervised classifiers get wrong, 61% have a wrong label, versus 11.1% overall. The fewer images a screen lets through, the more of them are mislabeled, along approximately one curve. Fit on one model family, this curve predicts the screens of two held-out model families with a mean error of 2.4 percentage points, and replays of ImageNet-D's and ImageNet-Hard's screens within 0.1 and 6.3 points. On new pools, ImageNet-V2 and CIFAR-10, enrichment at the strictest screens is stronger than the curve predicts: on ImageNet-V2, by human relabeling, 67% of the images that all 66 classifiers get wrong are mislabeled, against 46% predicted. Screens that let models choose among only some of the classes, as ImageNet-A's does (200 of 1,000), fall below the curve. By ReImageNet, 32% of ImageNet-Hard's ImageNet images have no correct label. ScreenAudit, which comprises an audit tool, a script that rebuilds corrected answer sets for the 5,464 decided ImageNet-Hard images (of 5,646) from ReImageNet's gated release, and per-image audits of 1,198 benchmark images, will be released later.

title: Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming for Prediction and Classification of Target Variables in Structured Datasets
summary: Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming for Prediction and Classification of Target Variables in Structured Datasets Weight-space programming fixes every parameter of a feed-forward network by hand, with no gradient descent anywhere in the construction. Every demonstration so far starts from a target function handed to the model as a rule system, making it a compilation problem. A supervised dataset withholds that specification, so the procedure must do the statistical inference itself and then express the result in the parameterisation it was given. We ask whether a large language model can do both. It is shown a small dataset in full, with the architecture of a feed-forward network, and writes out every weight and bias as a literal number, with no optimizer, no gradient, no code execution, and no chance to evaluate it first. Each construction is sealed and pre-registers its expected score. The graded suite runs from two toy problems, through nine synthetic problems disguised by a hidden rotation, to the classical benchmarks and one real engineering regression. The frozen network matches the closed-form optimum wherever that optimum is linear, reaches the irreducible error of the generating process on three rungs where it is not, and beats every fitted baseline on two of those, including the same architecture trained by gradient descent. It fails on two rungs, both times because the structure to be found is oblique to the coordinates it analysed. Three further constructors separate two failure modes a single score conflates: one returns no parameter vector at all on the hardest rungs, another delivers everywhere while writing networks worse than predicting the mean. One of those failures proves avoidable: another constructor solves the oblique-hinge rung by a margin that survives multiple-comparison correction. What predicts whether the hidden layer earns its keep is the training error of a linear separator, which the composite complexity index misses.

title: Staged Semantic Distillation: Preserving Free-Form Semantics in a Low-Compute Non-LLM Surrogate of a Staged LLM Agent
comment: Main text 7 pages; 18 pages total; 3 figures, 16 tables
summary: Staged Semantic Distillation: Preserving Free-Form Semantics in a Low-Compute Non-LLM Surrogate of a Staged LLM Agent Main text 7 pages; 18 pages total; 3 figures, 16 tables Staged LLM agents make market and social simulators realistic, but one 102-day run of a 200-agent, ten-index market simulator issues 203,100 language-model calls and returns one realization. Conventional low-compute distillation drops their free-form intermediate state. We present staged semantic distillation, a low-compute method that preserves non-structured semantics in a non-LLM student trained from one recorded trace. A frozen encoder maps each teacher output to a 1024-d vector; the student sees typed stage-tagged vectors with stage-specific visibility, is jointly supervised, and trains with scheduled self-history. One TwinMarket trace yields a 13.2M-parameter deterministic student that trains in 1,658 seconds on one 8-GB GPU and runs with zero teacher or decoder calls and no text generation (0.14 ms per decision). Its analysis stays close to the teacher (cosine 0.943), and swapping semantic inputs between agents moves 64.7% of decisions against 12.8% for a matched donor, so the channel is preserved and live. We use the surrogate to study what the transfer carries. It reaches 0.8347 balanced accuracy on the teacher-forced replay and 0.7783 [0.766,0.791] on the deployment decoder; the five-seed gain over a no-semantic retrain is +2.2 [1.21,3.14]. Against the teacher's own re-sampling level, round-one R is 97.1% [95.8,98.4] and 92.3% [89.0,95.4]; R is a diagnostic, not an accuracy. A five-seed content-by-schedule study isolates the gain: scheduled self-history carries it (+2.2 [1.21,3.14]); shuffled and constant content controls reproduce it, while content matters teacher-forced. The design rule: invest in the deployment schedule, let content earn its place at the teacher-forced operating point. A 20-seed, 200,000-decision sweep takes 12 minutes with zero LLM calls, versus three hours for the teacher. The paper is a method-and-case-study contribution on one simulator and trace.

title: Macro Control and Capability Evaluation of Black-Box World Models: A Two-Regime Framework for LLM-Agent Markets
summary: Macro Control and Capability Evaluation of Black-Box World Models: A Two-Regime Framework for LLM-Agent Markets 19 pages; 6 figures, 17 tables Large language model (LLM) agents can be organized into multi-agent markets that act as world models, mapping macro information to emergent macro dynamics while the evaluator observes only macro inputs and outputs. This paper separates a model's capability into two stages that a single aggregate score cannot separate: information simulation, from macro information to micro behavior, and macro emergence, from micro behavior to the macro outcome. We introduce a soft macro-control method that announces a public reference path day by day without touching individual decisions, orders, or matching, and a two-regime evaluation framework that measures both stages from macro observations alone. In the reference-only regime the symmetric true and flipped references share a common level R, which measures realization under the announced reference, while their paired gap B measures structural bias; in the information-injection regime external information dilutes the reference, so only the true-flipped gap Delta remains interpretable. On five single-index LLM-agent markets, announcing a target path shifts the realized path toward the announced target on both announced references under both information conditions. Relative to the no-reference path, the tracking score is higher by 0.306 and 0.415 without news and by 0.183 and 0.329 with news; within the stock/cash scan structural bias is lowest at 70/30 (B=0.042); realization peaks at a 3:7 technical share (R=0.894 versus 0.358 for technical-only); and Delta is 0.0341 with fundamental data and 0.0487 with news. Both stages use the same two observable scores, each read in the regime where it is interpretable.

title: Hardening Agentic Web Populations Through Multi-Criterion Competitive Co-Evolution: Lessons from Wargame Strategy Optimization
comment: Accepted at the 1st NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Agentic Web: Decentralized, Continually-Adapting Agent Ecosystems ( this https URL )
summary: Hardening Agentic Web Populations Through Multi-Criterion Competitive Co-Evolution: Lessons from Wargame Strategy Optimization Accepted at the 1st NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Agentic Web: Decentralized, Continually-Adapting Agent Ecosystems ( ) Agents on the open web will face adversaries that keep adapting, so a defense that is only tested once will eventually be found and broken. We propose treating jailbreak attacks and safety guardrails as two populations that evolve against each other, rather than as a fixed attacker probing a fixed defense. This idea comes directly from wargame strategy optimization, where two-population competitive co-evolution with alternating evolution cycles and cross-play evaluation has already been shown to produce strategies that are robust to a moving opponent, and where a companion line of work has shown that the same machinery can measure how much competitive pressure a population must absorb. However, real-world applications can never rely on a single criterion as a key performance indicator, rather must use multiple conflicting criteria, such as, cost and efficiency. We describe how this mechanism transfers to language model safety, argue why the resulting multi-criteria, competitive and coevolutionary arms race is a genuinely networked, population-level problem rather than a two-agent toy setting, and lay out the open problems that stand between the wargame version of this idea and an agentic web version of it.

title: The Data Debt of Stockouts: Partial Identification and Minimax-Regret Inventory Control
summary: The Data Debt of Stockouts: Partial Identification and Minimax-Regret Inventory Control Problem definition: Inventory decisions select which demand enters sales logs. Unrecorded forecasts can leave demand frequencies unidentified even when stocking levels are recorded. We study which multistage ordering decisions these logs can justify and what finite samples can guarantee. Methodology/results: Nested stockout thresholds yield exact sets of compatible demand laws and finite representations for policy evaluation. We choose one deterministic inventory rule to minimize its largest expected cost gap from the informed optimum under the same law. This population value is data debt for the specified information and policy class. Under independent demand, carryover can create positive debt despite common optimal actions in every isolated period. Finite samples add learning error above debt. The required sample count grows linearly with the selection bound, with upper and lower orders matching up to logarithmic factors. This rate requires fixed demand and cost bounds, sufficient revelation, and a uniformly positive probability of clearing all feasible stock across the confidence sets. Controlled and semi-synthetic studies separate policy improvements from tighter guarantees. Managerial implications: More records can tighten guarantees while debt persists. Deeper revelation can establish common optimality without fully identifying demand. Using these guarantees requires validated logging, a credible selection range, and a regret tolerance in cost units. Information acquisition must distinguish tighter assurance from operating savings.

title: NI-ACT: A Neural Intent Interface for Brain-Embodied Manipulation
summary: NI-ACT: A Neural Intent Interface for Brain-Embodied Manipulation Intracortical brain-computer interfaces can drive robotic arms, but they keep the user inside the fast sensorimotor loop: every approach, correction, and grasp must be neurally specified. Whether intracortical population activity can instead serve as a task-level condition for a learned embodied policy, without symbolic commands or hand-designed skill libraries, remains unknown. NI-ACT addresses this question with a hierarchical brain-embodied framework: a brief motor-cortical signal is read once as a persistent intent, and a visuomotor policy then closes the perception-action loop from vision and proprioception. In a counterfactual grasping task where the scene cannot specify the target, the neural intent alone determined which object the robot grasped; replacing the intent changed the behavior accordingly. Passing the full population latent as a dedicated intent token, rather than a one-hot decoded direction, raised grasp completion from 69% to 81% over 132 held-out scenes, whereas a continuous direction alone did not improve on a one-hot label. Where the signal was read also mattered: in one dual-array session, with the readout window matched, premotor (PMd) intent completed more grasps than primary motor (M1) intent (77% vs. 53%), and the conventional post-cue M1 readout reached 42%. Preparatory activity was itself sufficient: in a center-out task, intent read only from PMd before the go cue (that is, before any movement) drove complete grasps, and in one recording it completed more grasps than the same animal's post-cue readout. These results show that how a neural signal is represented, and where and when it is read, jointly determine how effectively it conveys movement goals to an embodied agent.

title: From Mutation to Medication: Characterizing Failures of Clinical LLMs to Respect Genomic Resistance
comment: Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the Machine Learning for Health (ML4H) 2026 Symposium
summary: From Mutation to Medication: Characterizing Failures of Clinical LLMs to Respect Genomic Resistance Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the Machine Learning for Health (ML4H) 2026 Symposium Language models are increasingly proposed to support molecular tumour boards, but may recommend cancer therapies despite genomic evidence of resistance. We evaluated ten models on 1,464 resistance cases from five curated oncology knowledge bases, collecting 58,910 judgments. Models endorsed resisted therapies in 21.8-81.4% of cases. However, raw rates can reflect a tendency to agree rather than an ability to distinguish resistance from drug sensitivity: one open-weight model endorsed 81.4% of resistance cases and 82.3% of sensitivity controls. We therefore compared endorsement within matched gene and evidence-level groups. This analysis is exploratory because it was specified after the pre-registered analysis, which yielded null-to-weak results. Measured failures depended strongly on the reference knowledge base and evidence strength. When a second source independently confirmed resistance, four models across three vendors endorsed at most 2.4% of cases; at weaker evidence tiers, discrimination was not measurable. Models sometimes acknowledged resistance yet recommended the therapy. Repeating a model's own resistance conclusion reduced endorsement to 0.0-3.5% on cases where it had stated resistance. Falsely attributing the opposite conclusion increased endorsement above baseline for all seven hosted models, reaching 95.2% for GPT-4o; an instruction without an attributed conclusion changed endorsement by only 0.9 percentage points. Providing the correct curated evidence reduced unqualified strong recommendations to 0.3-3.5%, testing evidence use under an oracle condition rather than retrieval.

title: Information Limits of Replay-Free Recurrent State Migration
summary: Information Limits of Replay-Free Recurrent State Migration When a recurrent model is replaced, its old state may not determine what the new model would compute from the same history. We characterize the information that must be retained before the replacement is known. For a time-invariant affine linear family, the minimum continuous causal memory for order-$k$ local migration equals the reachable dimension of a lifted coefficient system minus the information in the anchor state. A controllable $d$-state model with scalar input needs at most $kd$ additional real coordinates, even when arbitrary matrix replacement directions are revealed only after streaming. A single rank-one direction can already require all $kd$. Conditional singular values and auxiliary-bit bounds distinguish this local information law from recovery at a fixed tolerance. We also give invariant-subspace and future-output constructions. Controlled experiments compare the resulting representations. In a small language model, equal-memory cubic interpolation improves mean state fidelity over third-order coefficients but provides no meaningful predictive gain. An analytic history basis preserves useful adaptation more economically in a coupled identification task. With repeated slow poles, eight history coordinates meet normalized output error $10^{-4}$ across five fitted seeds despite substantial full-state error. Splitting the poles raises the smallest tested successful width to 64.

title: Attention U-Net Cellular Automata for Multi-Class Land Use and Land Cover Change Simulation in Lucknow, India: Evaluation Against Null and Classical Baselines
summary: Attention U-Net Cellular Automata for Multi-Class Land Use and Land Cover Change Simulation in Lucknow, India: Evaluation Against Null and Classical Baselines 10 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables Convolutional networks are often used to learn the transition rules of land-use cellular automata (CA), yet their predictions are seldom compared with a null model that predicts no change. We built AttentionUNet-CA, which reads a 32 x 32 neighbourhood of land-cover states with four drivers (elevation, distance to major roads, distance to the central business district (CBD) and population density) and predicts the state of each cell ten years later. We tested it on Lucknow, India, with GLC_FCS30D land cover for 1990, 2000, 2010 and 2020, a 30 m series mapped consistently over time, and compared its built-up class with GHSL and ESA WorldCover. AttentionUNet-CA was trained on 1990-2010, selected on held-out spatial blocks and evaluated once on 2010-2020, with three seeds. Baselines were the null model, a random-forest CA (RF-CA) and a U-Net CA without attention; each network was trained with and without class weights. Only 8.1% of the study area changed in the test decade, so no model matched the overall agreement of the null model (91.9%). On change, measured by the figure of merit, the class-weighted networks scored highest (U-Net CA 22.0 +/- 1.2%, AttentionUNet-CA 21.0 +/- 1.4%), ahead of RF-CA (20.3%), but by margins comparable to seed-to-seed variation; the networks estimated the amount of change better than RF-CA. The attention gates did not improve accuracy. Population density and distance to the CBD were the most useful drivers. Projected to 2030, built-up land grows by 22-35%, mostly at the city edge.

title: One Run Is Not Enough: Reminding a small Gemma 4 coding agent of its last finding made no measurable difference in a paired test
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures. Code, data and the commit history of the pre-registration: this https URL
summary: One Run Is Not Enough: Reminding a small Gemma 4 coding agent of its last finding made no measurable difference in a paired test 10 pages, 2 figures. Code, data and the commit history of the pre-registration: When a coding agent runs out of room, its earlier findings are cut and it forgets them. We tested a simple fix: automatically putting the agent's last finding back in front of it. We fixed the rules in advance and ran 98 paired coding tasks with and without this reminder, using Gemma 4 31B (QAT, 4-bit) in the Gemma 4 Developer Agent harness. The reminder made no measurable difference: across all 98 tasks, 47 were solved with it and 48 without (-1.0 points, 95% interval [-8.3, +6.3], exact McNemar p=1.0). The primary outcome (a documented deviation from our preregistration), the first 48 pairs, was 29/48 with memory against 25/48 without (+8.3 points, [-2.1, +18.3], p=0.22); the extension of 50 tasks, decided after that result, pointed the other way (18/50 against 23/50, -10.0 points, p=0.125), so the sign did not replicate. With 19% of tasks flipping between two identical no-memory runs, the combined interval excludes harms larger than about 8 points and gains larger than about 6, and the design had 80% power only for effects of about +-12 points or more. The model almost never wrote notes (2 of 16 and 4 of 32 runs), and memory cost context: the first request is larger and something was injected at only 47% to 65% of compactions. The registered secondary, repeated actions per compaction, was also null. Two directional hypotheses found on Modal did not replicate on Kaggle. We also report an A/A calibration and a validity funnel (129 tasks, 105 valid). Together these results show that single-run memory claims on task sets of this size sit inside run-to-run noise. The treatment is a harness mechanism and does not test agent-written memory.

title: Does a completed simulation run mean a usable urban wind result for AI agents?
summary: Does a completed simulation run mean a usable urban wind result for AI agents? AI agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now configure and run computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solvers, but a completed run does not ensure that delivered metrics can be recomputed from raw outputs. This gap was examined for urban wind simulation, where multi-case comparisons must hold non-target conditions fixed and reported values must be traceable to raw samples. UrbanWind-AgentBench, comprising 200 tasks and 367 cases in 10 engineering task families, was constructed. Public task contracts specify variable factors, fixed conditions, numerical thresholds and deliverable requirements, and two-layer scoring separates a structural score for deliverables, run provenance and raw evidence from a numerical score obtained by independent recomputation against references. WindPilot was then proposed as an execution framework that incorporates contract parsing, execution provenance, deterministic verification and bounded acceptance review into the LLM execution loop. On 30 OpenFOAM tasks with independent references, at least the structural maximum of 60 points was reached by a base agent on 28 tasks, but numerical credit was obtained on only 6. With the same model name and budget, WindPilot increased the number of tasks with numerical credit to 17, full-score tasks from 0 to 3 and the mean task score from 62.5 to 72.5. Mean action steps fell from 130.4 to 104.9, and mean token consumption decreased by 12.9%. The mean gain for atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) tasks was 18.5 points. A completed simulation run is therefore not sufficient for a usable urban wind result; usability depends on checks that tie reported metrics to raw evidence during execution.

title: SARGO: Agreement-Gated Reinforcement and Suppression via On-Policy Self-Guidance for Visual Hallucination Mitigation
summary: SARGO: Agreement-Gated Reinforcement and Suppression via On-Policy Self-Guidance for Visual Hallucination Mitigation Vision-language models remain susceptible to visual hallucinations, often mixing grounded information with unsupported claims in the same response. Response-level reinforcement learning assigns a shared advantage to all tokens in a response, causing negative updates to suppress correct information alongside unsupported claims. To reduce hallucination while preserving useful visual information, we introduce SARGO (Self-guided Advantage-Routed Grounding Optimization), a post-training framework for selective reinforcement and suppression through on-policy self-guidance. Direct and reciprocal weighting gives better-supported tokens stronger reinforcement on positive updates and weaker penalties on negative updates. Agreement between overall and hallucination-specific advantages selects when to apply this guidance. At the response level, a reference-calibrated reward couples factuality with the retention and expansion of grounded information, discouraging lower hallucination scores obtained through omission. Experiments on Qwen3-VL-4B, Qwen3-VL-8B, and Gemma3-4B demonstrate that SARGO outperforms the evaluated mitigation baselines across Obj-Hal, AMBER, THRONE, and SHR evaluations. SARGO achieves these gains while preserving useful visual information and general multimodal capabilities.

title: Screen Before You Add: Reducing Candidate Inference in Model Ensembles
summary: Screen Before You Add: Reducing Candidate Inference in Model Ensembles 42 pages, 4 figures, 10 tables, including appendices As new models become available, existing ensembles must be updated to be competitive, making them intrinsically dynamic. Deciding whether to add a candidate model can require inference on an entire annotated dataset. Such a screening becomes prohibitive for models with costly inference especially when they ultimately add no value. Even under simple convex aggregation, relying on benchmark scores can be misleading as strong standalone performance does not guarantee ensemble improvement, and fitted ensemble weights can hurt test performance. In this work, we study candidate screening and show how early rejection can be achieved safely, exploiting residual geometry for stratification and rejecting the candidate when the best possible remaining predictions cannot achieve the necessary improvement. The key result that justifies this approach is that, under convex aggregation and squared or Brier loss, the population optimum improves if and only if a candidate induces a prediction change positively aligned with the residuals of the population-optimal existing ensemble. An optimistic quadratic program (QP) provides certified early rejection, while posterior-scenario sampling offers an alternative heuristic. We evaluate the approach by showing the tradeoff between saved calls and screening accuracy, which refers to recovering the same accept/reject result as for the entire annotated dataset. We assess empirically whether full-dataset decisions predict candidate usefulness on a held-out test set. On two LLM panels, stratified screening with certified QP rejection saves 21-23% of candidate calls while keeping 100% screening accuracy. In our experiments, sampling posterior scenarios further increases call savings to approximately 37%, with a loss of less than one percentage point in screening accuracy.

title: Rethinking Offline On-Policy Distillation: From Scalar Advantages to Distributional Supervision
summary: Rethinking Offline On-Policy Distillation: From Scalar Advantages to Distributional Supervision On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher capabilities through token-level feedback on student-generated trajectories, but repeatedly evaluating fresh rollouts with the teacher is computationally expensive. Offline methods such as Lightning OPD reduce this cost by caching recorded tokens' teacher log-probabilities on fixed reference rollouts. By extending the idea to a multi-turn agentic search setup, we find that it consistently underperforms the SFT starting point trained by the same teacher. We empirically observe greater teacher--reference mismatch than in mathematical reasoning and post-training distributional flattening, and theoretically show that scalar advantage supervision on fixed rollouts admits solutions with flattened output distributions under suitable conditions. Motivated by these findings, we propose Distributional On-Policy Distillation (DistOPD), a simple yet effective offline OPD method that retains candidate-token probabilities from both reference and teacher at selected positions and aggregates the remaining parts into a residual token. On agentic search, DistOPD achieves performance comparable to online OPD while improving student--teacher alignment and using training GPU-hours comparable to Lightning OPD.

title: Algebraic Interaction: A Recipe for Neural Architecture Generation
summary: Algebraic Interaction: A Recipe for Neural Architecture Generation We introduce an algebraic foundation for neural architecture design in which convolution, attention, state-space models, and equivariant layers are expressed through compositions of bilinear product operators over two structures: a position algebra governing positional routing and a feature algebra governing feature interactions. This decomposition makes routing, feature algebra, and operator composition explicit design focus on the feature-algebra axis through an Algebraic Recipe: fix the routing and operator composition of an existing architecture while replacing its feature algebra. This preserves the information-flow structure while allowing computational and symmetry properties to be modified through algebraic instantiate the recipe in linear attention, Mamba, and equivariant networks. Structure-constant and Clifford algebras improve accuracy at comparable parameter count in linear attention; structure-constant algebras yield up to $3\times$ faster training and inference in Vision Mamba at competitive accuracy; and an $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-representation algebra provides rotational equivariance by construction. These results demonstrate that feature algebra alone can control accuracy, efficiency, and symmetry without redesigning positional turns algebraic structure into an explicit design variable and reduces architecture design, within our framework, to algebraic specification.

title: MeltKV: Memory-Aligned KV Cache Compression via Variable-Bit Packed Vector Quantization for Long-Context LLMs
comment: 9 pages, 10 figures, 5 tables. To appear in the IEEE/ACM International Conference on Computer-Aided Design (ICCAD 2026)
summary: MeltKV: Memory-Aligned KV Cache Compression via Variable-Bit Packed Vector Quantization for Long-Context LLMs 9 pages, 10 figures, 5 tables. To appear in the IEEE/ACM International Conference on Computer-Aided Design (ICCAD 2026) Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on long contexts, making Key-Value (KV) caches dominate memory usage and inference latency. Existing vector quantization (VQ) methods effectively compress KV caches to sub-4-bit levels but often overlook inefficiencies in memory alignment and decoding speed. This work introduces MeltKV, a memory-latency co-optimized KV cache quantization framework for long-context LLM serving. MeltKV employs a memory-aligned variable-bit index packing scheme that adaptively assigns bit-widths to grouped key channels and compactly stores indices within standard data-types, eliminating redundant bits. Additionally, head-wise codebook sharing reduces the total codebook size while maintaining accuracy. Experiments demonstrate that MeltKV effectively compresses KV representations to sub-4-bit levels down to 1 bit and, at comparable perplexity, achieves 48.1% lower memory usage and 52.9% lower latency than state-of-the-art VQ methods.

title: Earth World Model: Physics-constrained latent dynamics for forecasting and environmental scenario analysis
comment: 20 pages, 5 figures, 11 tables; includes Supplementary Information
summary: Earth World Model: Physics-constrained latent dynamics for forecasting and environmental scenario analysis 20 pages, 5 figures, 11 tables; includes Supplementary Information World models have been widely applied to multi-agent planning and forecasting, but exogenous environmental changes are rarely incorporated as replaceable drivers in a unified state-evolution process. This limits assessment of whether environmental perturbations propagate through physical systems with faithful dynamics. We propose the Earth World Model (EWM), an Earth-centred forecasting framework that compresses heterogeneous multi-source observations into a reusable low-dimensional latent state representing the system's history and current condition. Given explicit exogenous drivers, a shared transition operator recursively updates the latent state, and physics-constrained decoding produces multi-step forecasts. Replacing the drivers enables environmental scenario analysis and evaluation of dynamic-response fidelity. We evaluated EWM for power forecasting and environmental-perturbation response at six photovoltaic sites and one wind-power site. Across four photovoltaic sites and three forecast horizons, three independent training runs yielded mean $R^2$ values of 0.8578-0.9095. In a separate six-site decoder ablation, the mean net per-unit response $\rho$ under the prescribed irradiance intervention increased from 0.180 with a multilayer perceptron decoder to 0.922 with an analytic physical decoder, close to site- and horizon-specific analytic references. The wind model achieved an injection elasticity of $0.9990 \pm 0.0006$, while pre-intervention outputs remained unchanged. These results show that forecast fit and intervention response should be evaluated separately and that the tested EWM configurations preserved response amplitude and temporal boundaries under the prescribed interventions.

title: Beveridge: Open Weight System One Decision Models with Calibrated Probabilities
comment: 23 pages, 11 figures, 8 tables. Models: this https URL , this https URL , this https URL . Code: this https URL
summary: Beveridge: Open Weight System One Decision Models with Calibrated Probabilities 23 pages, 11 figures, 8 tables. Models: , , . Code: Many production systems need a model to make a narrow decision about a document (route a ticket, check a limit, refuse a request, pick the next step of a browser agent) rather than to write text about it. We present Beveridge, a family of open weight System One decision models that take a document and up to 15 typed questions (yes/no, choice among described options, or a level on an ordered scale) and return, in one forward pass without generating text, an answer with a calibrated probability for every option. Beveridge-Large-C (398M parameters) adds a 3.5M parameter decision network to ModernBERT-large: typed number and date features in the input, exact facts from a rule engine, question-to-document evidence attention, a three-step recursive core with learned halting and an exact yes/no path. Beveridge-Pro-C adapts Gemma 4 26B-A4B with LoRA to score option letters, and Beveridge-Pro-C-Web extends it to the next step of a browser agent. On held-out tests the 0.4B model reaches 93.0% on our operations-document benchmark against 91.1% for the best of five general LLMs (31B-675B) and 87.9% for a commercial System One API, and, because its confidences are calibrated (ECE 0.029 on that benchmark), it can hand over 76% of decisions automatically at 95% accuracy, where no general LLM we tested can hand over any. It answers in 4.9 ms per decision on one NVIDIA H200 GPU and 60 ms on the 14 core CPU of an Apple M4 Pro laptop. Beveridge-Pro-C-Web raises next-step accuracy on web pages from unseen site types from 49.4% to 98.2% and completes live browsing tasks without losing document accuracy. We describe the models, the training recipes and an evaluation on 19 held-out test sets against a commercial System One API and five general LLMs, including where the models are weak. Weights and inference code are released under Apache 2.0.

title: ECOD: Experience-Calibrated On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Turn Agents
summary: ECOD: Experience-Calibrated On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Turn Agents Sparse and delayed rewards make reinforcement learning challenging for long-horizon language agents. On-policy distillation (OPD) complements environmental rewards with dense teacher feedback on student-generated contexts. Standard OPD can misalign supervision with relative teacher competence, student trajectory outcomes, and the temporal structure of task execution. Recent variants adjust guidance through divergence-based weighting and temporal schedules, while joint calibration from task-completion experience remains underexplored. We introduce Experience-Calibrated On-Policy Distillation (ECOD), which allocates teacher supervision at the task, trajectory, and turn levels. ECOD compares teacher and student success-rate posteriors under matched task conditions, restricts direct supervision to failed student trajectories, and derives a temporal prior from successful teacher lengths. The resulting weight applies to teacher losses or teacher-derived advantages. We evaluate ECOD on ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Under matched teacher settings, ECOD improves standard OPD by up to 4.06% in relative ALFWorld unseen success. Across both model scales, ECOD-assisted SOD, TCOD-F2B, and ATOD configurations yield average paired relative gains of 6.20% on ALFWorld unseen and 7.05% on WebShop, with WebShop gains ranging from 2.29% to 21.60%. These results support experience-calibrated supervision allocation as a reusable mechanism across distinct distillation objectives.

title: SART: Sign-Absolute Reformulation Theory for Binary Variable Reduction in Neural Network Verification
summary: SART: Sign-Absolute Reformulation Theory for Binary Variable Reduction in Neural Network Verification OOPSLA 2026 Complete formal verification of neural networks is crucial for their deployment in safety-critical domains. A key bottleneck stems from encoding complexity: traditional methods assign one binary variable per unstable ReLU neuron. We propose the Sign-Absolute Reformulation Theory (SART), which fundamentally breaks the conventional one-to-one mapping between unstable neurons and binary variables by establishing formal reducibility criteria. This allows for finer-grained modeling, where each unstable neuron corresponds on average to fewer than one binary variable, thereby reducing verification complexity at its source. Based on SART, we derive a theoretical lower bound on the number of binary variables required for complete verification and, under the assumption that $P \neq NP$, prove that variables in the final layer can be compressed by 50\%, while the number of variables in intermediate layers cannot be further reduced. To overcome the apparent ``last-layer-only'' limitation, we recast verification as a sequential process and, crucially, show that the gain lifts to the entire network: LayerABS, a SART-based progressive tightening verifier, iteratively treats intermediate layers as temporary final layers and propagates tight bounds that shrink the global search space and binary-variable counts. Furthermore, we reveal a structural law influencing verification complexity: when the signs of weights of unstable neurons satisfy numerical symmetry, with positive and negative weights equal or differing by at most one, the worst-case verification complexity achieves the theoretical optimum, offering theoretical guidance for the design of verification-friendly architectures. As a general-purpose underlying encoding, the value of SART is independent of specific algorithms.

title: Rethinking the Verification of Machine Unlearning
summary: Rethinking the Verification of Machine Unlearning Machine unlearning claims require evidence that a model has removed the influence of specified training data. Yet widely deployable post hoc verifiers. infer unlearning largely from predictive behavior, the final model response that remains under the provider's control. We make this limitation concrete through Output-Level Deceptive Response (ODR), an attack that produces responses accepted by output based verifiers while preserving the original representation state. By separating output conformity from internal unlearning, ODR motivates a rethinking of machine unlearning verification, shifting the audit target from what the model returns to what changes inside it. We operationalize this shift through Representation Unlearning Verification (RUV), a gray box verifier that compares intermediate forward representations in the original and unlearned models. RUV traces a four-stage response through activation reorganization, representation displacement, neighborhood disruption, and loss of manifold support. Matched retained controls distinguish target specific responses from global model drift, while joint permutation calibration combines the four evidence views into an adaptive decision. Experiments spanning exact and approximate unlearning, class and sample level requests, multiple datasets, and diverse architectures show mean ODR deception success rates of $97.0\%$ and $97.7\%$, respectively. RUV achieves mean verification accuracies of $98.9\%$ and $94.9\%$, while rejecting $99.5\%$ and $99.8\%$ of the corresponding ODR submissions.

title: Stagewise Adaptive Boosting
summary: Stagewise Adaptive Boosting Stagewise algorithms and sparsity-inducing regularization are two influential approaches to high-dimensional modeling. Existing stagewise theory, however, largely centers on convex regularization, whereas stronger sparsity and other structural preferences are often pursued through fixed-level nonconvex optimization rather than generating an entire adaptive solution path. We develop stagewise adaptive boosting, a general framework that builds a monotone path by selecting the update consistent with structural preference. The framework can encourage sparsity along the path itself and also admits extensions that promote other properties of the solution, including group selection, similarity across models for multiple outcomes, and known priorities or prerequisite relations among predictors. We study its theoretical property as well as finite sample performance using simulations and real-data analyses. Across these studies, the proposed pathwise approach often achieves predictive performance comparable to commonly used baselines while selecting substantially smaller models. These results suggest that adaptive stagewise learning provides a practical route to stronger sparsity and richer structural control without repeatedly solving separate weighted or nonconvex optimization problems.

title: Can a Vision-Language Model Tune Clustering In Context?
summary: Can a Vision-Language Model Tune Clustering In Context? Clustering is a widely used unsupervised learning method, but selecting an appropriate algorithm and set of hyperparameters for a specific dataset can require many possible configurations and evaluations. In this work, we investigate whether a Vision-Language Model can instead visually evaluate clustering results and use those decisions to then tune an explicit clustering algorithm. We study this through three progressive experiments using Qwen3.5-27B and five controlled synthetic clustering scenarios. First, we test whether the VLM can distinguish the best clustering result from a pair of plots. Second, we test whether it can assign numerical scores to those plots where a higher score represents a better result. Finally, we use these judgments within an agentic loop in which the VLM scores a k-means clustering and proposes updated hyperparameters that may result in better clustering. Our exploratory results show that the VLM performs well when clear cluster structure is present, while struggling on more ambiguous and noisy settings. In the full agentic experiment, the VLM produces clustering configurations with silhouette scores relatively close to those of grid search and Bayesian optimization, while terminating in much fewer iterations. Overall, these results provide an initial proof of concept that VLM-based visual feedback can be used to autonomously tune an explicit clustering algorithm.

title: Gradient-Guided Hardware-Native MIXFP4
summary: Gradient-Guided Hardware-Native MIXFP4 Blackwell tensor cores support native inference with 4-bit weights and activations (W4A4), but NVFP4 leaves a perplexity (PPL) gap to BF16. Choosing a format for each 16-element block can improve accuracy, but current matrix multiply instructions cannot execute choices this fine. Applying these rules at hardware-compatible tiles loses most of their benefit. We introduce FlipQuant, which selects E2M1 or E0M3 for each MMA weight tile. It keeps both quantized weight candidates fixed and learns a binary format map from end-to-end gradients of a bucketed KL loss to a BF16 teacher, re-evaluating them after each update. Native kernels execute 16 x 64 tiles on SM120 and 256 x 64 tiles on SM100 with median GEMM overheads of 1.9% and 1.7%, respectively. Across six language models and two corpora, FlipQuant at 16 x 64 closes 42.5% of NVFP4's PPL gap to BF16 on average, compared with 13.3% for FourOverSix. Code is available at .

title: SearchChord: Prompt Preselection and Field Recomposition for One-Step Image Editing
summary: SearchChord: Prompt Preselection and Field Recomposition for One-Step Image Editing 10 pages, 3 figures, conference Finding effective prompts and seeds for one-step image editors requires balancing edit fidelity, source preservation, and computational cost. To address this challenge, we explore a large collection of candidate edits, where each candidate is defined by a unique prompt-seed pair, and generate corresponding images on demand. We present SearchChord, a training-free framework that leverages a large pool of such candidates, combining text-based preselection, image verification, and latent-field recomposition. Our ablation studies across pool sizes up to 200 candidates show that a pool of 100 offers a cost-effective operating point. Compared with feeding all 100 candidates into recomposition, TextSim preselects a subset of 10 candidates. Rather than uniform averaging, we incorporate image-verifier scores to weight each candidate during recomposition. Experiments on PIE-Bench and the proposed CropWeed-EditBench reveal a trade-off: candidate selection improves target-text alignment, while recomposition better preserves unmodified source content. The oracle verifier achieves the best performance in both preservation and target-text alignment. Practical verification partially recovers semantic alignment, but recomposition still compromises edit fidelity, including in agricultural image edits. These results motivate text-first preselection and stronger verification to balance preservation, fidelity, and cost. Code and data will be made publicly available.

title: FDAM: A Frequency-Direction-Aware Multi-Task Framework for Pavement Crack Grid Localization
summary: FDAM: A Frequency-Direction-Aware Multi-Task Framework for Pavement Crack Grid Localization Pavement crack grid localization remains challenging for thin and tiny cracks due to weak visual cues and background interference. Box detection often misses these cracks, while supervised semantic segmentation faces limited pixel-wise annotations and high labeling costs. In this paper, we propose a Frequency-Direction-Aware Multi-Task framework (FDAM) with box detection and grid classification branches. The core grid classification branch comprises Frequency-Domain Enhancement (FDE) and Directional Feature Refinement (DFR). FDE adaptively weights spectral bands and fuses reconstructed features with spatial features. DFR captures thin crack patterns through multi-scale strip convolutions, direction-sensitive modulation, and feature recalibration. Sparse positive cells and ambiguous local predictions motivate adaptive grid supervision. Adaptive Importance Reweighting emphasizes uncertain predictions and local label transitions, with focal supervision for all cells. Our contribution is to couple the box detection and grid classification branches through shared feature learning for pavement crack grid localization. We validate FDAM on our RoadDistress2026 dataset of thin and tiny cracks and further evaluate it on public datasets Crack500 and DeepCrack. The code is available at

title: DEFDVO: Deformable Deep Visual Odometry for Equirectangular Images
summary: DEFDVO: Deformable Deep Visual Odometry for Equirectangular Images Accepted to WACV 2027 Omnidirectional ($360^\circ$) cameras capture the full surrounding scene in every frame, providing a strong advantage for visual odometry (VO) over pinhole sensors with a limited field of view. However, their equirectangular projection (ERP) introduces latitude-dependent distortion, an artificial seam at the image border, and a sampling bias toward the poles. Existing $360^\circ$ VO methods address these challenges only partially. DEFDVO closes this gap with a patch-based deep VO method that operates directly on ERP imagery, combining spherically initialized deformable feature extraction, end-to-end seam-aware estimation, and spherical-gradient patch selection. The deformable feature extractor combines spherical geometric priors with learned sampling offsets, while seam-aware processing preserves ERP continuity, and spherical-gradient selection reduces polar sampling bias. Trained exclusively on synthetic TartanAirV2 ERP imagery, DEFDVO improves the best prior average absolute trajectory error (ATE) by $4.8\times$ (0.201 m to 0.042 m) on the TartanAirV2 evaluation set defined by 360DVO and achieves the lowest average ATE on both splits of the real-world 360DVO benchmark. Code is available at

title: DecoEdit: Beyond Flat Control for 3D-Aware Unified Image Editing
summary: DecoEdit: Beyond Flat Control for 3D-Aware Unified Image Editing While recent advances in multimodal image editing have achieved impressive results, current frameworks remain largely confined to ``flat" 2D controls (e.g., text prompts, bounding boxes, or masks). Precise 3D-aware geometric manipulation -- such as coordinating an object's location, physical scale, and 3D orientation while strictly preserving its fine-grained identity -- remains an elusive challenge, typically suffering from severe detail degradation or requiring expensive per-instance fine-tuning. In this paper, we present DecoEdit, an all-in-one image editing framework that goes beyond flat control by seamlessly integrating 1D textual, 2D spatial, and 3D volumetric inputs under a unified architecture. First, to power this unified model, we establish a data curation pipeline and curate a large-scale dataset, namely DecoDataset, containing 1.6 million samples, encompassing diverse multi-dimensional (1D/2D/3D) tasks and their complex compositions. Furthermore, we establish a comprehensive image editing benchmark named DecoBench to systematically evaluate multi-task editing performance. Finally, to address the fundamental trade-off between complex spatial transformations and identity preservation, we propose a novel decoupled pipeline: DecoEdit factorizes the editing process by utilizing structural guidance from SAM-3D to anchor the target geometry, scale, and spatial orientation, while concurrently leveraging a detail-preservation path to lock in high-fidelity textures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DecoEdit achieves state-of-the-art results. Notably, on the challenging 3D spatial pose and orientation control tasks, DecoEdit significantly outperforms leading closed-source models such as Seedream 5.0 in both geometric accuracy and identity consistency.

title: Puzzle: One Pass Is Not Enough for Open-Vocabulary Remote Sensing Segmentation
summary: Puzzle: One Pass Is Not Enough for Open-Vocabulary Remote Sensing Segmentation Open-vocabulary remote sensing image segmentation (OVRSIS) enables the segmentation of unseen classes without additional annotation or retraining. By analyzing the predictions of existing OVRSIS methods, we find that many misclassified patches coexist with visually similar, correctly classified patches of the same class within the same image. Unfortunately, most of these methods stop after a single inference rather than using their predictions to guide further inference. Motivated by this observation, we propose \textbf{Puzzle}, a plug-and-play iterative re-inference framework that combines prediction history with a visual-similarity prior to progressively refine patch-level attention. Puzzle employs a lightweight history-conditioned controller to regulate each patch's contribution as an information source and its reliance on visually similar patches, while an adaptive stopping rule determines when to stop. It keeps the segmentation model frozen and reuses the same controller across different models and datasets without retraining. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent performance improvements across diverse OVRSIS models and datasets, highlighting the strong transferability of Puzzle. Moreover, Puzzle can further improve the performance of SOTA methods.

title: From zero-target transfer to target-site personalization: multi-source training across fall-detection models
summary: From zero-target transfer to target-site personalization: multi-source training across fall-detection models Video-based fall detection could support timely assistance when a person cannot call for help. Unfamiliar cameras and scarce local labels challenge deployment. We examine whether joint training improves cross-dataset detection and subsequent local training. We analyze 2,697 clips from eight OmniFall datasets and one AI-Hub dataset. Positive clips contain a fall or collapse transition, while negative clips do not. We hold out each dataset in turn, training on the other eight. We evaluate three vision-language models (VLMs), Qwen, LLaVA, and InternVL, and three visual baselines, CLIP-temporal, VideoMAE, and Pose-TCN. We evaluate the stored source model without target data for training or selection. For each label budget, we update a separate copy using labeled clips from the held-out target dataset. We call this target-site personalization. We compare the Source-initialized model with Target-only, which skips source training but uses identical target clips and updates. Across nine targets, source training raises mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) from frozen-model values of 0.821 to 0.912 for Qwen, 0.883 to 0.947 for LLaVA, and 0.939 to 0.962 for InternVL. With five target examples per class and 26 updates per run, 95% confidence intervals for the AUROC benefit over Target-only lie above zero for Qwen, CLIP-temporal, VideoMAE, and Pose-TCN. With full-target training, they lie above zero only for Qwen and LLaVA. Separate VLM analyses reveal threshold sensitivity and post-fall false detections. The benefit varies by model and label budget.

title: EviRef: Evidence-Specific Memories for Logical Anomaly Detection across Capture Conditions
summary: EviRef: Evidence-Specific Memories for Logical Anomaly Detection across Capture Conditions Logical anomalies arise when every component looks normal but their combination violates the scene rules. In practical inspection, these rules must hold under varying backgrounds, illumination, and imaging quality, with only a few dozen normal images per scene, whereas existing methods couple normality with appearance and merge different constraints into one reference. We model logical normality as decomposable constraints and propose EviRef, a training-free method that builds a separate reference memory for each family of evidence. Component prototypes built once per scene parse images under any capture condition into one label space, on which occupancy and relation constraints are verified. Semantic constraints are verified with whole-image embeddings independent of parsing, and additional evidence such as text is admitted through a task-level gate without modifying existing memories. On VID-AD, EviRef attains a mean image-level area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 92.1% (88.9% with visual evidence alone), the highest among the compared methods under each of five capture conditions, with a standard deviation of 0.5. Even with memories built from only 20 normal images per task, it surpasses all compared methods that use 50 normal images per task.

title: WA-JEPA: Goal-Aware Predictive Feedback Action Refinement for a World-Action Model
comment: 16 pages, 5 figures, including supplementary material. Code available at this https URL
summary: WA-JEPA: Goal-Aware Predictive Feedback Action Refinement for a World-Action Model 16 pages, 5 figures, including supplementary material. Code available at JEPA-based world models predict action consequences in latent space, but representative planning approaches rely on candidate-action search, requiring repeated evaluation of action sequences and incurring substantial online computational cost. Direct action generation avoids this search, yet how to leverage latent predictions to guide action generation given task goals remains a key challenge in translating learned physical dynamics into effective decisions. We introduce WA-JEPA, a world-action model that couples action generation, action-conditioned latent prediction, and goal-aware feedback. The model first generates an action proposal and predicts the resulting future scenes and proprioceptive states, then refines the proposal through two complementary feedback paths, using the task goal as a reference. Goal-discrepancy residual feedback (GDRF) uses differences between the latent representations of predicted scenes and the task goal to guide chunk-wise action refinement. Future-scene context feedback (FSCF) preserves fine-grained predicted scene representations to guide subsequent action refinement.
