Building on this signal, we develop PG-based Reasoning Optimization (PGRO) to optimize reasoning generation with sentence-level rewards, supported by a custom causal attention mechanism for efficient PG computation. Additionally, an auxiliary PG-based Reasoning Utilization (PGRU) task adaptively strengthens reasoning-conditioned prediction to complement PGRO. Extensive experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate that GainReason consistently outperforms competitive baselines and achieves substantial performance gains from reasoning.

title: Subprocess-Constrained Markov Decision Processes
comment: To appear at NeurIPS '26. Code available at this https URL
summary: Subprocess-Constrained Markov Decision Processes To appear at NeurIPS '26. Code available at Constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs) typically bound expected cumulative cost from an initial state. Such a guarantee can be insufficient when a policy must remain feasible after every history it may encounter. We introduce \emph{subprocess-constrained MDPs} (S-CMDPs), which require the expected discounted cost of each continuation, conditional on any reachable history, to satisfy a bound determined by the current state. This stronger requirement changes the structure and complexity of the problem: we show that stationary policies can be strictly suboptimal, and finding even an approximately optimal stationary policy is NP-hard. We adapt a recently introduced value-set iteration framework to show that history-dependent policies surprisingly overcome both obstacles. Our polynomial-time algorithm represents such a policy implicitly: its expected reward is within $\epsilon$ of the optimal feasible value, it violates each subprocess cost bound by at most $\delta$, and its action distribution can be computed in polynomial time for any given history.

title: Generative AI and the Crisis of Higher Education Assessments: Examining 'AI-Proofing' Strategies for College-Level Assessments
summary: Generative AI and the Crisis of Higher Education Assessments: Examining 'AI-Proofing' Strategies for College-Level Assessments Higher education is confronting an academic-integrity challenge unlike any in its history. Students can now outsource homework, take-home assignments, and online examinations to large language models (LLMs) that complete them in seconds. Existing research on evaluating LLM performance on academic assessments has focused largely on standardized examinations, or on questions from college-level courses drawn from a single discipline. Far less is known about how LLMs perform on college-level assessment questions spanning multiple disciplines, that instructors have purposely designed to be AI-resistant, and about which features of such questions, if any, meaningfully constrain LLM performance. We address this gap by collecting 75 questions from authentic college coursework assessments, spanning 17 disciplines, which were contributed by 37 faculty members from ten U.S. universities and one U.K. university. Of these, 61 questions were intentionally designed by faculty members to be 'LLM-proof', while the remaining 14 questions were sourced from online courses. We then (i) evaluate three state-of-the-art LLMs' ability to correctly answer these questions with and without supplementary course materials; (ii) identify five strategies, through thematic analysis, that faculty used to make their questions harder for LLMs to solve; and (iii) test whether these strategies impact LLMs' ability to answer the questions accurately. Our experimental results show that the best-performing model scored approximately 83% without supplementary course materials and 85% with them, and we observed noteworthy differences across models, answer formats, and instructor tweaking strategies. We discuss implications for assessment design, academic-integrity policy, and the broader ethics of deploying LLMs in educational settings.

title: Safe Resemblance, Silent Propagation: Limits of Text-Similarity Guardrails for AI Agent Safety
summary: Safe Resemblance, Silent Propagation: Limits of Text-Similarity Guardrails for AI Agent Safety When AI agents relay information to one another, an output can preserve an injected instruction's effect on downstream agents even after its wording changes, yet legitimate quotation and template reuse can produce high textual overlap with the source, so text-similarity guardrails that attempt to flag the former risk conflating these two cases. We test this distinction using DonkeyRail, a public classifier combining BLEU, ROUGE-L, and METEOR features, deployed in a controlled three-agent email relay, defining a behavioral measure in which an output counts as functional (the injected procedure induces fresh computations in two subsequent agents) independent of the detector's score, alongside legitimate controls that explicitly authorize quotation and reuse. At its default threshold the classifier misses 8 of 19 functional outputs while flagging 70 of 192 legitimate replies, with every completed quotation and template-reuse reply triggering a false alert; calibrating for low false positives on one template set does not transfer, as the recalibrated threshold detects only one functional output and still produces 15 false alerts on new templates. We also identify an operating-point error in all 21 published classifier configurations, where ROC interpolation replaces direct threshold application, and show formally that high AUC against a surface-level text criterion provides no distribution-free guarantee of high AUC against the behavioral target, while the existing evaluation labels lack the joint observations needed to estimate the gap. An authorization analysis further shows that identical visible transcripts can require different safety decisions depending on the governing policy, a distinction no observation-only classifier can resolve. These results argue for behavioral and policy-grounded evaluation over text-similarity guardrails.

title: Procedure without Judgment: What Small Language Models Learn under an Exact Verifier
summary: Procedure without Judgment: What Small Language Models Learn under an Exact Verifier 17 pages When an authorization policy blocks an agent's tool call, the audit log should name the facts that forced the decision and nothing more. For an executable policy over an enumerable context space this minimal sufficient reason can be computed exactly, so an explanation is scored against ground truth rather than a proxy for it. We use that exactness to ask what a model can learn from a verifier that has no error in it. The explainer sees one request and one decision, never the policy, and has thirty turns in which it may call the policy on altered requests and ask whether a candidate set of facts is sufficient. Frontier models find the exact reason about half the time with the tools alone, and one sentence telling them to shrink the answer lifts Haiku 4.5 from 58% to 75%. A 4B model fine-tuned on 2000 traces of the deletion algorithm reaches 92% on the policy it was trained on. Teacher kind is what moves this: at matched data size the algorithm-taught student leads the frontier-taught one in all three training seeds, and the two arms never overlap. What the student learns is a fixed schedule of sufficiency checks, and the schedule does not travel. On three public policies it never saw, its answers stay sufficient (94%) and stop being minimal (48%), while Haiku under the same sentence is exact on all 47 episodes. Reinforcement learning from the exact reward leaves held-out accuracy where it was and inverts the strategy, from probing the policy to spending the entire budget on sufficiency checks. The oracle made the effect of training legible, but it did not make training better.

title: SciResearch-Eval: Evaluating Scientific Judgment in Autonomous Experimental Agents
comment: 28 pages, 7 figures. Code and leaderboard: this https URL
summary: SciResearch-Eval: Evaluating Scientific Judgment in Autonomous Experimental Agents 28 pages, 7 figures. Code and leaderboard: We introduce SciResearch-Eval, an interactive benchmark of scientific judgment built on a standard laboratory problem: measuring a material's thermal properties by heating it and fitting a heat-conduction simulator. An agent designs its own experiments, uses a supplied simulator that may be under-resolved or physically wrong, and reports each property with a 95% interval. To our knowledge it is the first benchmark to combine agent-designed experiments, a deliberately flawed simulator, and proper scoring of calibrated intervals against exact ground truth. On a held-out split (93 tasks, 9 models, 2,511 episodes), models handle procedural traps. When the simulator is missing physics, most report wrong values while stating they are 95% sure: their ranges contain the truth in 20-62% of cases, against 94% for GPT-6 Astra and 99% for Claude Fable 5.2. At default effort the failing Claude 5.5 models rarely diagnose the missing physics (Opus in 35% of episodes, against 66% for Astra), and even when they do, their ranges often miss; Astra and Fable design experiments in which the flawed simulator is accurate, such as gentle heating, which keeps Astra calibrated even when it does not name the cause. Asking for wider intervals does not help; stating the strategy improves interval scores 1.6-2.5-fold, replicated on a pre-registered fresh split, but coverage barely moves. A pre-registered effort ablation shows that the correction is latent in the Claude 5.5 models: at maximum effort Opus improves more than tenfold and is no longer detectably behind Astra at default, but only with 13-31 times more reasoning; older and open-weight models gain nothing. Fable 5.2 is the most accurate model at default effort (interval score 1.9 times better than Astra's) but writes 6 times as many tokens, and at Astra's token count it falls short. We release the environment, graders and harness.

title: Right Reason, Wrong Advice: Evaluating Recourse in LLM Explanations of Denied Requests
summary: Right Reason, Wrong Advice: Evaluating Recourse in LLM Explanations of Denied Requests 21 pages Language models increasingly write the explanations people receive when a rule system denies their request. If several rules deny the request independently, an explanation can name a true reason and still leave the person denied after they fix it. We call the missing property recourse validity: changing what the explanation cites, without changing what was asked for, can flip the decision. We compute it exactly, and a hitting-set argument predicts from the policy alone when a correct reason fails. In six of seven rule systems ported from access control and US benefit eligibility, a single correct reason almost never gives recourse when several reasons apply. Across 20 LLMs, checks of whether the cited reasons are correct, computed or asked of an LLM judge, are close to chance at spotting this failure, as the argument predicts. A strong judge asked whether acting on the explanation would work does spot it. Stronger and reasoning models do better but still fail on many denials with four or more independent reasons. Asking for every rule helps every open model with room to improve. Explanations of eligibility decisions should be built from the decision function and judged by whether acting on them works.

title: An XAI Approach to Deep Learning Models in the Detection of DCIS
summary: An XAI Approach to Deep Learning Models in the Detection of DCIS 12 pages, 5 figures The results showed that XAI could indeed be used as a proof of concept to begin discussions on the implementation of assistive AI systems within the clinical community.

title: Fast Catch-Up, Late Switching: Optimal Batch Size Scheduling via Functional Scaling Laws
comment: 34 pages, accepted by ICLR 2026 as a conference paper
summary: Fast Catch-Up, Late Switching: Optimal Batch Size Scheduling via Functional Scaling Laws 34 pages, accepted by ICLR 2026 as a conference paper Batch size scheduling (BSS) plays a critical role in large-scale deep learning training, influencing both optimization dynamics and computational efficiency. Yet, its theoretical foundations remain poorly understood. In this work, we show that the functional scaling law (FSL) framework introduced in Li et al. (2025a) provides a principled lens for analyzing BSS. Specifically, we characterize the optimal BSS under a fixed data budget and show that its structure depends sharply on task difficulty. For easy tasks, optimal schedules keep increasing batch size throughout. In contrast, for hard tasks, the optimal schedule maintains small batch sizes for most of training and switches to large batches only in a late stage. To explain the emergence of late switching, we uncover a dynamical mechanism -- the fast catch-up effect -- which also manifests in large language model (LLM) pretraining. After switching from small to large batches, the loss rapidly aligns with the constant large-batch trajectory. Using FSL, we show that this effect stems from rapid forgetting of accumulated gradient noise, with the catch-up speed determined by task difficulty. Crucially, this effect implies that large batches can be safely deferred to late training without sacrificing performance, while substantially reducing data consumption. Finally, extensive LLM pretraining experiments -- covering both Dense and MoE architectures with up to 1.1B parameters and 1T tokens -- validate our theoretical predictions. Across all settings, late-switch schedules consistently outperform constant-batch and early-switch baselines.

title: ChartSync: A Benchmark for Visuo-Logical Cascading Chart Editing
summary: ChartSync: A Benchmark for Visuo-Logical Cascading Chart Editing Generative image editing models struggle with structured statistical charts when data modifications require geometric synchronization. We formalize this task as Visuo-Logical Cascading Editing (VLCE). However, existing methods remain confined to localized text substitutions and struggle with dependency-aware cascading updates. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce ChartSync, an expert-validated benchmark constructed via a programmatic rendering pipeline that guarantees deterministic visuo-logical coupling for the ground truth. ChartSync comprises 870 triplets across 9 chart categories and 4 task types, including 235 geometry-coupled VLCE instances that specifically test cascading text-to-geometry synchronization. We further evaluate these instances via a two-tier framework combining objective visual metrics with a vision-language model judge paradigm to assess low-level fidelity alongside multimodal comprehension and reasoning. Evaluating 14 image editing models and one code-mediated pipeline reveals a nuanced capability gap: most open-source models suffer severe drops in geometric synchronization, while only two frontier proprietary models show emerging VLCE capability, with their residual errors mainly involving semantic isolation and background corruption. Our detailed error analysis deconstructs these failure paradigms to identify core meta-abilities for guiding future multimodal architectures. The ChartSync dataset and code are publicly released at .

title: Multiaccuracy as an Error Benchmark for Learning with Distribution Shift
summary: Multiaccuracy as an Error Benchmark for Learning with Distribution Shift Agnostic learning has a well-developed theory of computational and statistical complexity. For learning with distribution shift, even the choice of an appropriate error benchmark remains challenging. Testable learning with distribution shift (TDS) was introduced to develop computational foundations for this setting: using labeled training data and unlabeled test data, the learner must either produce a predictor with low test error or detect distribution shift. However, standard agnostic TDS guarantees allow a constant-factor amplification of the optimum error even when the training and test distributions coincide. They therefore do not directly recover the guarantee of classical agnostic learning. We introduce shift multiaccuracy, a stronger error benchmark inspired by multiaccuracy from algorithmic fairness. This yields a TDS formulation that becomes equivalent to multiaccuracy when there is no shift. Using a recent nontrivial reduction from agnostic learning to multiaccurate prediction from prior work, we obtain the first TDS framework that formally generalizes agnostic learning through an efficient reduction preserving the training marginal. The framework retains existing algorithmic upper bounds and inherits computational lower bounds from agnostic learning. Moreover, we establish a direct connection between our model and identity testing, yielding the first statistical characterization of agnostic TDS learning, in terms of Rademacher complexity. More broadly, we argue that shift multiaccuracy might be of independent interest in unsupervised domain adaptation, as it leads to sharper out-of-distribution generalization guarantees, and can be minimized directly, since its definition does not involve the unobserved test labels.

title: Sample-Efficient Ensemble Reinforcement Learning at Scale
summary: Sample-Efficient Ensemble Reinforcement Learning at Scale 10 pages, 3 figures Ensemble methods such as MeanQ have been shown to improve the sample efficiency of relatively small model-free deep reinforcement learning (RL) architectures, including DQN and similarly sized variants such as Rainbow. However, to our knowledge, the effects of ensembling on large-scale architectures such as Bigger Better Faster (BBF) have not been studied. In this work, we present MeanQ-BBF, a hybrid model-free algorithm that combines the principles of MeanQ and BBF. Through statistically rigorous evaluation on the Atari 100K benchmark, we show that in contrast to naive scaling of the network size of BBF, which degrades performance, MeanQ-BBF is able to leverage the increase in model capacity to improve performance over BBF. Moreover, MeanQ-BBF does this in a computationally efficient way by organizing the added parameters into largely independent learners. Finally, we discuss the performance-cost tradeoff in the context of practical sample-efficient RL.

title: Exploration of Reinforcement Learning in Generative Recommendation Models
summary: Exploration of Reinforcement Learning in Generative Recommendation Models Traditional cascaded recommender systems balance accuracy and efficiency over large item spaces, but misaligned stage-wise objectives hinder end-to-end optimization. Generative recommendation unifies these stages in an autoregressive framework, providing a natural interface for reinforcement learning (RL) to optimize the entire generation process. However, directly applying RL often leads to unstable optimization and degraded recommendation quality. We revisit Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and other ratio-based objectives through a unified logit-gradient view. We identify three issues: (i) clipped surrogates create dead-gradient regions, under-utilizing samples; (ii) negative-advantage updates can become effectively unbounded as importance ratios grow, allowing a small subset of negatives to dominate optimization; and (iii) ratio-based control lacks sensitivity to absolute policy confidence, so updates on high-confidence cases may fail to vanish. Motivated by this diagnosis, we propose \emph{Gradient-Bounded Policy Optimization} (GBPO), a simple objective with stop-gradient normalization that is simultaneously (a) fully gradient-active, (b) sign-symmetrically bounded for both positive and negative updates, and (c) explicitly confidence-weighted under current policy probabilities. This ensures that updates gracefully vanish for $\pi\!\to\!1$ positives and $\pi\!\to\!0$ negatives. Across the evaluated settings, GBPO achieves competitive recommendation performance with more stable training than competing RL methods.

title: When Does an AUROC Comparison Survive a Change in Population Mix?
comment: 30 pages, 5 figures. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: When Does an AUROC Comparison Survive a Change in Population Mix? 30 pages, 5 figures. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible Does an AUROC comparison survive a change in the proportions of tasks, populations, or image corruptions? A pooled-AUROC ranking of failure detectors or uncertainty scores describes one particular mix of groups. We study two fixed scores for a common binary target under mixtures of fixed group-conditional laws. Using the cross-group AUC decomposition, we prove that every rational symmetric quadratic comparison geometry is realizable by finite scalar-score distributions. Universal dominance is thus coNP-hard, and even exhaustive checks of every mixture on fewer than $K$ groups can miss a $K$-group reversal. A grid bound gives a dimension-uniform approximation certificate with sharp $1/m$ order. Common score marginals across groups make the comparison numerator linear, with an error envelope for imperfect alignment. These results yield exact finite-bank audits, explicit reversal mixtures and distances, and simultaneous population statements. For failure detection with a frozen ResNet-50 on ImageNet-C, 15 of 18 confidence-score comparisons win in every corruption family on a discovery split, and all 15 are finite-bank certified over all family mixtures on a held-out split; over all 15 corruption types, of 14 discovery winners the corrected grid certifies 10, leaves 3 unresolved, and finds one confirmation reversal of at least 0.05 AUROC. An audit of all 11,019 released Stable LM 2 12B outputs and 35 uncertainty methods finds 66 confirmation-set comparisons that win within all four tasks yet reverse under mixing. Discovery-fitted marginal rank alignment removes all 66; an alignment-error envelope certifies 83 comparisons. Label checks also change several selected reversals. The findings distinguish robustness of frozen scores from robustness after calibration; they do not establish human-error detection, robustness to unseen corruptions, or generalization beyond the evaluated banks.

title: PISG: Constraint-Aligned Signal Amplification for Diffusion-Based Combinatorial Optimization
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (poster). 32 pages. Code: this https URL
summary: PISG: Constraint-Aligned Signal Amplification for Diffusion-Based Combinatorial Optimization Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (poster). 32 pages. Code: Diffusion-based solvers have become a prominent approach to neural combinatorial optimization. At inference time, they assign each decision variable a prediction score. A greedy decoder ranks candidates by these scores and checks hard constraints to ensure feasibility. Top-ranked candidates should be both promising and jointly feasible, making prediction-constraint alignment critical. When this alignment is weak, greedy decoding skips constraint-violating candidates and falls back to lower-ranked alternatives, degrading solution quality. Existing test-time methods improve search, sampling, or decoding, but do not directly strengthen this alignment before decoding. We observe that trained denoisers already carry constraint-aligned structural signals. Building on this observation, we propose Perturbed Instance-Structure Guidance (PISG), a training-free method that amplifies these signals at test time. At each denoising step, PISG constructs a structure-degraded prediction and extrapolates the unperturbed prediction away from it. The resulting guided prediction improves candidate rankings before constrained decoding. Signal analysis shows that this guidance concentrates on constraint-critical variables rather than uniformly rescaling scores. Under greedy decoding and without downstream refinement, PISG improves all 16 TSP solver-scale pairs across DIFUSCO, T2T, FastT2T, and StruDiCO, and all four MIS-ER solvers, with MIS-ER solved-cost gains up to +4.8%. The gains persist on most large-scale settings after 2-opt, and a preliminary study extends PISG to a Transformer-based solver. These results identify prediction-constraint alignment as an effective test-time enhancement direction for diffusion-based combinatorial optimization. Code is available at .

title: Exact Sparse Assignment with Costly Target Embeddings: Fixed-Realization Certificates and an Empirical Audit
comment: 7 pages, 2 figures. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Exact Sparse Assignment with Costly Target Embeddings: Fixed-Realization Certificates and an Empirical Audit 7 pages, 2 figures. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible Embedding-based one-to-one association is common in vision and data integration: detections are associated with tracks and records are linked across databases. Such pipelines often solve a sparse optional assignment whose edge scores add a cheap term to an inner product of neural embeddings. When target embeddings are costly, one can acquire them selectively and stop once a certificate proves that the current assignment is optimal. We give such a certificate for unit-norm embeddings. It bounds the unknown part of every reassignment by a support function and maximizes the resulting robust gains with a second sparse assignment; a shared owner-centred bound dominates any fixed-centre triangle bound. We make precise what is certified when network features are not batch-invariant: the realized values of the acquired rows and every unit-ball completion of the rest, not a second forward pass in a different batch. Auditing against a separately batched cache tests a different property; on our first pilot it produced a spurious $2.49\times10^{-6}$ objective failure. We audit the corrected protocol on four public text entity-matching benchmarks with two frozen encoders; no image data is used. All 96 certificate simulations and 120 online selective timings were exact on their own realization (largest objective gap $6.82\times10^{-13}$). At group size 8 the shared certificate acquires on average 60% of candidate-active targets, against 74% (mean centre), 69% (MEB) and 60% (zero centre): it beats the mean and MEB centres but not the zero centre, and savings concentrate in one benchmark (7% acquired). The prespecified runtime claim is contradicted: selective execution is +0.510 s slower per run (dataset-cluster 95% interval [+0.248, +0.772]). Uniform-microbatch re-encodings preserved the optimum in only 5 of 8 encoder-dataset cells, and 45 of 120 online runs disagreed with an eager cache at near-ties.

title: How Should Parallel Langevin Chains Share Noise?
comment: 48 pages, 6 figures, 36 tables. NeurIPS 2026 (poster). Code: this https URL
summary: How Should Parallel Langevin Chains Share Noise? 48 pages, 6 figures, 36 tables. NeurIPS 2026 (poster). Code: Parallel Langevin sampling usually draws an array of independent Gaussian vectors, one row per chain. The average row drives the ensemble mean, with variance $1/K$ per coordinate for $K$ chains. Yet the unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA) specifies only each row's distribution. Subtracting the column means and rescaling, as in classical antithetic sampling, makes that variance zero. Each chain keeps its ordinary ULA path law for any finite run. For quadratic targets we derive the joint covariance of linear estimates computed from the ensemble mean, including coefficient estimates, time averages and predictions. The identity separates contributions from initial states and Gaussian draws. The coupling changes the second through one scalar, which is zero whenever the draws sum to zero across chains. For nonquadratic targets we bound the remaining variance. Centering has a price: for a quadratic form in the mean-subtracted Gaussian state, the ensemble average has variance $1/(K-1)$ relative to one chain, compared with $1/K$ under independent draws. On three tempered logistic posteriors, eight centered chains reduced the variance of the posterior-mean estimate, summed over coordinates, by two to three orders of magnitude compared with eight independent chains. They also beat 128 independent chains on variance and on variance times sampling time. Under Metropolis correction the reduction shrank to about three- to eightfold: rejected draws no longer balance accepted ones. The measured variance ratios were consistent with a leading-order prediction from rejection frequency and noise energy.

title: Eliciting Research Taste in LLMs through Future Research Direction Choice
comment: Accepted at the LM4Sci Workshop at COLM 2026. 23 pages, 7 figures, 18 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Eliciting Research Taste in LLMs through Future Research Direction Choice Accepted at the LM4Sci Workshop at COLM 2026. 23 pages, 7 figures, 18 tables. Code and data: Research taste is increasingly discussed in the context of AI scientists, yet remains little studied or measured in LLMs. This judgment matters especially in open-ended research, where a direction must be chosen before a verifiable objective is available. We operationalize research taste through one task of the scientific workflow: choosing which future research direction to pursue given a research goal and current results. Rather than predicting downstream scientometric metrics or treating author choices as objectively correct, we evaluate models against human-authored future-work directions and report author alignment, stable divergence, and unstable choice as behavioral measures of research-direction preference. We construct an order-controlled evaluation of 80 pairwise comparisons from 19 ML papers published between December 2025 and February 2026 across four subdomains. Each query presents a research goal, hypotheses tested with key results, and two candidate future directions: one author-recommended direction and one plausible distractor sampled from a similar paper. Across eight LLMs, author alignment ranges from 45.0% to 67.5%, while stable divergence ranges from 15.0% to 36.2%. These divergences largely persist under similarity controls, prompt ablations, and an author-preference framing check, and inter-model agreement suggests that some non-author preferences are shared across models. We characterize what models diverge toward using transition-category labels and selected reasoning examples, finding recurring movement toward scaling/generalization and trade-offs between methodological and infrastructure/data extensions. We view this as an early descriptive evaluation for eliciting research taste profiles in LLMs, and as a step toward understanding and steering their research preferences as they take on more autonomous roles in novel open-ended scientific discovery.

title: The Sense Paradigm for World Models
summary: The Sense Paradigm for World Models 11 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables Latent world models predict the future in an embedding space rather than in pixels. An encoder trained only to predict collapses and maps every observation to the same point, so existing models add a mechanism against collapse, such as a target network, a variance penalty or a distribution penalty. These mechanisms keep the embedding from collapsing, but they leave its distances without meaning, and the model cannot tell a reversible transition from an irreversible one. We propose Sense, a single cross-entropy loss over the directed distance $d(x\to y)=\sum_i \mathrm{ReLU}(y_i-x_i)$ that replaces these mechanisms. The loss avoids collapse on its own, and since the encoder no longer needs the predictor, the predictor is fitted afterwards to fixed embeddings by plain regression. On four pixel environments, the return distance learned by Sense detects irreversible transitions with an AUC between 0.95 and 1.00, where LeWorldModel stays between 0.39 and 0.59. On TwoRoom, the navigation benchmark of LeWorldModel, planning with Sense reaches the goal in 100% of episodes against 91% for LeWorldModel. As the goal moves farther away, the planning failure rate of every baseline grows, while that of Sense stays near zero in Cup, Cliff and Sokoban and is the lowest of all methods in Pendulum.

title: Barron Approximation and locally optimal weight densities for shallow neural networks
summary: Barron Approximation and locally optimal weight densities for shallow neural networks Mean field theories provide optimization results for shallow neural networks by analyzing the weight distribution in infinite width limits. Corresponding results for finite sized networks are obtained by particle approximations, for which sharp quantitative bounds are still an open problem. In this paper, we consider a modified mean field loss, which allows a more fine grained control over finite sized networks. We prove convexity and equidistribution properties, which directly lead to Barron type approximation results for networks sampled from local loss minimizers. We demonstrate that particle approximations of the new loss function naturally lead to gradient descent methods with dropout type regularization.

title: Multi-Branch Transformer
summary: Multi-Branch Transformer Project: Transformer language models are commonly scaled by making their blocks wider or stacking them deeper. In this work, we explore a complementary path: branching, the parallel composition of full Transformer blocks. We introduce the Multi-Branch Transformer (MBT), which processes the input through shared initial layers, executes independently parameterized branches of sequential blocks in parallel, and fuses their outputs before shared final layers. At comparable training compute, we study three MBT variants: Wide-Shallow preserves block width, Narrow-Deep preserves sequential depth, and Balanced interpolates between them. In controlled pretraining experiments at four mixture-of-experts scales (0.8B to 2.1B total parameters), 2-branch Wide-Shallow MBTs consistently outperform sequential Transformers under matched parameter and training-compute budgets. Balanced MBTs improve further and retain comparable quality as the number of branches increases. To improve inference efficiency at long contexts, we introduce Joint-KV, which constructs a shared KV cache from branch representations at each depth. Our final recipe combines Balanced MBTs with Joint-KV, supported by an inference engine that exploits branch grouping and shared-cache reuse. Fitted scaling curves indicate that standard Transformers require up to 1.26x as much training body compute to match our final models' validation loss. These models reduce full-model KV-cache storage by up to 34% and deliver up to 51.4% higher decoding throughput on a single H200 GPU. Ablation studies show that branching yields gains beyond changes in width and depth, enables an effective KV-sharing strategy (Joint-KV), remains robust across fusion functions, and performs best in the middle layers. These findings show that branching offers a practical path for scaling language models toward both better modeling quality and faster inference.

title: Reasoning in the loop: antibody lead optimization by probing mechanism and measurement
summary: Reasoning in the loop: antibody lead optimization by probing mechanism and measurement 31 pages, 19 figures, 8 tables Lab-in-the-loop systems, in which a model proposes molecules, automated assays measure their properties and the results retrain the model, are a popular approach to antibody lead optimization. These systems optimize for a specification defined with metrics computed from instrument signals, so their success depends on how well those metrics serve as proxies for the properties a drug candidate needs. When a metric is a poor proxy, neither a better model nor more data will fix it, and identifying the problem usually requires expert review. We report two campaigns run on BigHat Biosciences' Milliner platform, one on an anti-albumin nanobody (VHH) and one on an anti-mesothelin single-chain variable fragment (scFv), in which a research team and a general-purpose AI agent, Claude, brought scientific reasoning into the loop. Over seven rounds and about 1,010 design variants we built libraries from antibody lineage, structure and biophysics, and found from the raw curves that on each scaffold one thermal metric did not measure what its name implied. The libraries were built as controlled comparisons, so the results also show what each mutation contributes to each property. We fit a physical model of the curves, used it to choose metrics suited to each scaffold, and changed the experimental protocol, varying protein concentration and heating rate, to test the model against pre-registered predictions. Both leads improve on their parents in affinity, thermal stability and aggregation while improving or maintaining yield and purity.

title: GlyphAtlas: Disentangling Stroke Detail from Layout for Scene Text Synthesis
summary: GlyphAtlas: Disentangling Stroke Detail from Layout for Scene Text Synthesis Scene text synthesis requires stroke-accurate characters rendered in a specified layout, as well as visual coherence with the surrounding scene. To achieve this, existing methods commonly pre-render the target text at its intended locations to form a glyph image that jointly specifies layout and glyph structure. However, this representation ties the resolution of each glyph to its target region, limiting fine-grained stroke guidance for small, densely packed, or structurally complex text. To tackle this, we propose GlyphAtlas, a scene text synthesis framework that retains the glyph image as a spatial anchor and supplies fine-grained stroke references through a dedicated glyph atlas. The atlas renders and encodes each character or word in a separate cell, decoupling reference resolution from target-region size. We further introduce atlas-anchored attention, which lets each text region retrieve stroke detail only from its corresponding atlas cells to refine the coarse glyph structure provided by the glyph image. This coarse-to-fine conditioning simplifies stroke rendering while preserving explicit layout correspondence. We optimize GlyphAtlas with a mask-weighted flow matching objective and a timestep-weighted text perceptual loss for writing accuracy and background consistency. Random resolution augmentation of atlas cells supports adjustable atlas budgets at inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GlyphAtlas achieves stroke-accurate synthesis of small, dense, and structurally complex text, zero-shot transfer to languages unseen during task-specific training, and leading performance in scenes with many text regions. project page:

title: DoF-Query Transformer for Adaptive Fusion of Egocentric Vision and Forearm HD-sEMG in Continuous Hand Kinematics
summary: DoF-Query Transformer for Adaptive Fusion of Egocentric Vision and Forearm HD-sEMG in Continuous Hand Kinematics Continuous and accurate estimation of human hand kinematics is important not only for intuitive human-machine interaction, but also for capturing fine-grained human manipulation demonstrations that can provide action supervision for embodied-intelligence datasets and dexterous robot learning. However, individual sensing modalities may be insufficient for reliable estimation under varying operating conditions. We present a finger-unencumbered multimodal framework for continuous regression of 20 hand joint angles from egocentric RGB images and 128-channel forearm high-density surface electromyography (HD-sEMG). The framework combines a Vision Transformer-based visual encoder, a Transformer-based EMG encoder, and a degree of freedom (DoF) query Transformer fusion decoder. To account for the varying informativeness of visual and EMG cues across joint DoFs and input conditions, the decoder assigns a separate learnable query to each DoF, enabling DoF-specific and context-adaptive fusion of the two modalities. The framework was evaluated on synchronized multimodal data from 10 participants. Averaged across participants, the proposed fusion model achieved a mean coefficient of determination ($R^2$) of $0.88$ and a mean absolute error (MAE) of $2.80^\circ$, compared with $0.82$ and $3.21^\circ$ for the vision-only model and $0.68$ and $5.13^\circ$ for the EMG-only model. It also outperformed the evaluated representative unimodal baselines and alternative fusion designs. DoF-wise analyses showed larger fusion gains for visually ambiguous joints and viewing conditions, while synthetic visual occlusion demonstrated greater robustness than vision-only estimation. These results highlight the complementary value of egocentric vision and forearm HD-sEMG for capturing fine-grained human hand kinematics, with potential applications in human demonstration acquisition and dexterous robot learning.

title: Radar Panoptic Transformer: Semantic-Guided Mask Queries for Dynamic Scene Understanding
summary: Radar Panoptic Transformer: Semantic-Guided Mask Queries for Dynamic Scene Understanding 9 pages, 4 figures Automotive radar provides long-range sensing and direct Doppler velocity measurements, but its sparse and non-uniformly sampled point clouds pose significant challenges for panoptic segmentation. Dynamic objects often yield only a few detections amid a dominant static background, providing limiting the geometric cues for separating object instances. We propose \emph{Radar Panoptic Transformer (RPT)}, an end-to-end point-based network that incorporates radar-adaptive feature extraction with semantic-guided mask prediction. Its backbone aggregates pose-aligned temporal context through grouped vector attention and learns per-point neighborhood radii conditioned on range, azimuth, and radar cross section (RCS). Point-wise semantic predictions initialize queries at likely foreground detections and guide masked cross-attention through query-point class agreement, producing instance masks without geometric clustering. An auxiliary RCS-consistency loss matches instance-level statistics between predicted and annotated instances. RPT achieves state-of-the-art performance on RadarScenes with $71.6\%$ mIoU and $82.2\%$ PQ. We further evaluate RPT on MAN TruckScenes, where it outperforms the evaluated baselines in a long-range, full-surround radar setting with sensing ranges up to $230\,\mathrm{m}$. RPT achieves real-time end-to-end inference at $31$\,Hz on RadarScenes, exceeding the sensor frame rate.

title: AstroPIE-53: Towards Understanding Failure Modes of Human Pose Estimation in Space
comment: 4 pages + references, 4 figures. Published in the Proceedings of SPAICE 2026 and i-SAIRAS 2026
summary: AstroPIE-53: Towards Understanding Failure Modes of Human Pose Estimation in Space 4 pages + references, 4 figures. Published in the Proceedings of SPAICE 2026 and i-SAIRAS 2026 Reliable monitoring of astronauts is essential for safety, situational awareness, and autonomous assistance in space missions. While modern computer vision enables accurate human detection and pose estimation on Earth, its robustness in space environments remains largely unquantified due to limited data availability. We present AstroPIE-53, a pilot dataset of 53 annotated astronaut videos collected from publicly available mission footage. To respect copyright restrictions, we release video identifiers, reconstruction scripts, and dense annotations rather than raw videos. The dataset includes bounding boxes, challenge classes, and human-annotated pose failure tags. We benchmark state-of-the-art person detection and pose estimation models under realistic zero-shot deployment conditions and perform the first systematic failure analysis for astronaut monitoring. Our results reveal substantial performance degradation caused by occlusions, unusual body orientations, low contrast, and microgravity motion patterns.

title: Ocular Recognition: Interoperability, Multi-Resolution, and Spectrum Challenges

summary: Ocular Recognition: Interoperability, Multi-Resolution, and Spectrum Challenges Paper submitted to IEEE journal in revision process. Abstract reduces to 1920 characteres Ocular recognition is typically developed under controlled acquisition conditions, limiting its use in semi-controlled and on-the-move scenarios. A key obstacle is the lack of representative data spanning real-world capture conditions. At a border checkpoint, for example, images may range from low-resolution visible-light periocular crops (RGB) to high-resolution near-infrared iris images (NIR). Using this heterogeneous evidence raises three questions: whether resolution-specific processing improves recognition, how to compare templates from different processing routes, and how to allocate training data across resolution specialists. We investigate resolution-specific processing and parameter sharing using three AdaFace-based architecture families: fixed-resolution specialists; Independent Backbones with Shared Heads (IBSH); and models with resolution-specific front-ends for 40x40, 80x80, and 160x160 inputs, followed by a shared identity trunk and embedding projection. We evaluate each architecture with route-specific training subsets and with a full-pool strategy, in which every specialist uses the complete selected training set. Results reveal a trade-off among same-resolution specialization, cross-resolution interoperability, and common-route re-extraction. Route-specific training produces distinct performance profiles across routes, whereas full-pool training makes route performance more uniform and primarily benefits the 160x160 route. Thus, adding training data does not improve all resolution routes equally.

title: EvoMem3D: Adaptive-Depth Temporal Representation Memory for Multi-Camera 3D Detection
summary: EvoMem3D: Adaptive-Depth Temporal Representation Memory for Multi-Camera 3D Detection Modern multi-camera 3D detectors increasingly rely on large Vision Transformer (ViT) image encoders, making repeated full-depth encoding a dominant inference cost even though adjacent driving frames are highly redundant. We present EvoMem3D, an adaptive-depth temporal framework that caches the most recent full-depth detector-interface appearance representation as a read-only anchor and combines it with policy-selected partial features from the current frame. A lightweight pre-encoding controller chooses among semantic encoder exits before image processing, allocating shallow computation to stable frames and deeper computation when the visual state changes. To reuse appearance without carrying stale geometry, we decouple temporal appearance from geometric alignment: current-frame calibration defines the decoder geometry at every timestamp, while a motion-conditioned positional adapter accounts for anchor-to-current ego motion. On nuScenes, EvoMem3D achieves 61.50 NDS and 52.76 mAP while reducing end-to-end latency from 364.4 to 168.7 ms (x2.16) relative to standard dense DETR3D. With StreamPETR, it reaches 61.36 NDS and 52.55 mAP at a x1.92 speedup. Controlled studies isolate the effects of current evidence, temporal reuse, memory correction, and adaptive routing, while our audit confirms that the policy learns to distinguish semantic driving regimes.

title: Self-supervised learning for zebrafish embryo phenotype evaluation: Systematic comparison of algorithms, label-efficient classification, and transfer learning
summary: Self-supervised learning for zebrafish embryo phenotype evaluation: Systematic comparison of algorithms, label-efficient classification, and transfer learning Zebrafish embryos are a prominent model organism for image-based phenotyping and especially suited for large-scale imaging studies, for which machine learning (ML) models can automate evaluation. However, training ML models usually requires large labeled datasets, and differences in imaging conditions often impede reuse across laboratories. Self-supervised learning (SSL) addresses both constraints by learning transferable representations from unlabeled images. Yet central aspects like the choice of algorithm remain underexplored for domain-specific applications. To close this gap, we benchmark popular SSL algorithms on the public EmbryoNet dataset, explore label-efficient learning, and test transfer to an unseen setting. Using representations from our strongest model, a ResNet50 network trained with SwAV, a simple linear classifier reaches 86.4% accuracy and a non-linear classifier 87.1%, rivaling the fully supervised EmbryoNet model (87.1%). The SwAV model decisively outperforms supervised training from scratch when labels are scarce (70.2% vs. 45.7% accuracy with 5% of labels). On a three-class problem (normal, dead, falsely cropped) with a small, previously unseen zebrafish toxicity dataset, recorded in a different setting, our model reaches 81.3% accuracy without retraining, while EmbryoNet achieves 75.9%. Overall, self-supervised models for zebrafish embryos seem to mostly facilitate label-efficiency and transfer to new settings rather than improving supervised results.

title: Visual Marking as a Native Reasoning Capability for Multimodal LLMs
summary: Visual Marking as a Native Reasoning Capability for Multimodal LLMs Visual reasoning often requires maintaining intermediate spatial states that are difficult to express in text. Existing approaches either rely on external drawing tools or image generators, or encode these states in latent tokens without explicit spatial correspondence to the input image. We introduce SelfMark, which enables MLLMs to construct and use visual marks directly in their native visual feature space. By treating the visual token grid as a canvas, SelfMark establishes explicit spatial correspondence between marks and images. This is achieved through a locate-mark-read procedure, where the model identifies relevant locations, constructs task-dependent mark features, and reads the resulting visual features to guide its reasoning. We jointly train a single model on spatial planning, dense counting, high-resolution VQA, and line tracing. Across six benchmarks, SelfMark outperforms state-of-the-art MLLM-based methods specialized for individual tasks. These improvements also persist with a stronger backbone, demonstrating the effectiveness of visual marking across different model capabilities. Overall, SelfMark provides a unified approach to visual reasoning by integrating spatially grounded marks directly into the visual feature space of MLLMs.

title: CiGS: Conduction in Gaussian Splats for Interior Temperature Field from Thermal Images
summary: CiGS: Conduction in Gaussian Splats for Interior Temperature Field from Thermal Images 18 pages We present a method for inferring the interior temperature distribution of a solid object from registered multi-view visible-spectrum and thermal images, even when the thermal views cover only part of its surface. We formulate steady-state heat conduction as a Laplace boundary value problem and solve it with a direct boundary integral equation discretized over a point cloud: a Gaussian reconstruction of the visible-spectrum images supplies the boundary geometry, and the thermal images supply the boundary data. We do not build surface or volume meshes at any stage in our method. Instead, we sample collocation points from rendered depth without the pixels at depth discontinuities, and use a density subtraction that keeps the interior evaluation accurate up to the surface. The whole chain is differentiable, and we use it to recover the pose and depth of heating pipes, insulation defects, and the shape of cracks from thermal images. We validate our method through experiments on boundary value problems with Dirichlet-only and mixed Dirichlet and Robin boundaries, using synthetic and real captured data on scenes with challenging topology. These experiments show that our method matches analytical solutions and has better accuracy than FEM solvers.

title: PoCoAttn: Position-Content Collaborative Sparse Attention for Fast and High-Fidelity Video Generation
comment: 21 pages, 15 figures, 13 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: PoCoAttn: Position-Content Collaborative Sparse Attention for Fast and High-Fidelity Video Generation 21 pages, 15 figures, 13 tables. Project page: Video diffusion transformers rely on 3D full attention over tens of thousands of spatiotemporal tokens, and its quadratic cost dominates inference latency. Sparse attention reduces this cost, but existing methods face a dilemma: static methods apply predefined masks and cannot capture input-dependent attention, whereas dynamic methods reconstruct the sparse mask repeatedly, paying online to rediscover positional structure that is largely stable across inputs. To this end, we propose PoCoAttn, a training-free sparse attention framework that separates input-stable from input-dependent attention and resolves the former offline and the latter online. PoCoAttn features: (1) A relative-offset analysis of 3D query-key pairs, which shows that video attention decomposes into an input-stable positional prior that carries most of the attention mass and a small content-dependent residual. (2) A position-content collaborative sparse attention mechanism, which retrieves positional keys from offline-calibrated tables, selects content keys online with a head-adaptive ratio between the two sources, and compensates for the discarded keys to approximate full attention. (3) A step-adaptive budget allocation algorithm, which models how early-step sparse attention errors are amplified along the denoising trajectory and derives the optimal sparsity budget per step. Extensive experiments across four video diffusion models and three tasks show that PoCoAttn consistently achieves a better speed-fidelity Pareto frontier than state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods, improving PSNR by 1.9 to 5.0 dB over baselines and delivering up to 4.1$\times$ attention and 2.0$\times$ denoising speedups over dense FlashAttention-3 attention.

title: Unreasonable Confidence from Simulator Misspecification: Directional Robustness on the SPEED+ Sim-to-Real Benchmark
comment: 22 pages, 5 figures, 20 tables. Extended version of a paper at the Sim2Science workshop, NeurIPS 2026. Code, per-image predictions and pre-registration record: this https URL
summary: Unreasonable Confidence from Simulator Misspecification: Directional Robustness on the SPEED+ Sim-to-Real Benchmark 22 pages, 5 figures, 20 tables. Extended version of a paper at the Sim2Science workshop, NeurIPS 2026. Code, per-image predictions and pre-registration record: Vision-based navigation systems for orbit must be trained almost entirely on synthetic imagery, because real labelled images of a given spacecraft in flight rarely exist. Benchmarks like SPEED+ are built for that situation: the training set comes from a simulator, and the test sets are real images of a satellite mockup under two kinds of lighting. That simulator approximates how light reflects off mylar and aluminium, and like every scientific simulator it is misspecified. Its error is radiometric, since it misses the specular highlights, hard shadows and sensor saturation common in real images. We probe the resulting synthetic-to-real gap, the central risk for such systems, with a deliberately simple monocular pose estimator. In a 2x2 study of backbone adaptation and photometric augmentation, trained on synthetic images and tested on both real hardware-in-the-loop domains, we find three things. (1) The model does not know it is failing: regions conformally calibrated to 90% on synthetic data cover only 9-15% of rotation errors on sunlamp and 21-38% on lightbox, so a wrong pose carries the confidence of a correct one. (2) Transfer is asymmetric: scaling data and features improved synthetic rotation error from 1.65 to 1.03 rad but moved the harshly lit sunlamp domain by only 0.05 rad, under twice its seed s.d., whereas adapting the backbone's last stage carried 63-83% of its extra synthetic gain to both real domains. (3) Once the backbone adapts, augmentation helps only in the direction it models: our photometric stack improved the diffusely lit lightbox domain from 1.17 to 0.99 rad on every seed but moved sunlamp no more than seed-to-seed variation, while with the backbone frozen it helped sunlamp more. Every post-review experiment was pre-registered, and the code, per-image predictions and pre-registration record are at .

title: Words Speak Louder? Exploring the Language Shortcut of LLM-Driven Incomplete Multimodal Learning
comment: 19 pages, 7 figures, 14 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Words Speak Louder? Exploring the Language Shortcut of LLM-Driven Incomplete Multimodal Learning 19 pages, 7 figures, 14 tables. Project page: Is a face or a voice still heard once the words are known? Incomplete multimodal learning increasingly uses large language models (LLMs) as fusion engines: modality features enter as token blocks and missing modalities become placeholders. We find that LLM-driven fusion can override non-verbal evidence it can read. Contrasting its full-input prediction with counterfactual views, the same model shown one modality or no content, we identify language shortcuts. We build MR-Bench: MR-Bench-A types every test sample of four sentiment benchmarks; MR-Bench-H contains 900 human-validated clips (620 language-shortcut, LS; 280 non-verbal-shortcut, NS) from seven sources, and every model is scored on all of them. Zero-shot MLLMs solve at most 32.7% of the LS clips; adding the transcript to the muted video lowers vision-language accuracy by 46.1-53.1 points. Yet inverting a text-only model's answers solves 94.4%, so LS accuracy alone cannot establish use of non-verbal evidence. Inside the fusion LLM, fused states align increasingly with the text view late in the decoder. Counterfactual-View Reliability learning (CoVeR) trains views as unimodal judges and withholds fused supervision where they disagree. It achieves state-of-the-art results on five benchmarks without extra inference cost in accuracy mode. On MR-Bench-H, it reaches 61.7% LS and 93.6% NS accuracy; robust mode raises LS accuracy to 63.0% while lowering NS accuracy to 84.8%. Among LS clips solved without text, adding text causes errors on 30.1% with CoVeR versus 32.2% with LLM-Fusion. Project page: .

title: Sivia: Learning to Draw, Learning to Learn
summary: Sivia: Learning to Draw, Learning to Learn A paper's overview figure is often the first thing readers see: it must explain the method correctly and look polished. We present Sivia, an overview-figure system that reads the paper, plans its relations, adapts visual organization from recent top-conference papers, and composes a design for image generation. Sivia improves with use through human-guided recursive self-improvement (RSI) at two levels: learning to draw revises its drawing skill from feedback on accuracy and presentation, and learning to learn revises the updater that proposes those revisions. A personal profile adapts presentation to its user's aesthetic preferences while the scientific content stays fixed. A diagnostic study of 1,964 overviews for 445 papers (17,973 relation judgments) shows that most errors are omissions and that source-derived relation plans raise required-relation accuracy (RRA) by up to 19.85 points. On 48 test papers, learning both levels reaches 93.54\% RRA, 15.31, 9.38, and 8.33 points above the initial skill, the Fixed-updater, and the GEPA baselines, while readability and visual quality rise from 3.95 and 4.00 to 4.70 and 4.78 on five-point scales. Learned presentation profiles raise liking from 4.02 to 4.73 and adoption from 34 to 45 of 48 tasks. Code and released artifacts are available at

title: RoboACE: Adversarial Co-Evolution for Robot Self-Improvement
summary: RoboACE: Adversarial Co-Evolution for Robot Self-Improvement 13 pages, 5 figures Robot agents can improve reusable skills, planning procedures, and recovery strategies from execution feedback, yet a fixed practice source leaves the search for new weaknesses unchanged. Useful practice depends on the agent's current capabilities, so the procedure that chooses practice must also be revisable. We present RoboACE (Robot Adversarial Co-Evolution), a framework that jointly evolves curriculum and execution harnesses around frozen foundation models. The curriculum harness uses accumulated capability evidence to propose informative challenges, while the execution harness responds with reusable revisions that expand execution capabilities. Alternating updates hold one side fixed as the other changes, and admitted challenges form fixed snapshots for comparing execution revisions. Starting from a compact set of LIBERO practice conditions, the resulting frozen deployment outperforms the evaluated controllers and agent systems across four LIBERO-family panels. On LIBERO-PRO, it reaches 74.0% success, exceeding the initial deployment by 15.0 percentage points and direct execution by its VLA controller by 13.5 points. Case studies document changes to evidence-guided practice selection, drawer-skill grounding, and controller intervention.

title: One Question, Four Voices: How Advice for Alzheimer's Caregiving Differs Between Caregivers, Clinicians, and Large Language Models
comment: Accepted to ACM CSCW 2026. 35 pages, 7 figures
summary: One Question, Four Voices: How Advice for Alzheimer's Caregiving Differs Between Caregivers, Clinicians, and Large Language Models Accepted to ACM CSCW 2026. 35 pages, 7 figures Online caregiver forums are an important source of emotional and informational support for Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD). We compare responses to 85 real caregiver questions from ALZConnected across four responder groups: peer caregivers, physicians, ChatGPT, and a retrieval-augmented CareGPT grounded in peer discussions. Using 28 measures spanning linguistic form, emotional support, informational support, and topic scope, we examine how these voices differ when answering the same questions. Peers provided time-anchored narratives and community grounding; clinicians offered concise, advice-forward, clinically bounded guidance; and LLMs produced a formal, verbose, highly structured consultation style. CareGPT showed minimal measurable separation from ChatGPT, suggesting that retrieval plus prompt injection alone was insufficient to shift communicative stance. LLM outputs scored higher than peers on politeness and emotion-support markers and were comparable to clinicians on informativeness and physician-alignment measures, but were less narrative and less contextually situated. Topic modeling showed that LLM responses concentrated on advice-oriented themes, whereas peers covered a broader range, including emotional processing, legal and financial concerns, and daily care. These findings suggest that AI can complement, but not replace, human contributions to ADRD caregiver support and motivate hybrid systems that combine structured AI delivery with the distinct strengths of human voices.

title: Syntactic Complexity Convergence in Dialogue: Analysis of the Phenomenon and Application to LLM Detection
summary: Syntactic Complexity Convergence in Dialogue: Analysis of the Phenomenon and Application to LLM Detection EMNLP 2026 main camera-ready We revisit the under-explored phenomenon of syntactic complexity convergence in dialogue. Extending prior topic-level analyses to full conversations, we examine five human-human datasets and a set of human-LLM dialogues. We integrate and evaluate a multidimensional set of syntactic complexity metrics to quantify structural variation in dialogue. Our analyses reveal robust syntactic complexity convergence across human-human datasets, especially in task-oriented interactions, and statistical tests confirm that these effects are not due to chance. In contrast, human-LLM dialogues show no significant convergence under individual metrics; however, linear-CKA uncovers a distinct cross-metric convergence pattern. Motivated by these differences, we use syntactic complexity as a feature for detecting LLM-involved dialogue, achieving 96\% accuracy. Our classification results demonstrate its potential without relying on likelihood-based signals such as surprisal, which require a language model as the estimator.

title: Justification of Emotional Appeal in Computational Argumentation
summary: Justification of Emotional Appeal in Computational Argumentation EMNLP 2026 main camera-ready Emotional appeals (EAs) are often treated as fallacious in computational argumentation, yet they may be justified when warranted by the context. We introduce the task of predicting EA justification and present the first human-annotated dataset for this task, covering 1,176 argument--context pairs. Grounded in philosophical literature, our framework evaluates EA justification along logical and emotional dimensions. Human annotations show that justification criteria form a shared latent judgment space, with evidential proportionality and normative acceptability most strongly associated with overall justification. We further find that EAs without logical support are not always judged fully unjustified, and stronger EAs are not necessarily judged less justified. Finally, LLM experiments show that EA justification prediction remains challenging.

title: Understanding Failures in LLM Reasoning by Learning Structured Representations of Chain-of-Thought
summary: Understanding Failures in LLM Reasoning by Learning Structured Representations of Chain-of-Thought Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Conference (Findings) Chain-of-Thought (CoT) is central to improving reasoning in large language models, yet existing evaluation methods focus on step-level signals and ignore the underlying structure of reasoning traces. This raises a key question: what aspects of reasoning quality (i.e., correctness, efficiency, and failure patterns) are encoded in the structure of a CoT trace? We introduce \textbf{CoT2Graph}, a framework that represents CoT traces as directed dependency graphs, making relationships between reasoning steps explicit and capturing patterns such as backtracking, branching, and subtask merging. We model these graphs with graph neural networks and use attribution-based explanations to identify structural patterns associated with reasoning quality. CoT2Graph reveals distinct patterns of successful and failed reasoning: correct CoTs place greater importance on early planning, whereas incorrect CoTs are associated with overloaded synthesis steps and dependency violations. We further show that graph-based signals better predict whether a CoT leads to a correct answer, outperforming previous tree-based structural methods by up to 2.5\% and simple length-based baselines by 7.8\%, while also improving Best-of-$N$ selection. Overall, our results demonstrate that reasoning structure encodes rich signals about reasoning quality, motivating a shift from sequence-level evaluation to structural analysis.

title: When Helpful Agents Cause Financial Harm: Evaluating LLM Agent Safety in Executable Economic Worlds
comment: Accepted (Oral) at EMNLP 2026 Workshop on Financial NLP (FinNLP)
summary: When Helpful Agents Cause Financial Harm: Evaluating LLM Agent Safety in Executable Economic Worlds Accepted (Oral) at EMNLP 2026 Workshop on Financial NLP (FinNLP) As LLM agents become increasingly capable of making consequential economic decisions, their safety under economic pressures remains poorly understood. We introduce EconSafeBench, the first benchmark for systematically evaluating the safety of LLM agents in executable economic environments. EconSafeBench contains 828 cases across five economic scenarios and four categories of safety violations. A key design is the matched evaluation of three sources of safety pressure, including explicit user requests, pressure from other actors, and pressure arising from the agent's own pursuit of a performance objective. We further evaluate safety at both static and dynamic scales through 30-period interactions with persistent memory and matched controls. Across eight LLMs, all evaluated models exhibit safety violations on the static benchmark, with overall violation rates ranging from 8.5% to 40.6%. We further find that violations can occur even without an explicit unsafe request, and that initially compliant agents may begin to violate as performance pressure increases over time. These findings highlight the need for stronger safety alignment and rigorous evaluation before LLM agents are deployed in high-stakes economic environments.

title: The Judge Is Not Impartial: Self-Preference in Medical LLM Evaluation
summary: The Judge Is Not Impartial: Self-Preference in Medical LLM Evaluation 17 pages, 3 figures, 8 tables Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to evaluate model-generated medical content, creating a potential circularity: an LLM judge may favor outputs generated by the same model independently of clinical quality. To characterize LLM judge self-preference in medical settings, we measured same-model affinity in single-turn specialist question answering and multi-turn standardized-patient encounters. We evaluated eight models, two from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Qwen, on 620 real point of care questions from clinicians (Real-POCQi). The same eight models also generated and judged 200 standardized patient-clinician scenarios (MedSP1000) up to 8 visible turns. In total, our analysis spans 13,760 LLM judgments. We define three complementary measures of self-preference. Answer Rank Bias, our primary measure, compared the rank assigned to a fixed response by its own-model judge with its average rank from outside judges. Answer Score Bias made the analogous comparison using rubric scores. Own-Answer Win Rate measured how often a judge ranked its own model's response above a competitor. Higher values across all these measures indicate greater degrees of self-preference. In Real-POCQi, pooled Answer Rank Bias was $+1.22$ positions, and all eight judges favored their own answers. Self-preference persisted both with and without a grading rubric. Revealing generator identities modestly weakened self-preference by an average of $-0.094$ positions. In MedSP1000, pooled Answer Rank Bias ranged from $+0.53$ to $+0.62$ positions, with no clear difference by conversation length ($p=0.17$). LLM judges systematically favored responses generated by their own models across multiple formats. Clinical AI deployments should exercise increased vigilance including multiple evaluation measures and judge panels spanning differing model families when deploying LLM-as-a-judge systems.

title: Which Mathematical Context Supports Target-Aligned Conjecture Generation? A Paired Ablation Study
comment: 16 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. To appear in the Proceedings of the 4th Workshop on Mathematical Natural Language Processing (MathNLP 2026)
summary: Which Mathematical Context Supports Target-Aligned Conjecture Generation? A Paired Ablation Study 16 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. To appear in the Proceedings of the 4th Workshop on Mathematical Natural Language Processing (MathNLP 2026) Generating mathematical conjectures from natural-language context is challenging because theorem-relevant information is distributed across multiple forms of mathematical context, including definitions, objects, assumptions, and constructions. We study which of these contextual signals help a model recover the specific claim supported by the surrounding setup, using 61 main theorems from 12 papers across four mathematical domains. For each theorem, we redact the result and represent the remaining setup using six context components. A paired ablation design compares full context, six leave-one-out conditions, and six single-component conditions, yielding 793 generated conjectures. Context components were largely complementary: removing one component usually had little effect, whereas retaining only one substantially reduced expected-theorem alignment. Local Mathematical Objects provided the strongest standalone signal, while Structural Constraints and Conditions produced the largest alignment decrease when removed. These findings suggest that target-aligned conjecture generation depends on combining information that identifies relevant objects with information that constrains admissible claims.

title: Evaluating the Robustness of Fact-Checking LLMs on Multilingual Evidence
comment: 13 pages, 16 figures Accepted at COLM Sci-FM 2026
summary: Evaluating the Robustness of Fact-Checking LLMs on Multilingual Evidence 13 pages, 16 figures Accepted at COLM Sci-FM 2026 Automated fact-checking benchmarks typically pair claims with clean, curated evidence in high-resource languages, but real-world evidence is often incomplete, misleading, or written in a language where models are weaker. We evaluate the robustness of fact-checking LLMs for different languages. Building on EuroVerdict, we construct gold evidence sets for 190 claims in each of English, German, Greek, and Romanian, then apply four corruption strategies at two severity levels. We test LLMs on a set of claims, providing them with evidence from the sets above. A rubric-based LLM-as-a-judge scores reasoning quality. Verdict accuracy proves highly sensitive to both factors: Misleading edit cut Llama 3.1 8B's English accuracy from 80.00% to 16.84%, and losses widen as language resource level decreases. Machine-translating Greek and Romanian claims into English recovers much, but not all, of the low-resource gap. Judge scores decline more slowly than accuracy, suggesting that automated reasoning evaluation underestimates degradation. These results caution against deploying LLM fact-checkers on noisy multilingual evidence, and we release our evidence datasets and evaluation code to support future work.

title: Skill Transfer: Adapting Agent Skills from Strong to Weak Agents
summary: Skill Transfer: Adapting Agent Skills from Strong to Weak Agents Agent skills are modular bundles of instructions, code, and resources that an agent loads on demand, increasingly authored and validated on frontier models and shared as an open standard. The same skill behaves differently across models: a strong model turns it into a large performance gain, while a weak model realizes little of that gain and sometimes does worse than with no skill at all. Cost and resource constraints, however, often restrict real deployments to exactly these weaker agents. We hypothesize that the strong model silently supplies procedural steps the skill leaves implicit, which the weak model omits, and formalize closing this gap as \emph{Skill Transfer}: holding the skill's capability ceiling and the model's parameters fixed, we adapt the skill so a specific weak agent can execute it well. Our method abstracts strong and weak trajectories into typed execution structures, localizes their structural divergence with a graph edit distance (GED), and repairs the skill through an iterative diagnoser-patcher loop. Across three benchmarks and two model families, Skill Transfer raises pass rate over the unmodified skill significantly and well over other skill-evolution baselines. The adapted skill also improves the strong agent it was never adapted for, and transfers out of distribution to a structurally related, unseen task. Code is available at

title: Interpretability-Guided Auditing for Clinical Language Models for Discharge Prediction
summary: Interpretability-Guided Auditing for Clinical Language Models for Discharge Prediction Clinical natural language processing (NLP) models for hospital discharge prediction are vulnerable to explicit discharge-related lexical cues in clinical notes, even when note timestamps are temporally filtered. These cues may act as proxies for future outcomes, leading models to rely on shortcut-like signals rather than clinically meaningful evidence. We propose AuditBERT-Discharge, a lightweight framework that reframes interpretability as a training-time auditing mechanism. Token-level SHAP attributions from an initial BioClinicalBERT model are used to identify highly attributed discharge-related tokens, which are subsequently masked in the training corpus before model retraining. We evaluate the framework on a retrospective cohort of elective spine surgery encounters from a single academic medical center. Qualitative attribution analysis and preliminary evaluation suggest that SHAP-guided auditing reduces reliance on explicit discharge-proxy language and yields more conservative, better-calibrated predictions, although improvements in discrimination are not uniform. These findings demonstrate the potential of interpretability-guided auditing as a practical strategy for identifying and constraining shortcut-like lexical dependencies in temporally sensitive clinical NLP tasks.

title: Conditional Optimal Transport and Triangular Maps for Imitation Learning
summary: Conditional Optimal Transport and Triangular Maps for Imitation Learning 38 pages, 5 figures We introduce a unified formulation of imitation learning from demonstrations as a conditional sampling problem solved by triangular transport: a policy is the second block of a triangular map that transports a reference distribution to the conditional distribution of the action chunk given the observation history. Unlike in Diffusion Policy, where it is a fixed Gaussian, the reference becomes a design variable; we take it to be the empirical distribution of the demonstrated action chunks and introduce three instances of the formulation: an optimal transport policy (OTP), a flow matching policy (FMP), and a stochastic interpolant policy (SIP). On the Push-T and robomimic Square tasks, the three policies are competitive in task performance with Diffusion Policy and Consistency Policy while using considerably smaller networks and shorter training, and the informative reference accounts for a substantial part of their performance when few network evaluations are used. The three instances offer different trade-offs rather than a single best method: OTP generates an action chunk with a single evaluation of the smallest network (0.23 million parameters on Push-T) and is suitable for settings in which inference time and model size matter, whereas SIP attains the highest scores among the proposed policies at a higher cost.

title: GraphPass: A Study of Graph Neural Networks for Compiler Pass Selection
summary: GraphPass: A Study of Graph Neural Networks for Compiler Pass Selection Compiler pass selection is usually governed by fixed pipelines (-O2, -O3) or hand-written heuristics. We study whether a graph neural network (GNN) over a program's control-flow graph (CFG) can select among a fixed menu of five pass sequences in a single forward pass. GraphPass encodes each CFG with a graph attention (GAT) or graph convolutional (GCN) encoder and classifies it into one of the five sequences. On a synthetic benchmark of 5,000 generated CFGs in five program families, both encoders agree with the benchmark's reference label on about 92% of held-out programs, versus 68.4% for a hand-written rule-based heuristic and 85% for a flat MLP.
