This paper proposes a dual stacked intelligent metasurfaces (dual-SIM) architecture that performs semantic alignment entirely in the wave domain. By jointly exploiting programmable metasurfaces at both ends of a link and the wireless channel, the proposed architecture realizes an end-to-end linear transformation between heterogeneous latent spaces. We show phase-only multilayer SIM can approximate both supervised linear aligners and zero-shot Parseval-frame equalizers. We investigate single-SIM, disjoint asymmetric and symmetric dual-SIM, and jointly optimized dual-SIM configurations, considering channel equalization and constructive channel exploitation. For joint design, we develop an alternating projected gradient algorithm with convergence guarantees to first-order stationary points. We further introduce a deep-unrolled network that unrolls gradient-based iterations to reduce computational cost of SIM reconfiguration under channel variations. Numerical results with heterogeneous vision transformer encoders show accurate semantic alignment from moderate to high signal-to-noise ratios. The joint and symmetric disjoint dual-SIM designs achieve the highest accuracy over compact channels, the joint design leads at shallow stack depths, and the advantage over single-SIM designs diminishes at equal depth.

title: Equilibrium measures for anisotropic exponential interaction energies with applications to transformers
summary: Equilibrium measures for anisotropic exponential interaction energies with applications to transformers 23 pages, 3 figures We study the minimization of anisotropic exponential interaction energies over probability measures on the sphere, motivated by mean-field models of self-attention in transformer architectures. For every symmetric positive definite interaction matrix, we relate the minimizer to a corresponding anisotropic Brownian motion and use the Feynman--Kac formula and elliptic regularity theory to show that it admits a smooth, strictly positive density on the sphere. We further show that it is the only stationary measure with full support for the dynamics considered. We use the stochastic viewpoint to derive an algorithm for sampling from the minimizer. In dimension two, we also propose a numerical scheme for approximating its density based on a Mathieu series expansion.

title: Geometric Stability and Sample Complexity for Compositional Function Priors
comment: 25 pages. An extended abstract was accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Symmetry and Geometry in Neural Representations (NeurReps), non-archival. Ancillary file: companion document with extended proofs and examples
summary: Geometric Stability and Sample Complexity for Compositional Function Priors 25 pages. An extended abstract was accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Symmetry and Geometry in Neural Representations (NeurReps), non-archival. Ancillary file: companion document with extended proofs and examples We study when compositional structure yields dimension reduction in supervised learning. We frame learning as empirical risk minimization with a function-space prior: a regularization functional selects a subset of functions with favorable approximation and metric entropy. The models are compositions $f(x)=g(Ax+\Delta h(x))$, where $A\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d}$ is a linear base map, $\Delta h$ is a nonlinear correction, and $g$ is an outer function; that is, $f$ is an arbitrary smooth function of a $k$-dimensional representation of the input that is linear up to a correction. We prove covering-number bounds showing that the statistical complexity of this class interpolates between an intrinsic regime, parametric in the $kd$ entries of the linear map and nonparametric only in the representation dimension $k$, and an ambient $d$-dimensional nonparametric rate; the interpolation is controlled by the correction size $\varepsilon=\|\Delta h\|$. We then connect $\varepsilon$ to data geometry. If the data lie in a small tube around a $k$-dimensional manifold and the regression target depends on the input only through its nearest point on that manifold, then locally the target factorizes exactly as $g(Ax+\Delta h(x))$ with $A$ a tangent chart and a correction whose Sobolev norm scales linearly with curvature at the localization scale. Patching such local models over an atlas gives a finite-sample excess-risk bound for a least-squares estimator over a finite net of local models, whose ambient term vanishes with curvature. For a one-dimensional model problem we also prove a converse: on curved data, every affine compositional predictor faces an error floor unless its correction budget scales with curvature, while the matching curved model class attains the intrinsic rate. The correction size $\varepsilon$ is thus the effective-dimension parameter linking curvature to statistical complexity.

title: Steering Bayesian Inference and Decisions through Data Poisoning
summary: Steering Bayesian Inference and Decisions through Data Poisoning 64 pages, 13 figures Adversarial machine learning has revealed that statistical models can be manipulated through poisoned data, and Bayesian inference is no exception. Earlier work has shown that subtle poisoning attacks can drive the posterior toward a distribution of the attacker's choosing. Such posterior attraction attacks require a fully specified target posterior; however, attackers typically care about only a few posterior quantities or, more consequentially, about a downstream decision. Herein, we study how an attacker can alter Bayesian inference and decisions by deleting or replicating a few observations, chosen to minimize the maximum mean discrepancy between the resulting posterior and a target distribution. A suitable kernel lets the attacker steer selected posterior moments without specifying the rest of the target. Because Bayes actions depend on the posterior only through expected utilities, which are themselves posterior moments, the same approach can target a decision directly. We construct the attacks with a gradient-based heuristic that requires only posterior samples, and analyze its convergence. Experiments with regression and hierarchical models compare moment-based and full-posterior attacks, and illustrate how deleting a handful of observations can flip a Bayesian decision.

title: NAP-Wave: A Neural Adaptive Plane-Wave Architecture for High-Frequency Helmholtz Problems
summary: NAP-Wave: A Neural Adaptive Plane-Wave Architecture for High-Frequency Helmholtz Problems 35 pages, 15 figures, 7 tables Training neural networks to simulate highly oscillatory wavefields presents optimization challenges, often hindered by spectral bias and poorly conditioned physics-based loss landscapes. To address these challenges and enhance convergence, we propose NAP-Wave, a joint neural architecture and training strategy that expands the target scattered wavefield in an adaptive neural plane-wave basis. The basis functions are extracted from all hidden layers and modulated by trainable plane-wave carriers, embedding the high-frequency oscillatory physics directly into the network's trial space. NAP-Wave is trained on a physics-informed loss built from the Lippmann-Schwinger integral equation, so no differentiation of the network with respect to its input is required. We develop a decoupled optimization strategy in which Adam updates the parameters of the neural plane-wave basis, while the linear combination coefficients are computed exactly by a least-squares (LS) solver. We couple this with an adaptive-depth training strategy in which the network starts shallow and grows progressively layer-by-layer. At each growth step, we avoid the loss spikes typical of dynamic network growth using the LS-computed coefficients, the warm-started parameters, and the preservation of the first- and second-order optimizer moments of the previous stage. Ablation studies confirm that the plane-wave basis, the exact coefficient solve, and the progressive schedule independently accelerate convergence and improve accuracy. Validated on exact-solution benchmarks, NAP-Wave achieves relative L2 errors of order 1%. On highly heterogeneous geophysical benchmarks, it achieves relative errors of 5%, 9%, and 10%, significantly outperforming published PINN methods in both accuracy and convergence time. To ensure reproducibility, the code is available at .

title: SG-LegalClarify: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Legal Reasoning and Ambiguity Recognition in Singapore Law
summary: SG-LegalClarify: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Legal Reasoning and Ambiguity Recognition in Singapore Law Singapore offers a distinctive testbed for legal reasoning by large language models (LLMs). Its legal system combines inherited English common law with jurisdiction-specific statutes, requiring models to distinguish local doctrine from generic common-law intuition. This setting also highlights the challenge of recognizing underspecification in lay legal queries, because the facts material to a legal outcome depend on the governing doctrine. Yet legal benchmarks rarely cover Singapore law or test this form of ambiguity recognition. To address these gaps, we introduce SG-LegalClarify, a large-scale benchmark for open-ended legal reasoning and ambiguity recognition in Singapore law. SG-LegalClarify contains 1,100 lawyer-authored source questions spanning 10 legal domains, including 340 fully specified and 760 underspecified questions. Each underspecified question has a fixed hidden-fact assignment and a fully specified counterpart, yielding 1,860 evaluation instances. Responses are graded with lawyer-authored Issue, Rule, Application, and Conclusion (IRAC) rubrics. We evaluate 19 LLMs, closed-book and with web search, using a multi-turn pipeline in which models decide whether to answer or clarify, and a user simulator reveals hidden facts only when asked. We find the benchmark far from saturated: the best models satisfy only 69.8% of mandatory rubric items closed-book (average 53.8%) and 77.8% with web search (average 63.0%). Models also struggle to recognize when clarification is necessary. We will release the public split of our benchmark, the model outputs on it, and the evaluation pipeline to support future research.

title: Tabular Foundation Models as Emulators for Forecasting Terrestrial Ecosystem Dynamics
summary: Tabular Foundation Models as Emulators for Forecasting Terrestrial Ecosystem Dynamics Process-based terrestrial biosphere models such as the Ecosystem Demography (ED) model underpin global carbon budgets, but their cost limits global, high-resolution and scenario-rich simulation. Deep emulators such as DeepED reduce that cost but require task-specific architectures and training. Tabular foundation models offer a different route: TabPFN predicts new rows by in-context learning, without being trained on the task. We compare TabPFN-3.5 with two DeepED baselines, $DeepED_{LSTM}$ and $DeepED_{Transformer}$, on CarbonGlobe's overall evaluation, which trains on a uniform 1/16 sample of sites and tests on the other 50,779, predicting the 40-year state of all seven ED outputs. We then test every model, trained on present-day data only, on ED runs forced by SSP1-2.6 and SSP5-8.5 for 2021--2060 in six continental forest regions. With no training, TabPFN-3.5 has the lowest present-day height error of the three models and is within 4% of $DeepED_{LSTM}$ for soil carbon, but is less accurate for AGB, LAI and the carbon fluxes. In 2060, errors are several times larger than at the same sites under present-day forcing, and every model underestimates the biomass that ED gains. Under SSP5-8.5, TabPFN-3.5 is the most accurate model for height, AGB, soil carbon and LAI, with the lowest AGB error in all six regions, although, unlike ED, it predicts no larger biomass gain than under SSP1-2.6. Under SSP1-2.6, no model is best overall.

title: Model Immunization Beyond Condition Numbers: The Importance of Plateau Regions
summary: Model Immunization Beyond Condition Numbers: The Importance of Plateau Regions Accepted by NeurIPS 2026 Harmful fine-tuning can rapidly compromise safety alignment in Large Language Models, underscoring the vulnerability of deployed models to post-release modification. While prior work motivates model immunization by inducing ill-conditioned curvature to slow harmful optimization, this approach is not scalable due to the high computational cost of Hessian estimation. We refine this paradigm by extending the theoretical framework to prioritize plateau regions alongside curvature. We further introduce an immunization algorithm based on efficient Hessian estimation and bounds on the extremal singular values of the Hessian. We demonstrate the proposed immunization framework in three applications: (i) Fine-tuning-as-a-service settings where benign user data may be mixed with poisoned harmful data, (ii) open-weight settings where an adversary can fine-tune on harmful-only data with varied training dynamics, and (iii) robust unlearning, where immunized models better resist relearning attacks after unlearning. Extensive experiments confirm that our approach achieves robust defense against adversarial fine-tuning while largely maintaining general utility and downstream trainability. Our code is available at .

title: Improving X-Ray Baggage Instance Segmentation with Shared Point-Based Mask Refinement
summary: Improving X-Ray Baggage Instance Segmentation with Shared Point-Based Mask Refinement 12 pages, 8 figures, 11 tables Overlapping projections and complex object contours make prohibited items difficult to delineate in X-ray baggage images. This study investigates shared point-based mask refinement to improve instance segmentation within Cascade Mask R-CNN. The framework combines a ResNet-101 backbone with an attention-based feature pyramid and progressively updates uncertain mask locations, increasing mask resolution from $28 \times 28$ to $112 \times 112$. A single refinement module is shared across cascade stages and refinement levels, with transformer and multilayer perceptron (MLP) variants used to examine the role of interactions among selected points. Ten configurations were evaluated on the official PIXray split across three training seeds using the original target-instance annotations for evaluation. The transformer and MLP refiners achieved mean mask average precision (AP) of 71.79 and 72.47, respectively, compared with 70.50 for the unrefined detector, yielding gains of 1.29 and 1.97 AP points. The MLP achieved the highest mean mask AP among the evaluated configurations. Both variants also improved boundary agreement on commonly detected objects, supporting improved mask delineation, while detection diagnostics did not establish a corresponding positive gain. These findings demonstrate that shared point-based refinement can improve segmentation quality in the tested cascade architecture using existing target-mask annotations, without additional occluder supervision. Evaluation on independent X-ray datasets is needed to determine how well these improvements generalize.

title: Beyond Seeing: Fine-Grained Preference Validation and Severity-Aware Alignment for Mitigating Visual Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Includes a 4-page supplementary appendix with experimental details, equations, prompt templates, and additional comparisons
summary: Beyond Seeing: Fine-Grained Preference Validation and Severity-Aware Alignment for Mitigating Visual Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models 9 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Includes a 4-page supplementary appendix with experimental details, equations, prompt templates, and additional comparisons Large vision-language models can produce fluent responses containing objects, attributes, or relations unsupported by the image. We study an implemented alignment pipeline that normalizes released fine-grained hallucination supervision, validates chosen-rejected preference pairs with vision-language judges, repairs rejected chosen responses, and trains LLaVA adapters with standard or severity-aware direct preference optimization. The study uses 16,143 normalized feedback records and 8,386 released preference pairs, comparing direct training with zero-shot and two-shot judged severity-margin variants. The zero-shot variant reduces Object HalBench CHAIRs from 53.00 to 36.00 and CHAIRi from 15.72 to 10.41. Across aligned models, AMBER-Hal decreases from 35.90 to 25.10-26.90, accompanied by reduced visual coverage. In contrast, the base model retains the highest valid POPE adversarial F1, 84.18 versus 83.87-83.91 after alignment. These results support benchmark-dependent reductions in generative hallucination rather than uniform superiority of severity-aware alignment. We distinguish implemented pipeline components from the preference paths used in the reported experiments and discuss the limits of attributing gains to judging, repair, or the training objective individually.

title: LINK: Lightweight and Inductive Node-to-Node Propagation Rule Learning for Traffic Kriging
summary: LINK: Lightweight and Inductive Node-to-Node Propagation Rule Learning for Traffic Kriging Spatio-temporal traffic kriging aims to reconstruct traffic time series at unobserved locations with no historical traffic observations by leveraging spatial and temporal dependencies across the road network. Existing Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based approaches primarily rely on neighborhood aggregation to capture spatial dependencies, thereby modeling traffic interactions implicitly and making it difficult to accurately recover traffic magnitudes at locations without historical observations. To address this limitation, we propose LINK, a Lightweight and Inductive Node-to-node propagation rule learning paradigm for traffic Kriging. LINK introduces three key designs: 1) a propagation-centric traffic kriging paradigm that explicitly learns a shared node-to-node transition rule; 2) a context-aware Spectral Propagation Network that performs traffic-state propagation in both the spectral and time domains; and 3) TraffiKrig, a realistic traffic kriging benchmark that preserves heterogeneous road-segment characteristics and road-specific metadata while enabling systematic comparison of representative kriging methods under a unified metadata-enhanced setting. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LINK achieves strong reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency. Compared with the strongest baseline on each subset, LINK achieves an average MAE reduction of 54.7% over original baselines. LINK also achieves substantial efficiency improvements, reducing training time by 66.5% and inference time by 86.6% compared with the fastest competing methods. Zero-shot experiments further demonstrate the transferability of the learned propagation rule across regions.

title: GranularGPT: Natural-Language-Driven End-to-End Discrete Element Method Simulations
summary: GranularGPT: Natural-Language-Driven End-to-End Discrete Element Method Simulations 21 pages, 9 figures Discrete element method (DEM) simulations are widely used to investigate granular and particulate systems, but their application often requires specialized expertise in particle physics, numerical modelling, and simulation post-processing. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to simplify these workflows by enabling users to interact with simulation tools through natural language. This study offers GranularGPT, an LLM-assisted agentic framework for end-to-end DEM simulation workflows, from natural-language problem descriptions to simulation execution and automated post-processing. The framework enables users to generate DEM simulation cases, execute and monitor simulations, and automatically extract and report physical and process-level metrics. Evaluation across 60 normal-condition cases covering 12 DEM scenarios and parameter variations achieve a simulation success rate of 91.7%. In the error-handling evaluation, all 10 repairable errors are detected and 9 are successfully resolved, while all 5 non-repairable cases are correctly identified and reported. The framework automatically extracts a range of DEM-relevant metrics, including particle size distributions, packing and density measures, velocity profiles, discharge rates, mixing indices, contact force characteristics, and thermal quantities. GranularGPT provides a foundation for improving the accessibility and efficiency of DEM simulation workflows while reducing the specialized expertise required for their operation.

title: AsymEEF: Bimanual Manipulation with Asymmetric End Effectors
summary: AsymEEF: Bimanual Manipulation with Asymmetric End Effectors Teleoperated demonstrations are costly to collect and rarely reusable across end-effectors with different kinematics and action spaces. This burden grows in bimanual manipulation, where each end-effector pair may require new data. We present AsymEEF, a framework for executable cross-end-effector demonstration generation and unified bimanual policy learning. Given a small source dataset, AsymEEF transfers demonstrations to heterogeneous combinations of two-, three-, and five-fingered end-effectors without additional teleoperation. Kinematic teacher anchors provide geometric supervision, while sparse real-world X-Calib anchors correct discrepancies in grasp execution. A shared encoder maps wrist poses and actuator states to a morphology-agnostic latent space, and a morphology-conditioned decoder reconstructs target commands. Generated trajectories undergo replay filtering for task-level executability. The representation also supports a unified bimanual visuomotor policy trained across multiple pairs. Across four simulated and six real-world tasks, AsymEEF improves replay success over adapted transfer baselines, achieves a mean replay-valid expansion gain of 16.6 times in simulation, and is evaluated through downstream policy training on real robots. Project website: .

title: One-Shot Calibration via Model Editing
summary: One-Shot Calibration via Model Editing Model editing aims to correct errors in large, pretrained models by replacing model generations with user-provided responses. Existing editors assume a single target answer for each edit. However, many real tasks inherently entail uncertainty, resulting in multiple plausible answers with varying likelihoods in user feedback. Such feedback forms a target distribution to not only correct but also calibrate model generations. We therefore propose SoftEdit, the first model editor to leverage uncertainty in user responses and perform one-shot calibration during editing. To generalize calibration to unseen samples, SoftEdit uses co-plausibility relationships between answers while preserving real distributional shifts, balancing the new distributional generality-locality tradeoff. Across three language models, three vision-language models, and two large datasets, SoftEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance, ultimately showing that uncertainty in user responses enables generalizable calibration of pretrained models beyond single-answer corrections.

title: Memory-Efficient Speculative Decoding with Quantized Draft KV Cache
comment: Accepted at the AXIOM Foundations of Efficient Deep Learning Workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Memory-Efficient Speculative Decoding with Quantized Draft KV Cache Accepted at the AXIOM Foundations of Efficient Deep Learning Workshop at NeurIPS 2026 Speculative decoding reduces generation cost, but it stores two KV caches: one for the target model and one for the draft model. We reduce this extra memory by quantizing the draft cache. The target cache and verifier remain in BF16, so that compression cannot change the target model's final correction rule. We first study how to divide precision between keys and values. A naive per-token quantizer makes keys appear much more sensitive: splitting a 12-bit budget, K8V4 beats K4V8 in acceptance by 10.87pp. However, with grouped per-channel keys, the gap becomes -0.25pp. A controlled Qwen test confirms that changing only the key quantizer can erase or reverse the preferred bit split. Hence, following KIVI, we propose K4V4 quantization with per-channel keys and per-token values. Across six model pairs, our method reduces draft cache memory by 66.20%, and combined memory across both caches by 23.95%. Mean acceptance drops from 57.93% to 57.14%, only 1.36% relative. Overall, quantized draft caches can make speculative decoding more memory efficient; as a predictive principle for efficient AI design, key and value precision must be co-designed with the quantizer layout.

title: Weight-Space Programming Changes How an LLM Uses Python for Computational Biology
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 6 main tables, and 1 supplementary table
summary: Weight-Space Programming Changes How an LLM Uses Python for Computational Biology 16 pages, 3 figures, 6 main tables, and 1 supplementary table Weight-space programming allows a language model to edit another model's weights without gradient-based training. We used Claude Opus 5.5 to edit Qwen3.5-0.8B and investigated how the edits changed its use of Python on computational biology problems. We compared four initial edited checkpoints with the original model on 50 test problems across three test seeds, yielding 600 paired evaluations. Strictly correct answers increased from 44 to 77, and technically correct answers, which included correct final values rejected for formatting, increased from 64 to 100. Repeated Python calls decreased from 1,834 to 1,044. Among the 64 pairs in which only the edited response was technically correct, the original model had already computed the correct value in 36 but did not submit a technically correct final answer. The edited model corrected the computation in 13 of the 64 pairs. With six additional checkpoints on the same 50 problems, technically correct answers rose from 96 to 154 across 900 pairs. We explored three selected problems with ten test seeds for each of ten checkpoints. On the melting-temperature problem, correct Python outputs decreased from 60 to 22 while technically correct final answers increased from 0 to 18. Weight editing changed both the calculations Qwen ran and whether it submitted a correct answer.

title: Language Models Meet Vibration Testing for LEO Constellation Satellites with Calibrated Response Prediction from Few-show Sweeps
summary: Language Models Meet Vibration Testing for LEO Constellation Satellites with Calibrated Response Prediction from Few-show Sweeps Large language models (LLMs) increasingly drive engineering analysis end to end, turning textual records into the inputs of numerical programs, but a plausible and wrong value can pass silently into a decision. We propose deterministic validation gates for LLM-driven engineering analysis, a general paradigm in which a typed configuration produced by LLMs is consumed only after it passes deterministic checks on units, physical consistency, verbatim quotes, agreement between independent models, consistency with measurement exports and the applicability of trained models. The gates target hallucinations from two directions, since quote checking catches fabricated content while agreement between models catches errors of omission that quote checking misses. We instantiate the paradigm on sine vibration acceptance testing for low Earth orbit mega-constellation satellites, where DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Qwen-plus read Chinese test records and extract a configuration of 76 fields. Fact-level F1 ranged from 0.98 to 1.0 on five input variants, with all repairs frozen on development inputs and evaluated on held-out inputs. With all gates, 20 of 20 configurations produced notching results bit for bit identical to the gold run, and all 17 real and injected errors in consumed fields were stopped, of which 16 would have run without gates. Retraining the bound model on a dataset built from an LLM configuration reproduced its results within GPU nondeterminism. We also report a negative result of practical value. Direct LLM curve forecasting only matches linear extrapolation, whereas a small physics-structured network reduces the over-notched bandwidth by 86% to 89% at calibrated coverage c = 0.90, which delineates where direct LLM prediction should give way to a trained model.

title: Same Papers, Different Verdicts: Tracing Version Drift in LLM Peer Review
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures. Results of the registered tests that need the ICLR 2027 decisions will be added after 16 December 2026
summary: Same Papers, Different Verdicts: Tracing Version Drift in LLM Peer Review 19 pages, 5 figures. Results of the registered tests that need the ICLR 2027 decisions will be added after 16 December 2026 Venues and benchmarks read LLM review scores as measurements of a paper, while providers replace their models within months. We audit twenty frontier models from OpenAI, Google and Anthropic on ICLR 2027 submissions while they were under review, with tests registered before the decisions. Between an earlier and a later version of Claude Opus and of Gemini, the share of papers placed on the accept side falls by 52 and 53 percentage points on 183 and 60 randomly drawn submissions, and by 43 to 79 points in six further paired comparisons, with no paper moving up in any of them. Stating a 30% acceptance rate in the prompt leaves a gap of 79 points between the two Opus versions. When score-stripped critiques are swapped between versions, the later critiques alone lower the accept share by 35 points for Opus and 51 for Gemini; for Opus the drop is 35 points under a third-party scorer and 24 after a rewrite that keeps each technical point and removes evaluative wording. On 57 papers, the percentiles of Opus 4.6 and 5.5 correlate at 0.73 while their accept shares differ by 44 points. On 99 to 119 submissions, the self-estimated percentiles of three models correlate with two human reviewers more strongly than a third reviewer does (point estimates 0.17 to 0.21, 95% intervals between -0.04 and +0.42). All twenty models give a 2 or a 3 in 473 of their 475 reviews, against 60 of 72 human reviews. Retrospective tests on decided papers can draw on memory. Claude Opus 5.5 names the true first author of 27 decided ICLR 2026 papers from their titles alone, with no wrong name, and Claude Opus 4.6 accepted all 11 decided papers it said it recognized, against 5 expected. Thresholds on LLM-reviewer scores therefore have to be validated against human decisions for each model version; our tests against the ICLR 2027 decisions follow on 16 December 2026.

title: Newton-PINet: A fast physics-informed neural network with Newton linearization for meta-learning nonlinear PDEs
summary: Newton-PINet: A fast physics-informed neural network with Newton linearization for meta-learning nonlinear PDEs Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Scientific machine learning has opened new avenues for solving parameterized partial differential equations (PDEs), enabling models to learn a family of PDEs and generalize to unseen instances. In this context, data-driven operator learning methods typically require large training datasets, while physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) suffer from difficult optimization and limited generalization, especially for nonlinear PDEs. We propose Newton-PINet, a physics-informed network enhanced by Newton linearization, offering an effective meta-learning framework for nonlinear PDEs. Newton-PINet (i) employs a physics-informed multilayer network with skip connections, where the output-layer weights are solved by least squares; (ii) adopts a two-stage learning strategy that first leverages gradient-based training to learn robust representations from the available training tasks, and then performs gradient-free fine-tuning on the output layer for fast task-specific generalization; and (iii) incorporates a Newton linearization method to speed up the least-squares iteration for nonlinear PDE problems. On a challenging nonlinear reaction-diffusion benchmark, Newton-PINet achieves up to three orders of magnitude lower relative error than recent neural solvers, while using 16x fewer training tasks and over an order of magnitude less training time (about 5 minutes versus several hours). This work advances the meta-learning of PINNs toward data-efficient, fast, and generalizable physics solvers. The code and datasets are publicly available at: .

title: A Geometric Understanding of Denoising Autoencoder with Applications to Image Denoising
summary: A Geometric Understanding of Denoising Autoencoder with Applications to Image Denoising Denoising autoencoders have shown strong empirical performance in recovering clean data from their noisy observations, yet their underlying statistical behavior remains underexplored. In this paper, we study denoising autoencoders under the manifold hypothesis, assuming that clean data are supported on low-dimensional smooth manifolds embedded in a high-dimensional ambient space, while noisy observations are generated by isotropic Gaussian noise. We establish generalization guarantees in three geometric scenarios: a single manifold, a pairwise separated finite union of manifolds, and a finite union of intersecting manifolds. Using local chart representations, partitions of unity, and neural network approximation, we derive upper bounds for the expected squared reconstruction error for denoising autoencoder. In the single-manifold and separated-union scenarios, the error consists of a sample-dependent statistical term of order $n^{-2/(d+2)}\log^4 n$, a residual term of order $d\sigma^2/D$ caused by tangential noise, and an exponentially small tail term associated with failure of the manifold projection. Here $D$ is the data ambient dimension, $d$ is the intrinsic dimension of the clean-data manifold, and $\sigma^2$ is the expected squared noise magnitude. In the scenario of intersecting manifolds, we further identify an additional ambiguity term determined by the probability mass near the intersection neighborhood. Numerical experiments on synthetic manifolds and real image datasets support the predicted sample-size scaling law and illustrate the additional reconstruction ambiguity near manifold intersections.

title: Attacker Diversity Reduction in Adaptive LLM Red Teaming
summary: Attacker Diversity Reduction in Adaptive LLM Red Teaming Reinforcement learning can make automated red-teaming more successful while narrowing the attacks it produces. Co-training an attacker and a defender with group-relative policy optimization (GRPO) has been reported to reduce attacker diversity. This experiment reproduces attack diversity reduction using three runs with a Qwen2.5-14B attacker and a Phi-4-mini defender trained by direct preference optimization (DPO). The attacker receives a success-only reward and uses a length-unbiased loss, bounded updates, warm-up and ratio clipping. The attacker is evaluated on 26 AdvBench behaviors. Training ended after 12 rounds, following a decision based on development checkpoints, so the reported intervals are nominal. Attack Diversity Retention (ADR) compares the within-behavior of the trained attacker spread with the untrained attacker. In order for an attack diversity to be consider as having been reduced, a criterion requires the ADR to be below a 0.75 target with a 95% confidence interval together with continued attacker effectiveness. Therefore, if an attacker narrows its attack vector by 25% consistently its considered less diverse. After 24 attacker and 12 defender LORA-based updates, ADR for the three runs were 0.63, 0.61 and 0.63, respectively. Each run met the criterion at round 12; the earlier checks at rounds 4 and 8 fell short. Despite attacks being less diverse, attack success continued to improve as the attacker was updated after each training run.

title: Minimax Estimation of Discrete Distributions under Hockey-stick Divergence
summary: Minimax Estimation of Discrete Distributions under Hockey-stick Divergence We initiate the study of estimating a discrete distribution with respect to the hockey-stick divergence from independent samples. We provide non-asymptotic upper and lower bounds on the minimax expected loss in terms of the alphabet size, the number of samples, and the divergence parameter. The upper bounds are achieved by add-constant estimators, while the lower bound is derived via a Bayes risk argument. Both upper bounds and lower bounds reveal a transition between polynomial and exponential regimes as the parameters of the problem vary.

title: Cache or Denoise Less? Residual Reuse in a Flow-Matching World Action Model
comment: Honorable Mention at the CoRL 2026 Workshop on Efficient Foundation Models for Real-Time Embodied AI (EEAI). Code and data available at this https URL
summary: Cache or Denoise Less? Residual Reuse in a Flow-Matching World Action Model Honorable Mention at the CoRL 2026 Workshop on Efficient Foundation Models for Real-Time Embodied AI (EEAI). Code and data available at Flow-matching robot policies generate each action chunk through repeated network evaluations, one per denoising step. Cross-cycle caches such as C$^3$ache reuse computation from earlier replanning calls, but whether they beat simply taking fewer steps is unclear. We compare the two in Fast-WAM, a 6B-parameter world action model, on LIBERO-Goal. Two uncached steps keep the success of ten: on all 500 initial states they are non-inferior within two percentage points, for one checkpoint and noise seed. Under PyTorch's default compile mode, they also cut a replanning call on an RTX A6000 from 202 to 92 ms. This leaves little room for caching. A cache that keeps two fresh steps cannot be faster than two uncached steps: every call still encodes the images, runs the video expert and computes those two steps. Caching the first of two steps, refreshed every fourth call, saves at most 11--14% of a call by our cost model. Cached policies are also fragile. Their losses tracked the share of the flow path the cached steps cover: under Fast-WAM's current time shift, C$^3$ache's eight cached steps cover 80% of the path instead of 44%, and the cached policy succeeds on 63% of states against 95% uncached. Resampling the noise on every call cost caches covering 60% or more of the path 14--40 points. These results argue for fewer-step baselines and for testing reuse under the deployed sampler and noise settings. We release our evaluation harness, logs and a checklist.

title: Joint Learning of Factual and Counterfactual Worlds for Causal Prior-data Fitted Networks
summary: Joint Learning of Factual and Counterfactual Worlds for Causal Prior-data Fitted Networks Estimating treatment effects is central to science across many disciplines and requires counterfactual reasoning about alternative worlds. In the real world, however, each unit reveals its outcome only under the factual world. Thus, the factual and counterfactual outcomes can never be jointly learned by any model trained on real data. The problem is therefore tractable only in synthetic settings, where both worlds can be generated. Recent progress on prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) has shown that models pre-trained purely on synthetic data can transfer to real-world prediction. This paradigm has since carried over to causal effect estimation. Despite this fully synthetic setup, existing causal PFNs carry the real-world constraint into their training objective, confining learning to a single world's outcome per unit. The dependence between the two worlds is thereby lost, and the density of the treatment effect relies by default on independence, which is implausible in practice. We therefore propose joint learning, a training setup in which a causal PFN learns the joint distribution of the factual and counterfactual outcomes of each unit. From the joint distribution, we obtain both the response and the individual treatment effect densities, and at inference, we apply optimal transport across units to obtain an approximation of the average treatment effect density. Ours is therefore the first causal PFN approach to provide all three densities together while accounting for the cross-world dependence. We apply joint learning and optimal transport to existing causal PFNs and evaluate it across semi-synthetic, synthetic, and real benchmarks spanning diverse causal scenarios. The jointly trained models significantly improve upon their baselines in point estimation and uncertainty quantification in most settings, indicating that joint learning is a preferable training setup for causal PFNs.

title: Set-based State Estimation for Unknown Dynamical Systems from Noisy Output Data with Probabilistic Guarantees
summary: Set-based State Estimation for Unknown Dynamical Systems from Noisy Output Data with Probabilistic Guarantees We develop a methodology for set-based state estimation from noisy input-output trajectories, without a predefined model structure for the unknown state dynamics or access to training state measurements. We derive a bound on the state set diameter that depends on the sensor map and leverage it as a surrogate to formulate a tractable linear program balancing state set tightness against output trajectory coverage. Combining this certificate with deterministic or probabilistically certified measurement noise sets and leveraging the results from scenario optimization with relaxation, we provide joint a posteriori probabilistic guarantees for state inclusion and state set diameter. Numerical simulations corroborate our developed theoretical guarantees.

title: Found, but Not Fixed : From Software Vulnerability Discovery to Fixes with Iterative LLM Pipelines
summary: Found, but Not Fixed : From Software Vulnerability Discovery to Fixes with Iterative LLM Pipelines Software vulnerabilities persist as a critical threat despite the deployment of sophisticated detection tools and AI assistants. While detection has advanced, the subsequent code repair phase remains a primary bottleneck; manual intervention is inherently slow, costly, and prone to introducing secondary regressions and issues. In this paper, we investigate whether an iterative, LLM-based pipeline can provide a robust solution for the automated repair of vulnerable functions in real-world code. We propose a generalized framework that leverages the reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) through a multi-stage feedback loop. We benchmark this approach against state-of-the-art models, including GPT-4o, GPT-5.1, and Gemini 3 Flash, demonstrating that such a pipeline can achieve high-quality code repair. To support the broader security community, we provide our evaluation framework, fine-tuned weights, and comprehensive experimental dataset on our website:

title: Relax-and-Sparsify Approximation Algorithms for Sparse Ridge Regression
summary: Relax-and-Sparsify Approximation Algorithms for Sparse Ridge Regression This paper studies sparse ridge regression in the low-rank, high-dimensional setting that often arises when data collection is expensive. By exploiting the low-rank structure, we develop approximation algorithms within a relax-and-sparsify framework: solve a convex relaxation and then sparsify its solution to satisfy the original sparsity constraint. Specifically, we establish a tight rank-dependent sparsity bound for the convex relaxation by decomposing its support into two parts. This decomposition in turn motivates two approximation strategies, parameter reduction and binary redistribution, each exploiting a different part. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show that the binary redistribution algorithms outperform the benchmarks in most instances.

title: Where the Error Lives: Separating Lid-Edge and Body-Induced Error in Neural Pressure Prediction for 3D Cavity Flow
summary: Where the Error Lives: Separating Lid-Edge and Body-Induced Error in Neural Pressure Prediction for 3D Cavity Flow 37 pages, 10 figures Can a pressure surrogate score much better globally without better resolving the pressure around immersed bodies? We test this in a three-dimensional lid-driven cavity with an unregularized lid and centered pressure at native $128^3$ resolution. On 60 cases from 12 unseen geometries, with predictions sealed before the CFD truth existed, adding a body-free, Reynolds-conditioned reference correction to the same frozen $64^3$ surrogate lifted to $128^3$ lowers the mean full-volume relative $L_2$ error from 20.6% to 7.5%. In the post hoc regional analysis, the lid-edge junction occupies 1.5% of the fluid but holds 69% of the truth pressure energy and 95% of the uncorrected surrogate's squared error. Interior error changes by just +0.16% relative, and object-local peak error and recall change little on average. Retrospective ablations locate the learned term's contribution in the interior and near the bodies; rebasing on the reference lowers global error further with little change in cohort-mean near-body metrics. Reference-relative body-response error remains about 25% in the interior near-body band. Grid-refinement, lid-regularization and convergence checks delimit the numerical scope. In this benchmark, a large global gain chiefly reflects correction of a shared boundary field, not better resolution of the body response. We recommend reporting regional truth-energy and model-error shares alongside near-body and reference-relative body-response errors.

title: Learning Autoregressive Neural Operators on Solver-Defined Physical Constraint Manifolds
summary: Learning Autoregressive Neural Operators on Solver-Defined Physical Constraint Manifolds Accepted by KDD 2027 Autoregressive neural operators approximate time-dependent PDE solvers by repeatedly composing a learned transition, although the resulting states need not remain feasible under the discrete constraints of the numerical problem. We study this issue for incompressible flow, where each velocity state must satisfy solver-level incompressibility together with prescribed boundary values. We formulate autoregressive operator learning as a map between solver-defined affine feasible sets and introduce PCM-NO, a projected-residual realization of this feasible-transition principle. The neural backbone predicts a candidate state increment, a fixed tangent projection extracts its admissible component, and a metric retraction maps the advanced state to the prescribed feasible set. With exact affine constraint solves, the resulting transition is closed on the feasible set, while an affine identity separates admissible-update parameterization from state-level closure. With approximate solves, tangent-only residuals admit a cumulative upper bound, whereas per-step retraction resets feasibility to the residual achieved by the current solve. Experiments on periodic Navier--Stokes flow and lid-driven cavity flow demonstrate the superiority of PCM-NO in preserving solver-level constraints over long autoregressive rollouts and under parameter, boundary-value, and resolution shifts, while achieving lower rollout errors and better flow-specific diagnostics across both in-distribution and stress settings.

title: Ambiguous Examples Help, But Full Data Wins: Revisiting Dataset Cartography for Extractive Adversarial QA
comment: 37 pages, 30 figures, 20 tables. Accepted to Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EACL 2027. Code: this https URL
summary: Ambiguous Examples Help, But Full Data Wins: Revisiting Dataset Cartography for Extractive Adversarial QA 37 pages, 30 figures, 20 tables. Accepted to Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EACL 2027. Code: Dataset cartography argues that training dynamics can reveal regions of a dataset that matter differently for learning: easy-to-learn examples aid optimization, hard-to-learn examples often expose annotation problems, and ambiguous examples contribute strongly to out-of-distribution generalization. A striking implication of the original work is that a model trained on only 33% ambiguous examples can outperform full-data training on several OOD evaluations, including a QNLI reformulation of SQuAD evaluated on Adversarial SQuAD. We revisit this claim in a stricter setting: open-ended extractive question answering, where models must predict answer spans rather than classify question-sentence pairs. For each encoder family, we compute clean-source SQuAD training dynamics, train on full, random, easy-ranked, ambiguous-ranked, and hard-ranked subsets, and evaluate robustness on adversarial-only AddSent and AddOneSent rows. Ambiguous-ranked 33% subsets beat random 33% subsets on exact-match accuracy in all 14 model-evaluation cells and on F1 in 12/14 cells. However, full-data training beats ambiguous-ranked training in 12/14 exact-match cells and 12/14 F1 cells, with mean full-minus-ambiguous gains of 3.40 EM and 4.10 F1. The most thoroughly replicated ELECTRA-small panel is also the main exception to the ambiguous-over-random F1 gains. These results show that clean-source cartography remains useful for reduced-data selection, but its OOD advantage does not carry over as a general replacement for full-data training in extractive adversarial QA.

title: Tight Sequential Confidence Intervals for Online Kernel Regression
summary: Tight Sequential Confidence Intervals for Online Kernel Regression We characterize, in the worst case over kernels, the sharp minimax width of online confidence intervals for elements of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). This resolves the open problem posed by Vakili et al. (2021) in its original discrete-time form. A learner observes $y_i=f(x_i)+\epsilon_i$ at adaptively chosen points, with $\|f\|_{\mathcal H_k}\le B$ and i.i.d. $R$-sub-Gaussian noise, and reports the interval $|f(x)-\mu_n(x)|\le\rho_n(\delta)\sigma_n(x)$, where $\mu_n$ and $\sigma_n$ are the posterior mean and standard deviation of a surrogate Gaussian process model with regularization parameter $\lambda$. Writing $\rho_n^*(\delta)$ for the minimax confidence width for a fixed kernel, we show that, for the sum of a linear kernel and a periodic Sobolev kernel, all sufficiently large $n$, and all $\delta\in(0,1/4]$, $\rho_n^*(\delta)\asymp B+(R/\lambda)\sqrt{\gamma_n+\log(1/\delta)}$, where $\gamma_n$ is the maximal information gain and grows polynomially in $n$. Building on Lattimore (2023), we construct an adaptive design on a fixed two-dimensional domain for which, under Gaussian noise, the normalized error at a prespecified point is $\Omega(B+(R/\lambda)\sqrt{\gamma_n})$ with constant probability. This rules out the conjectured polylogarithmic width in the worst case over kernels and online designs.

title: Conditional Asset Pricing Transformer
summary: Conditional Asset Pricing Transformer In this paper, we propose a conditional asset pricing transformer (CAP-T) that captures nonlinear interactions among firms through attention to forecast excess returns. In the first stage, a transformer estimates conditional expected returns, and kernel-weighted principal component analysis of its residuals estimates the local factor loading space. Projecting the conditional mean onto this space separates factor risk compensation from conditional mispricing. Then, in the second stage, separate transformers learn these two components, whose predictions are combined to forecast returns. As a result, the proposed framework decomposes returns into conditional mispricing, factor risk compensation, a centered factor component, and an unpredictable innovation. We establish approximation and generalization bounds and characterize how first-stage prediction errors propagate through local factor estimation and component learning, providing statistical guaranties for conditional mispricing, factor loadings, and factor risk premia. Finally, simulations and empirical studies demonstrate the predictive and interpretive benefits of the proposed method.

title: Instructions Before Actions: Prospective and Retrospective Language Supervision for Driving Vision-Language-Action Data
summary: Instructions Before Actions: Prospective and Retrospective Language Supervision for Driving Vision-Language-Action Data Driving vision-language-action (VLA) models can accept navigation instructions, yet predicting a driver's trajectory does not establish that a model follows the instruction. We study how driving-language supervision is collected and evaluated, distinguishing prospective instructions issued before an action from retrospective labels written after observing it. We develop ADVLAT-Engine to synchronize spoken instructions, road-scene video, and vehicle trajectories, and compare three navigation apps on 48 replayed routes. On 87 maneuvers announced by both Google Maps and a passenger, the passenger uses more scene-dependent language. We evaluate four open driving VLAs before and after fine-tuning on prospective navigation-app drives. Fine-tuning reduces passenger-drive trajectory error by 23-59%, but instruction effects remain inconsistent. At real intersections, counterfactual instructions reveal stronger responsiveness: fine-tuned Alpamayo~2 Super gains 31 and 18 accuracy points at 15 and 5~m, while Qwen-Drive follows alternative maneuvers more reliably with a discrete command than with a sentence. We additionally collected retrospective annotations from four people for the driving recordings and describe controlled comparisons of annotation content, timing, and downstream learning; those analyses are pending. Our findings separate maneuver prediction from instruction-following and establish a framework for comparing prospective and retrospective supervision.

title: Safety-Preserving Medical LLM Fine-Tuning via Bilevel Data Selection
summary: Safety-Preserving Medical LLM Fine-Tuning via Bilevel Data Selection As general large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adapted for patient-facing medical applications, improving medical capability while controlling patient-facing risks remains a critical challenge. Large-scale medical instruction data are essential for acquiring domain knowledge through supervised fine-tuning (SFT), but unsafe responses can undermine existing safety alignment. To address this problem, we propose Scalable Bilevel Data Selection (S-BDS) for safety-preserving medical SFT. By controlling selection-weight concentration, S-BDS enables reliable sample ranking over large candidate pools and identifies training examples that improve medical capability while controlling patient-facing risks. We combine clinician-validated safe data and selected data with unscreened medical instruction data for SFT, and jointly evaluate medical capability and patient-facing safety on HealthBench and PatientSafetyBench, respectively. Experiments across Llama and Qwen models show that S-BDS achieves the highest safe rates among all compared methods, outperforming the strongest baselines by 4.64 and 3.00 percentage points, respectively, while maintaining competitive medical capability. Further experiments show that varying the safety-oriented weight during SFT controls the trade-off between medical capability and patient-facing safety.

title: Instrumenting Failure: Scoring Language Model Agents at Every Decision Node in Imperfect-Information Games
comment: Accepted at the Interpreting Agent Behavior (IAB) Workshop, NeurIPS 2026. 26 pages, 6 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Instrumenting Failure: Scoring Language Model Agents at Every Decision Node in Imperfect-Information Games Accepted at the Interpreting Agent Behavior (IAB) Workshop, NeurIPS 2026. 26 pages, 6 figures. Code: Agent evaluations report task success and rarely say what an agent did at each decision. We score every decision node of three 12B to 14B instruct-tuned language models (LMs) playing five zero-sum imperfect-information games against four opponents on eight properties from decision and game theory, five of them against a CFR+ equilibrium reference. At each node, the LM also states a belief about the opponent's hidden state in a separate call. Without memory and at temperature 0, stated beliefs sit 0.250 to 0.288 in total variation distance from the equilibrium posterior, and where the action responds to the state its agreement with that belief exceeds chance by -0.04 to 0.19. The two calls frame the opponent differently, so the result is a behavioural inconsistency and makes no claim about internal beliefs. Under one prompt and greedy decoding, the LM's action never varies with the state in 10 of the 38 cells where the reference varies its own. Memory lowers the constant-action share in 9 of 13 testable ladders at temperature 0; at temperature 0.2 the cells at 1 fall from 16 to 5 of the 46 informative cells, while the belief results hold. A gate withholds, with a stated reason, any belief score the run cannot support, and seven of the eight non-zero defect rates are attributable to the instrument, a representation, or the LMs.

title: MASTA: A Feedback-Scheduled Multi-Agent System for End-to-End Tamarin Modeling and Analysis
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Main Track, poster). 19 pages
summary: MASTA: A Feedback-Scheduled Multi-Agent System for End-to-End Tamarin Modeling and Analysis Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Main Track, poster). 19 pages Tamarin-based formal verification of security protocols requires expert-authored multiset rewriting rules and temporal-logic lemmas. Translating a natural-language protocol description into a complete formal model with an LLM is hard because syntactic, reachability, and property-level errors compound across the multi-step modeling process, and a single agent that both authors and self-evaluates cannot reliably localize them. We present MASTA, a multi-agent system that addresses these difficulties through three innovations. First, an operational--evaluative role decomposition assigns rule modeling to an Architect, property modeling to an Auditor, and pure dispatch to a dedicated Arbiter that holds no authoring duties. Second, the Arbiter implements a Tamarin-anchored scheduler that dispatches the next agent based on the latest verifier verdict and routes problem-tagged fixes through a modification list, with a six-class problem taxonomy and an LLM deduplication check preventing routing deadlock. Third, we construct a benchmark of 10 protocols paired with 139 mutation variants and five fine-grained metrics that jointly assess model correctness ($M_1$--$M_3$) and completeness ($M_4$--$M_5$). On this benchmark, MASTA on Qwen 3.5-plus improves over OpenCode on the same backbone by up to $+0.27$ on individual metrics and ranks first on both the correctness and completeness averages, surpassing Codex (GPT-5.5) and Claude Code (Opus 4.7) despite using a weaker LLM. Ablations on five protocols confirm that removing the Arbiter collapses property and verification scores to zero.

title: SpeCal: Spectral Calibration for Unsupervised RLVR
summary: SpeCal: Spectral Calibration for Unsupervised RLVR Accepted to KDD 2027 Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved the reasoning abilities of large language models, but its dependence on ground-truth answers or external verifiers limits its ability to exploit abundant unlabeled reasoning data. Unsupervised RLVR alleviates this bottleneck by deriving scalar rewards from the model's own rollouts. However, the reliability of such self-generated supervision varies substantially across rollout groups and individual responses, while existing methods construct or refine their rewards mainly from decoded outcomes and reward statistics. These endpoint signals reveal what answers the model produces, but provide limited information about whether the underlying rollout representations form a reliable structure for learning. Our key observation is that hidden-state spectra offer a complementary view of supervision reliability by characterizing both the organization of a rollout group and the support received by each rollout within that group. Based on this observation, we propose SpeCal, a bi-level spectral calibration framework for unsupervised RLVR. At the group level, SpeCal combines spectral mass with a Gaussian band-pass gate over normalized entropy-based effective rank, favoring rollout groups with substantial representation variation whose effective dimensionality lies in a preferred regime. At the rollout level, the same group effective rank determines how many dominant directions are retained in a leave-one-out spectral subspace formed by the remaining rollouts, within which the conditional support of each held-out rollout is measured. The resulting signals calibrate the original reward-induced advantages at the group and rollout levels without redefining the underlying unlabeled reward.

title: IndustrialKnowEval: A Benchmark for Evaluating Multi-Level Industrial Knowledge in LLMs
comment: 26 pages (13 pages of main text and 13 pages of appendix), 11 figures
summary: IndustrialKnowEval: A Benchmark for Evaluating Multi-Level Industrial Knowledge in LLMs 26 pages (13 pages of main text and 13 pages of appendix), 11 figures Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for industrial tasks, yet few benchmarks evaluate their mastery of industrial knowledge across different types of cognitive demand. We introduce IndustrialKnowEval (IndKnow), a benchmark for industrial knowledge and engineering question answering. It contains 43,282 samples covering 21 task types across seven industrial sectors, including aerospace, electric power, and metallurgy, organized into four levels of cognitive demand: memory, comprehension, reasoning, and engineering application. Enterprise-based domain specialists and experienced researchers participate in all stages of dataset construction and quality control. We conduct a series of experiments on 18 representative LLMs, with domain experts deeply involved in the evaluation. Building upon IndKnow, we propose the Industrial Cognitive Capability Gap (ICCG) metric to characterize the performance differential between foundational industrial knowledge and higher-order reasoning and application, and we analyze it alongside absolute performance to provide a more complete view of model capabilities. We anticipate that IndustrialKnowEval will support the benchmarking of LLMs in industrial scenarios and promote the development of robust industrial intelligence. Code is available at:

title: A First Look at System One Decision Models for Malware Detection
summary: A First Look at System One Decision Models for Malware Detection Malware detection needs scores calibrated at a fixed false positive rate (FPR) and decisions an analyst can read: feature-based detectors give the first, large language models (LLMs) on decompiled code the second, through generated text of uncalibrated confidence. System One decision models answer a typed question about a text with a probability over its declared answers in one forward pass. We present the first evaluation of these models for Windows Portable Executable malware detection, analyze how they decide, and propose S1Mal, an ensemble on the typed answers and the embedding of CLM-8B. In an isolated virtual machine, Ghidra and capa decompose each binary, and the host renders the records into a canonical textual state, a digest of headers, imports, MITRE ATT&CK capabilities and strings, optionally with decompiled functions, without class shortcuts. Three readouts score each model on the state: A0, the probability of one verdict question; A1, 32 atomic behavioral questions weighed by gradient-boosted trees; A2, heads on the model's state embedding. S1Mal feeds gradient-boosted trees with the atomic answers and the A2 score of CLM-8B. We evaluate CLM-8B, ten open decision models and two LLMs read through logits on BODMAS temporal splits, SOREL-20M out-of-distribution malware and 14,534 matched benign files. On BODMAS, A0 wastes the static evidence: its area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) spans 0.4025-0.8590 across 13 models. A1 recovers it, raising every model's AUROC by +54.61% on average; A2 lifts CLM-8B by +0.2749 to 0.9943, above a combiner on digest facts (0.9901), and reaches 0.9853-0.9948 on nine open models. S1Mal reaches 0.9946 and detects 93.47% of the malware at a realized FPR of 1.45%, and 59.15% at 0.1% FPR on the test ROC curve, against 46.59% with A2. S1Mal gives analysts calibrated decisions, each with the atomic answers behind it.

title: MemEmo: Evaluating Emotion in Memory Systems
summary: MemEmo: Evaluating Emotion in Memory Systems Memory systems address the challenge of context loss in Large Language Models during prolonged interactions. However, as an essential tool for warm companionship and personalized services, the effectiveness of memory systems in processing affective information remains underexamined. To bridge this gap, we propose an emotion-enhanced memory evaluation benchmark to assess the performance of mainstream and state-of-the-art memory systems in integrating and harnessing emotional information. First, we design a benchmark called \textbf{MemEmo} to assess the affective reasoning and tracking capabilities of memory systems across four dimensions: emotional information extraction, emotional memory updating, emotional memory question-answering, and emotional conflict detection. Second, we construct the \textbf{H}uman-\textbf{L}ike \textbf{M}emory \textbf{E}motion (\textbf{HLME}) dataset to provide an empirical foundation for scrutinizing memory systems. Finally, We evaluate five representative memory systems on the HLME dataset, reporting 11 performance metrics across four dimensions. Experimental results reveal that aggregating scores for all tested memory systems is up to 45\%, far below 100\% scale, exposing a profound disparity between memory system and affective intelligence.

title: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB: An Open and Efficient Small Language Model for Fast Conversational Agents
comment: Animated versions of Figure 3 are available in the blog: this https URL
summary: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB: An Open and Efficient Small Language Model for Fast Conversational Agents Animated versions of Figure 3 are available in the blog: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, an open and efficient small language model further post-trained from Gemma-4-E4B-it and optimized for speed and intelligence per GB of memory used for fast conversational agents. The model carries forward Gemma's strong conversational capabilities and further improves multi-turn tool use, instruction following, and input grounding for fast, local voice/device assistants, interactive personas, and embedded/Edge interfaces. The model combines natural conversation with multi-turn agentic capabilities to power voice/device assistants, interactive characters and robotic/IoT interfaces running on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and RTX/DGX Spark. Experiments on 21 benchmarks show that Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB achieves the highest average accuracy while generating the fewest output tokens in both reasoning and non-reasoning modes, compared with Gemma-4-E4B-it and Qwen3.5-4B. The model is released with a DFlash drafter. With DFlash, Bolt E4B achieves $2.74\times$ the per-user decode speed of inference without speculative decoding at concurrency~1, and $1.21\times$ the generation throughput of Gemma-4-E4B-it with MTP at batch size 1.

title: Auditing World-Model Explanations in Retail Forecasting: Faithfulness, Accuracy and Price Response
summary: Auditing World-Model Explanations in Retail Forecasting: Faithfulness, Accuracy and Price Response Forecasting models that read the price and promotion plan explain each forecast as a baseline, what would sell with nothing planned, plus the lift the plan adds. We test such explanations with eight checks, six with a pass rule fixed before any result, and find that passing them does not make an explanation right. In generated store data with known effects, a world model passes the checks of construction, stability, price direction and agreement with sales and with LightGBM, yet its lifts are 1.33 to 1.40 times the truth when merchants plan into high-demand weeks, and 1.23 to 1.42 times in eight variants of that world. It still picks the right weeks to promote, but stock ordered to its lift is off by 0.44 to 0.48 of the true lift. Its stated response to a lasting regular-price change is 4.7 to 6.5 times the true -0.5, and only a measured cause finds this. On Dominick's, 38 episodes in which a store's regular prices sat apart from its zone peers give a noisy benchmark: a pooled 8-week response of -0.33 (95% interval -0.68 to 0.01). For the final tuned world models of our companion paper on nine data sets, baseline and lift add up under each model's own plan, but a deeper price cut lowers the forecast in 29% to 83% of item-week steps on Dominick's (23% to 80% within prices seen in training), and the world model and LightGBM both state about twice the measured response. Across 703 configurations from the settings searches, checks passed were not related to forecast accuracy (Spearman 0.02, 95% interval -0.02 to 0.05); with no known answer for those versions, this concerns accuracy, while whether an explanation is right is measured only in the generated data.

title: The Cybersecurity Dataset Observatory: Which Data for AI in Cybersecurity?
summary: The Cybersecurity Dataset Observatory: Which Data for AI in Cybersecurity? AI is increasingly used for cybersecurity tasks such as intrusion and malware detection, in enterprise, industrial, vehicular and mobile networks. Its effectiveness depends on data: models need representative network traffic, both to be trained and to be evaluated realistically. Public datasets of cybersecurity network traffic, however, are scattered across laboratory pages, repositories and aggregators, and are continuously released, corrected and withdrawn: 92 of the 234 datasets we catalog were released in 2023 or later. At this pace, surveys that list them are outdated soon after publication, since they describe the field only as it was when they were written. We present the Cybersecurity dataset observatory, a public and continuously updated catalog of cybersecurity datasets based on network traffic. New datasets are added as they are found or submitted, every record is periodically re-checked against its original source, to which it links rather than hosting the data, and every change is recorded in a public change log. This paper documents the first release: we define a traffic-centered scope and a seven-axis taxonomy, and review 234 datasets (204 original captures and 30 derivatives) across 14 domains. The review shows a field that grows quickly but unevenly, where 91 datasets distribute only processed records, a few laboratories produce a large share of the data, and UAV, wireless and V2X networks have little public evidence, while 5G has few real captures. We then relate the catalog to common uses in AI research, outline a procedure for selecting datasets, and discuss benchmark pitfalls and open gaps.

title: Surprise-Gated Memory for Live Speaker Diarization
summary: Surprise-Gated Memory for Live Speaker Diarization 2 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables We transpose the Surprise-Gated Memory recipe, a frozen encoder plus a calibrated novelty signal that gates a one-shot episodic store consolidated by periodic replay, from continual visual learning to live speaker diarization. The moment-to-moment question a streaming diarizer must answer, whether an arriving voice belongs to an already-heard speaker or a new one, is a known-versus-novel decision, exactly the decision the surprise gate is built for. On a frozen fine-tuned DiariZen backbone, our online system SGM-Diar recovers 4.8 of the 9.2 diarization-error points separating a naive online baseline from the offline oracle on AMI-SDM (52%) and 1.9 of 2.3 points on VoxConverse (82%), in the end-of-meeting revisable mode, with calibration frozen on development data and transferred cross-domain without adjustment. These are single-seed runs on three AMI meetings and five VoxConverse sessions, so the ordering of conditions rather than the absolute rates is the result. Beyond error rate, we measure the gate's behaviour directly and find a coherent memory-like profile: one-shot speaker recall at 0.857, a novelty response that habituates as speakers become familiar, re-identification that is invariant to the length of intervening silence, and a false-novelty rate of 0.001. Two ablations reproduce, now on audio, the central prediction of the visual SGM work: a sliding replay window is worse than no replay at all. The memory is strictly intra-meeting and is wiped at the end, and no gradient touches the run-time system. We report SGM-Diar as a proof-of-concept and state its limitations explicitly.

title: PIRanNN: Random-Feature Pricing and Calibration under Jump-Diffusion and Stochastic-Volatility Models
comment: 29 pages, 4 figures, 14 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: PIRanNN: Random-Feature Pricing and Calibration under Jump-Diffusion and Stochastic-Volatility Models 29 pages, 4 figures, 14 tables. Code: We study a random-feature method for pricing and calibrating European options under jump-diffusion (Merton, Kou) and stochastic-volatility (Heston, SABR) models. The network has one hidden layer with a probit activation and fixed random inner weights, so fitting it to the pricing equation, the payoff and the boundary conditions is a single regularised least-squares problem, with no iterative training. For Merton and Kou the jump integral of each feature is explicit, so no quadrature is needed. One factorisation of the least-squares matrix gives the price at every state and time, its Greeks, and the exact derivatives of the prices with respect to the model parameters for gradient-based calibration. For the jump models, subtracting the Black-Scholes price removes the payoff kink and reduces the pricing error by about two orders of magnitude. The method is then about as accurate as a standard Crank-Nicolson finite-difference scheme at the same run time, although a finite-difference scheme that also subtracts the Black-Scholes price is about two orders of magnitude more accurate still. On the test problems of a recent physics-informed neural network study, the method matches that network's accuracy in seconds instead of about half an hour. The calibration experiments show that a solver can fit the quotes and still return wrong parameters when its pricing error is not small compared with the effect of the parameters on the prices: without the subtraction the solver misses the jump parameters by up to 50%, and with it they are recovered to within 3%. For Heston and SABR, used as an applicability study with boundary conditions that need no reference prices, pricing errors are about one percent and the calibrated parameters are within about 15% of the true values.

title: IANN: A Unified Framework for Equivariant InterAtomic Neural Networks with User-Friendly Implementation
comment: 31 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables; Supplementary Information included (49 figures, 11 tables). IANN is MIT-licensed. Code: this https URL - Documentation: this https URL - Curated DFT databases: this https URL - Foundation models: this https URL
summary: IANN: A Unified Framework for Equivariant InterAtomic Neural Networks with User-Friendly Implementation 31 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables; Supplementary Information included (49 figures, 11 tables). IANN is MIT-licensed. Code: - Documentation: - Curated DFT databases: - Foundation models: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) now approach density functional theory (DFT) accuracy at a fraction of its cost, but the practical benefit is limited by software fragmentation: each state-of-the-art architecture is released as a separate codebase, with its own data format, configuration system, training loop and molecular-dynamics interface. Comparing two architectures on the same dataset, or moving a trained model into a production simulation, therefore requires substantial re-engineering. We introduce IANN (InterAtomic Neural Network), an open-source PyTorch framework that reimplements equivariant graph neural networks - PaiNN, NequIP, MACE, Allegro, EquiformerV2, EquiformerV3 and UMA - behind a unified data object, a unified trainer and a single deployment route, so that the architecture is a one-word change in a configuration dictionary. Forces, stresses and virials are obtained for every architecture from one analytic differentiation of the energy with respect to the edge vectors of the atomic graph, exact under periodic boundary conditions. Distributed training is configured automatically from the SLURM, PBS or MPI environment, so the same script runs unchanged from a workstation to a multi-node GPU allocation. Self-describing checkpoints serve directly as ASE calculators, as ensembles reporting uncertainties, or as TorchScript models run inside LAMMPS through bundled C++ pair styles with single- and multi-GPU inference. Trained on a common dataset of millions of structures, the architectures can be compared under identical conditions. We further release PaiNN foundation models trained on 41.9 million curated DFT structures from MPtrj, Alexandria, OMat24, MatPES, OC20, OC22, OC25, MPr2SCAN and MatPESr2SCAN, spanning the PBE, RPBE and r2SCAN functionals. Additionally, IANN provides an agent interface to facilitate integration with autonomous agents.

title: Hermitian Positive Definite Neural Networks for Matrix-CFAR Geometric Signal Detection in Nonhomogeneous Clutter
summary: Hermitian Positive Definite Neural Networks for Matrix-CFAR Geometric Signal Detection in Nonhomogeneous Clutter 11 pages, 9 figures Matrix information geometry (MIG) detectors exploit the Riemannian geometry of Hermitian positive definite (HPD) matrices to achieve robust object detection in nonhomogeneous clutter. The matrix constant false alarm rate (matrix-CFAR) method is a representative MIG detector that relies on the geometric structures with respect to specific metrics. In most cases, computing representative HPD covariance matrices requires numerical methods, typically involving computationally intensive iterative optimization algorithms. Although explicit formulas are available for certain cases, such as the log-Euclidean (LE) mean, they are generally unavailable for many other matrix means and medians. To address this challenge, we propose integrating the Hermitian positive definite neural network (HPDNet) into the matrix-CFAR framework, replacing conventional numerical optimization procedures with a learned, geometry-preserving mapping that directly estimates representative HPD covariance matrices from data. In the simulations, the framework is evaluated for MIG detectors using both means and medians associated with the affine-invariant Riemannian metric, the LE metric, and the Bures--Wasserstein metric, on both simulated compound-Gaussian clutter and real IPIX sea clutter. In both cases, the HPDNet is trained solely on simulated data to assess its applicability to the study of real data. The results show a significant reduction of computational cost in testing, while maintaining detection performance and robustness.

title: EfficientSkill: Learning Skills for Token-Efficient Multi-Turn Agents
