summary: EfficientSkill: Learning Skills for Token-Efficient Multi-Turn Agents Reflective skill optimizers improve multi-turn LLM agents by revising instructions from failed and successful rollouts, yet accumulating edge-case rules bloats prompts, inflates token use, and pushes agents into long, error-prone loops. We introduce EfficientSkill, a two-step framework that first discovers a reliable skill without token penalties, and then warm-starts accuracy-guarded pruning from that skill to compress instructions, bound agent turns, and offload reusable code into workspace utilities with zero implementation prompt cost. Across four frontier, mid-tier, and open-weight models on MATH-500, ALFWorld, and SpreadsheetBench, EfficientSkill cuts output tokens over unconstrained EvoSkill on 11 of 12 configurations (by up to 80%) while raising mean accuracy on every benchmark, including +14.3 and +17.5 percentage-point gains on SpreadsheetBench with Gemini 3.8 Flash and Grok 4.1 Fast by replacing stalled loops with compact workflows. By shrinking both generated tokens and replayed history, EfficientSkill lowers total token usage and serving cost across every evaluated configuration, with or without full-prefix KV caching.

title: ProTTS: End-to-End Prominence-aware Natural and Controllable Text-to-Speech via Automatic Word Stress Discovery
summary: ProTTS: End-to-End Prominence-aware Natural and Controllable Text-to-Speech via Automatic Word Stress Discovery Natural speech conveys meaning not only through words, but also through the prominence on a few words. Yet most text-to-speech (TTS) systems remain prominence-unaware, existing prominence-aware TTS require external stress annotations, while unsupervised stress detectors operate in isolation, disconnected from synthesis. This creates a fundamental gap no existing system can automatically discover where stress should be placed, realize it as natural-sounding prosody, and offer user control over emphasis placement, all within a single model. To circumvent this, we propose ProTTS, a unified framework where stress detection emerges from the TTS model itself and, in turn, guides it to synthesize more natural and controllable speech. We incorporate a clustering head into the variance adaptor of FastSpeech_2 that discovers word stress directly from aggregated prosodic features. The discovered stress then drives emphasis variance predictors that modify pitch, energy, and duration for stressed words. The framework is trained end-to-end: TTS reconstruction and clustering losses jointly shape a stress-discriminative feature space without requiring stress labels at any stage. At inference, the same architecture also supports user-controllable emphasis by accepting a custom stress mask. We evaluate ProTTS on ISLE (non-native), LibriTTS, VCTK (native training), and three evaluation benchmarks (Tatoeba, TinyStress-15k, EmphAssess). Listeners prefer ProTTS over the baseline with a MOS of 3.96 vs. 3.12 and 83.5% preference rate. For stress detection, ProTTS achieves 0.839/0.861 F1 on ISLE (German/Italian L2), outperforming unsupervised (0.70) and supervised (0.82) baselines, and 0.933 F1 in zero-shot transfer to Tatoeba.

title: Passable for Whom? Few-Shot Personal Calibration of Sidewalk Accessibility Perception
summary: Passable for Whom? Few-Shot Personal Calibration of Sidewalk Accessibility Perception Whether a sidewalk is passable depends on who is trying to pass: people who use the same mobility aid disagree about the same image, so one label per scene, or per aid, is wrong for many of them. We introduce few-shot personal accessibility perception: from K answers of a person never seen before, predict their judgment of sidewalk scenes never seen before. PassCal separates a shared description of the scene from the person's interpretation of it. The description comes from the internal state of a frozen vision-language model (VLM) and from barrier type, severity and context properties predicted by a detector trained on 14.9k public audits; the interpretation, a calibration of the person's response style and a weighting of the properties, is fit from their answers. On 8,883 judgments in which each of 135 verified mobility-aid users rated the same 50 sidewalk scenes, with people and scenes both held out, eight answers lower the Brier score from 0.550 to 0.479. The same VLM prompted with those answers reaches 0.562, and the same calibration without the scene 0.521. Conformal risk control turns predictions into passable, blocked or "depends on you" statements with a bounded expected rate of wrong statements over people; at 5%, eight answers raise the share of decisive scenes from 27% to 42%. Audit-supervised properties improve all sixteen vision and VLM encoders we test and outperform attributes from a sidewalk navigation VLM.

title: Grounding Language Models in Speech Does Not Fix "AI Flavor": Calibrated LLM Judges, Goodhart Traps, and a Preference-Tuning Fix
comment: 11 pages, 2 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Grounding Language Models in Speech Does Not Fix "AI Flavor": Calibrated LLM Judges, Goodhart Traps, and a Preference-Tuning Fix 11 pages, 2 tables. Code and data: Chinese outputs of large language models carry a perceptible "AI flavor": formulaic sentence frames, stacked written-register connectives, repetition loops, and layout leakage. A popular hypothesis blames text-only training for the missing inner-speech layer of human writing; injecting speech or prosody signals should therefore reduce it. We test it with controlled interventions on a 0.6B model; all three fail: (i) phoneme-interleaved continued pretraining yields no spokenness gain under text-matched controls while raising repetition (+0.13 [+0.03, +0.23]); (ii) prosody-plan conditional generation reaches an adherence of only 0.257 against a pre-registered 0.50 gate; (iii) a rule-based reward built on TTS prosody-feature distance is imperceptible in double-blind evaluation by both humans (8/16) and a calibrated LLM judge (9/16). A root cause is evaluation: single-rater blind evaluation at n~20 only detects extreme (>=85%) preferences. We therefore build a calibrated LLM-judge protocol: the judge passes catch trials on known-answer pairs (16/16; single-text 22/24, same-topic pairs 24/24, versus 0.75 for the human rater), then annotates with two independent judges under A/B swapping, counting disagreement as a tie. Using the judge's agree labels directly as DPO pairs (no reward model), we obtain the first positive result: held-out blind win rate 0.833 [0.699, 0.972], repetition 0.114 to 0.000, unchanged MMLU. We further identify a Goodhart channel: the judge's length preference transduces into output-length collapse via pairwise DPO (median 75 chars vs a 300-char prompt); an SFT-anchor repairs it (w is a style knob: w=0.1 preserves gains, w=0.3 does not). Scaling preference data from 89 to 240 pairs yields no additional judge-visible gain. We release RA-Eval v0.1: a three-layer Chinese AI-flavor evaluation framework with 382 judge-annotated preference pairs.

title: NoLBERT-Calls: Reading Earnings Calls Without Hindsight
summary: NoLBERT-Calls: Reading Earnings Calls Without Hindsight Language models are now a standard tool for measuring what managers say on earnings calls, but the encoders behind these measures were usually pretrained on text from the same years a backtest covers. Holding out a test period does not remove that hindsight, because it sits in the features. We adapt NoLBERT, an encoder pretrained only on text published between 1976 and 1995, to earnings calls without letting it read anything dated after 31 December 2023. The calls supply the training signal themselves: every analyst question is followed by management's answer, and the model learns to pick that answer out from the other answers of the same call. We test on every US call from January 2025 to October 2026 (20,323 calls, 254,575 questions) and make every modeling choice on calls from 2024. The adapted model, NoLBERT-Calls-2023, ranks the true answer first for 78.0% of questions (95% interval 77.8-78.2; chance 8.0%), against 26.3% before adaptation. It is 1.0 point ahead of a call-adapted ChronoBERT, 3.4 points ahead of a call-adapted FinBERT, and 18.7 and 19.8 points ahead of the best off-the-shelf retriever and BM25. A year-by-year test over 2013-2026 finds no look-ahead premium: relative to a model adapted only through 2012, the released model does no better on the years it was trained on than on years it never saw. The price of the cutoff is compute: under one shared 150-minute recipe NoLBERT adapts least well of four encoders, and its lead comes from a longer, staged adaptation of about 13 GPU-hours.

title: ProcReverser: Multi-Agent Black-Box Microarchitectural Reverse Engineering for Processor Vulnerability Analysis
summary: ProcReverser: Multi-Agent Black-Box Microarchitectural Reverse Engineering for Processor Vulnerability Analysis When processor implementation details are unavailable, black-box microarchitectural reverse engineering helps security researchers identify hardware conditions related to security vulnerabilities. However, this process requires substantial manual effort to design experiments, develop test programs, and analyze results for each processor. We present ProcReverser, a multi-agent system that automates this process. ProcReverser uses execution feedback to improve experimental plans and test programs and identifies microarchitectural properties from measurements. We develop a comprehensive suite of property identification tasks focused on hardware mechanisms relevant to Spectre-class attacks, covering speculative execution, branch prediction, memory dependence, and cache behavior. We evaluate ProcReverser on the XuanTie C910, the gem5 RISC-V O3 CPU model, and the SiFive P550. ProcReverser achieves Pass@1 and Pass@5 scores of 81.3% and 93.8%, respectively, on C910, and 83.0% and 100.0% on gem5 O3. On the SiFive P550, ProcReverser further characterizes microarchitectural properties covered by the proposed task suite. These findings highlight the potential of automated microarchitectural reverse engineering to support processor vulnerability analysis and defense evaluation.

title: Evidence Diet: When Graph Evidence Helps LLMs Rank Competing Candidates
summary: Evidence Diet: When Graph Evidence Helps LLMs Rank Competing Candidates When several candidates have graph support, does it matter which candidate receives which supporter and path counts? We study how LLM rankers use collaborative evidence on Amazon Books and MovieTV. Swapping user-level evidence degrades ranking, while matched item substitutions have little effect. On fixed clean-trained checkpoints, unrelated catalog text lowers Hit@1 from 44.77% to 38.70%, with 99.9% of rankings still valid. Across all three paired seeds, the NDCG@5 difference between count and path prompts was larger after count training than after path training. Degree matching preserves target paths while giving more rivals support. Across the full degree-matched development pools, adding candidate-level graph records to history improves NDCG@5 by 2.28 points on Books and 2.54 on MovieTV. When the target and a rival both have support, path- and count-trained rankers benefit from retaining counts. On these development queries, adding counts numerically to history scores outperforms presenting them as text. For count-trained rankers, exchanging intact count pairs among supported candidates preserves support and token length, yet lowers NDCG@5 by 4.06 points on 141 Books queries and 3.26 on 104 MovieTV queries. A frozen evaluation on 274 previously unused Books users with supported targets and rivals confirms the attribution effect: correct assignment improves pairwise accuracy by 6.07 percentage points (95% CI [4.18, 8.00]).

title: EDITORS Know Your Style! Editing LoRA Subspaces for Stylistic Attribution and Imitation
summary: EDITORS Know Your Style! Editing LoRA Subspaces for Stylistic Attribution and Imitation Disentangling writing style from semantic content is a fundamental challenge in literary text modeling. Style-content entanglement causes models to rely on semantic content for authorship attribution (AA) tasks and memorize author-specific content for style imitation (SI) tasks. We propose EDITORS (EditingLoRA Subspaces), a diagnose-then-deflate framework that adapts pretrained large language models and prioritizes stylistic features, making it effective for both AA and SI tasks. EDITORS first trains a diagnostic LoRA adapter using style-neutral statements derived from the training corpus to identify a content-oriented subspace. It then trains the final style adapter under activation-space deflation that projects input activations away from the identified content-oriented directions. We empirically demonstrate that EDITORS is effective. On three AA benchmarks spanning literature, social media, and news, EDITORS achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, outperforming the strongest existing baseline by up to 29%. On SI, EDITORS generates stylistically faithful and diverse passages, outperforming baselines in achieving style similarity while adhering to content specifications.

title: MolReps: Taking SELFIES, Making SMILES, Teaching LLMs
summary: MolReps: Taking SELFIES, Making SMILES, Teaching LLMs The same molecule can be expressed in multiple, syntactically distinct representations, yet it remains unclear whether large language models (LLMs) can recognize and relate these equivalent encodings. We introduce MolReps, a pipeline that generates 9,600 question-answer pairs across ten representations for conversion, normalization, and 2D structure recognition. Post-training on MolReps improves text-only and multimodal models, MolQwen3-4B-Instruct (MQ3-4B-I) and MolQwen3-VL-4B-Instruct (MQ3-VL-4B-I), from $4.01\%$ to $75.13\%$ and from $7.11\%$ to $73.14\%$ (InChIKey match) on the molecule-overlap test set, respectively. On the molecule-disjoint test set, post-training increased validity from $20.35\%$ to $58.12\%$ for MQ3-4B-I and from $17.19\%$ to $59.34\%$ for MQ3-VL-4B-I. However, InChIKey match remained low, decreasing from $3.86\%$ to $3.09\%$ and from $6.44\%$ to $2.29\%$, respectively. Furthermore, the resulting models achieve a relative $27.84\%$ improvement in average over their base model on MolRepBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating molecular property prediction. These results show the effectiveness of targeted post-training for enhancing molecular representation understanding and its potential to improve downstream molecular tasks.

title: Scenario-Based Risk Certificates for Multi-Property Vulnerability Discovery in Parametric MDPs
summary: Scenario-Based Risk Certificates for Multi-Property Vulnerability Discovery in Parametric MDPs VMCAI 2027 Safety-critical systems such as network protocols and distributed algorithms depend on environmental parameters whose exact values are uncertain. Parametric Markov decision processes (pMDPs) model such systems by making transition probabilities symbolic functions of the parameters. For a single quantitative requirement, parametric verification asks which parameter valuations satisfy the requirement. In practice, however, engineers often monitor several safety and performance requirements at once, and one valuation may make several requirements vulnerable simultaneously. In this paper we study multi-property vulnerability discovery under requirement-wise semantics: given a pMDP and M quantitative requirements, we construct candidate regions of the parameter space that may contain violations, and study budgets for random testing under a specified parameter distribution. To solve this, we adopt a two-layered approach in which the scenario-approximation layer provides PAC guarantees on identifying conservative vulnerability regions for each requirement while the testing layer treats random parameter exploration as coverage of overlapping regions and yields a stopping certificate computed from the marginal region masses alone; a composition theorem then bounds the expected non-discovery score by the scenario approximation error plus the testing risk from the two layers. For confirmed discoveries, candidate hits are checked by model checking and budgets use independently certified discovery probabilities. Experiment evaluate these certificates using empirical surrogates and independent confidence bounds.

title: Re-Reading Is Not Free: Token Traces and Cache-Aware Energy Estimation for LLM Agents in Software Engineering
summary: Re-Reading Is Not Free: Token Traces and Cache-Aware Energy Estimation for LLM Agents in Software Engineering 21 pages, 13 figures, 18 tables As large language models (LLMs) evolve from conversational assistants into autonomous agents embedded in software development workflows, estimating their environmental footprint requires moving beyond conventional token-based accounting. Existing energy estimators focus on isolated request-response interactions, overlooking the repeated processing of accumulated context, cache reuse, and work delegated to subagents. We analyze nearly one billion tokens collected across 42 sessions and 752 task episodes over ten weeks of real-world AI-assisted software development. Cached-context reads make up 94.8% of all API-reported tokens, while uncached input accounts for only 0.017%; for every generated token, approximately 260 cached tokens are read. Context grows 5.3-fold over a session compared with 1.4-fold within individual tasks. To quantify the energy implications, we extend an existing analytical inference-energy model to account for cached-context processing, yielding a cache-aware hybrid estimator. It estimates approximately 250 kWh for the workload, compared with approximately 10 kWh from the output-based estimator EcoLogits, a 25-fold difference largely driven by cached-context reads. Neither estimator has been validated on long cached contexts, but no modeling assumption we varied closes the gap. Starting each task from a fresh context would lower our estimate by about 60%. We also find that parent-session logs report only a subagent's final internal call, undercounting delegated tokens by a factor of ten; for this workload the correction changes the energy estimate by about 5%, but token-volume studies are fully exposed to it. Our findings expose a substantial gap between how current energy estimators and agentic workloads treat context, highlighting the need for workflow-level energy accounting that captures context accumulation, cache reuse, and delegated execution.

title: Auditing a Moving Target: Evidence Anchoring and the Expiry of Fairness Audits of Provider-Served Language Models
summary: Auditing a Moving Target: Evidence Anchoring and the Expiry of Fairness Audits of Provider-Served Language Models Organizations increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for decisions about people, such as hiring, investment and employee evaluation, and rely on them over long periods of time. Fairness audits of such systems, however, are conducted only once. We examine how the biases of LLMs change over time. In a venture screening setting, models from five providers decided whether and how much to invest in startups whose founders differed only in gender, origin and university. We repeated this audit three times over 13 months (248,400 API calls). Study 1 shows that the same model, called under the same identifier one year later, displayed a significantly different bias pattern. Study 2 shows that the successors of retired models carried the same bias as their predecessors, but in a significantly different size and form. Study 3 shows that the bias does not depend on the industry of the startup. A document analysis further shows that providers change and retire models at their discretion, with notice periods of zero to six months. Drawing on these findings, we develop a theory of evidence anchoring. We theorize that bias resides in the model class and persists, whereas audit evidence is anchored to a single model and expires when the provider decides. We derive policy advice for organizations and regulators, namely audits of model classes instead of single models, a version record for every model response, and re-audits triggered by model changes.

title: Experience Rot: Experienced Agents Fail Where Novices Succeed
summary: Experience Rot: Experienced Agents Fail Where Novices Succeed Agents are increasingly built to learn from experience: they keep conversation histories, memory files, retrieved notes and skills, and reuse what worked before. We show that this experience turns against them when their tools change silently. We test a range of models with tools defined as in the Model Context Protocol (MCP). After a silent change, experienced agents fail on most tasks, while agents new to the task mostly succeed. We call this failure Experience Rot. Experienced agents copy their earlier call instead of checking the current interface, even when the tool definition shows the change. Then they report success. When the documentation is incomplete, experience is what makes agents succeed. After a change, the same experience leaves them worse off than no experience at all. The failure appears in every form of memory we test and grows with the amount of experience. Simple remedies fall short: announcing the update barely helps, and pointing the agent to the documentation fails whenever the documentation does not spell out the answer.

title: ReAccess: Look Once, Stay Focused with Efficient Test Time Memory
summary: ReAccess: Look Once, Stay Focused with Efficient Test Time Memory Project Page: Despite recent advances, vision-language models (VLMs) still struggle with fine-grained visual understanding, often failing to effectively utilize critical evidence already encoded in their visual representations. Existing approaches address this limitation through repeated visual processing or explicit reasoning, introducing substantial computational overhead. In this paper, we propose ReAccess, a lightweight framework that preserves and reuses question-relevant visual evidence through compact associative memory. Constructed during a single visual prefill, the memory supports progressive evidence retrieval that steers both attention queries and hidden representations, enabling effective visual grounding without repeated image encoding or explicit reasoning traces. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements in both general visual understanding and fine-grained perception, while achieving substantially faster inference than existing reasoning-intensive approaches, demonstrating a promising path to efficient multimodal reasoning.

title: vividRGB: Various visual cue detection in RGB photographs with forced focused attention
comment: 32 pages including supplementary material; 6 numbered figures and a graphical summary
summary: vividRGB: Various visual cue detection in RGB photographs with forced focused attention 32 pages including supplementary material; 6 numbered figures and a graphical summary Natural photographs contain dense, overlapping structures that can be weakly expressed in feature maps from whole-image vision encoders. We introduce forced focused attention (FFA) and its Python implementation, vividRGB. FFA is an encoder-agnostic inference-time procedure that applies a frozen encoder to enlarged, overlapping local crops, averages inverse-aligned reflections, and reconstructs a feature field in source coordinates. We evaluate 50 high-resolution photographs from grassland vegetation, fungal networks, airborne forests, coral reefs, and phytoplankton microscopy, using DINOv3 ViT-B/16. Across the five domains, FFA at 5% or 10% focus produces higher mean RGB-edge boundary F1 than direct DINOv3 encoding and automatic SAM3 masks. Domain means range from 0.244 to 0.596 for FFA, versus 0.028-0.076 for direct DINOv3 and 0.020-0.090 for SAM3. Qualitative feature maps also show finer appearance structure. These results concern RGB-edge preservation rather than verified species, traits, or biological segmentation. Narrower focus generally improves boundary preservation, while extraction time and GPU energy use increase sharply and gains diminish at finer settings. FFA may be useful for relatively small, high-resolution ecological image collections where dense visual cues matter. The alpha release vividRGB 0.1.0 and versioned research resources support reproducible cue inspection.

title: Sharp Gaussian Approximation for Q-Learning
summary: Sharp Gaussian Approximation for Q-Learning Gaussian approximation provides a foundation for online statistical inference in reinforcement learning. We establish sharp non-asymptotic Gaussian approximation rates in Wasserstein distance for asynchronous Q-learning with Polyak-Ruppert averaging. We prove an upper bound of $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/4})$, where $n$ is the number of iterations, together with a matching lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Q-learning is more challenging to analyze than linear stochastic approximation due to the nonlinearity of the Bellman operator. Asynchronous updates introduce further challenges due to Markovian noise. Our analysis separates the errors from Bellman nonlinearity, Markovian noise, and the finite-sample covariance discrepancy. In particular, we show that Markovian noise induces an unavoidable bias even when the Bellman operator is linear. The trade-off between this bias and the covariance discrepancy determines the convergence rate. We further extend our analysis to the synchronous setting and establish a sharp rate of $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/2})$.

title: Local Order Matters: A Lightweight CPU-Trainable CNN for Website Fingerprinting on Defended Tor Traffic
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure. Conference paper submitted to the 11th International Conference on Computer and Information Processing Technology (ISCIPT 2026)
summary: Local Order Matters: A Lightweight CPU-Trainable CNN for Website Fingerprinting on Defended Tor Traffic 5 pages, 1 figure. Conference paper submitted to the 11th International Conference on Computer and Information Processing Technology (ISCIPT 2026) Website fingerprinting (WF) attacks let a passive adversary infer which site a Tor user visits from the encrypted cell sequence. On undefended traffic, hand-crafted-feature attacks are already near-ceiling, so deep learning offers only a marginal advantage there. We show that the decisive regime is defended traffic: against the FRONT padding defense, which injects dummy cells that corrupt the volume and count features feature attacks rely on, a compact 95,103-parameter 1-D convolutional network trained on the raw cell-direction sequence, on CPU only, stays robust while three implemented direction-only feature baselines degrade. On the closed-world WFlib FRONT set (95 sites), our model reaches 54.2% top-1 accuracy versus 38.5% for the strongest implemented feature baseline (k-FP-style RF), a gain of 15.7 percentage points (3 seeds; seed-0 paired-bootstrap 95% CI [+14.5, +17.0] pp on per-trace correctness, excluding zero). On undefended traffic the CNN reaches 94.1% versus 92.3% for k-FP-style RF. A controlled order-ablation permutes only nonzero traffic cells within each trace, preserving direction counts, retained length, and trailing zero-padding positions while destroying traffic order. This collapses the CNN below every feature baseline (from 54.2% to 7.6%, a 46.6 pp drop), showing that the model depends strongly on order-derived information under FRONT.

title: Max-Min Throughput in RSMA-Aided SWIPT for Sustainable Internet of Underground Things: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach
summary: Max-Min Throughput in RSMA-Aided SWIPT for Sustainable Internet of Underground Things: A Deep Reinforcement Learning Approach 15 pages, 7 figures, and 3 tables Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-enabled wireless-powered underground sensor networks (WPUSNs) allow underground devices (UDs) to harvest radio-frequency energy from a UAV via wireless energy transfer (WET) techniques, enabling sustainable Internet of underground things (IoUT) applications. This paper integrates rate-splitting multiple access (RSMA)-aided simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT) into UAV-enabled WPUSNs to deliver information and energy to UDs. Within this framework, we investigate a max-min fairness problem that jointly optimizes the UAV transmit power, power allocation and message splitting, power-splitting ratios, and time allocation, aiming to maximize the minimum uplink throughput across UDs subject to per-UD downlink throughput requirements and a UAV energy-consumption constraint. To address this non-convex problem under dynamic underground environments, we develop an off-policy deep reinforcement learning approach based on the primal-dual truncated quantile critics (PD-TQC), where a TQC-based reward critic evaluates the fairness objective, cost critics estimate constraint costs, and an actor learns the resource-control policy with adaptive dual-variable updates. Simulations using in-situ soil volumetric water content measurements from a center-pivot irrigation farm demonstrate that PD-TQC achieves the highest annual average minimum uplink throughput compared with four benchmarks while satisfying the per-frame constraints in over 96% of the evaluated frames, and that this throughput advantage is preserved under different Rician factors, numbers of UDs, and downlink throughput thresholds.

title: Interactive Structured Environment Scaling for Large Language Model Agentic Reasoning
summary: Interactive Structured Environment Scaling for Large Language Model Agentic Reasoning Reinforcement learning via environmental interaction is a cornerstone post-training paradigm for evolving large language models into autonomous agents capable of multi-turn tool use and exploration. Because the environment defines what the policy observes and how actions are verified, its structure directly bounds the capabilities an agent can acquire. Yet existing structured and retrieval environments rely on upstream pre-filtering---extracting a compact subgraph around the gold answer or retrieving fixed passages before the policy acts. We show that such pre-filtering introduces a fundamental measurement confound: because per-question subgraphs enclose ground-truth paths, they compress the candidate space by orders of magnitude and leak answer locations via local topology, allowing a question-blind degree heuristic to surface gold answers far above chance. To restore path selection, candidate pruning, and optimal stopping as genuine policy decisions, we propose RISE (Interactive Structured Environment), which transitions structured reinforcement learning from static subgraphs to full-scale interactive databases along two coupled axes. First, Decision-Space Scaling exposes the unpruned knowledge graph via a five-stage graph-agnostic typed intent adapter under a bounded call budget and a multiplicative grounding reward gate. Second, Learning-Frontier Scaling overcomes within-group variance collapse under group-normalized objectives by uniting model-independent structural tier progression with a self-evolving competence-frontier bandit. Across nineteen benchmarks and three model backbones, RISE substantially advances in-domain and unseen-schema knowledge-graph reasoning, transfers zero-shot to open-domain passage retrieval, and significantly enhances out-of-domain mathematical and logical deduction.

title: First-order smoothed exact-penalty methods for equality-constrained regularized nonconvex optimization
summary: First-order smoothed exact-penalty methods for equality-constrained regularized nonconvex optimization We consider regularized nonconvex optimization over a closed convex set $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$, which involves a convex nonsmooth regularizer $r$ in the objective and $n$ smooth equality constraints. To find a near-KKT point of the problem, we propose a prox-linear first-order method, named as SEPi-Prox, based on a smoothed exact-penalty formulation. At each outer iteration of SEPi-Prox, a strongly convex prox-linear subproblem is formed and solved inexactly to a sufficient accuracy. Under a local non-singularity condition that is weaker than some other commonly used regularity conditions or constraint qualifications, SEPi-Prox finds an $\epsilon$-KKT point within $O(\epsilon^{-2})$ first-order oracle calls, matching the lower bound for unconstrained smooth nonconvex optimization. We employ Nesterov's accelerated proximal-gradient method (APG) and a dual cutting-plane method (DCP) for the prox-linear subproblems. Let $\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{FO}}$ and $\mathcal{C}_r$ denote the numbers of arithmetic operations of evaluating one first-order oracle and one proximal mapping of $r$ over $\mathcal{X}$, respectively. Then SEPi-Prox requires $\widetilde{O}(\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{FO}}\epsilon^{-2} + (dn + \mathcal{C}_r)\epsilon^{-5/2})$ and $\widetilde{O}((\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{FO}} + dn^2 + n\mathcal{C}_r + n^{3.373})\epsilon^{-2})$ total arithmetic operations to produce an $\epsilon$-KKT point, respectively by using APG and DCP as the subsolver. The latter result is preferable when $n$ is small and nearly matches the optimal dependence on $\epsilon$. Numerical experiments on instances of the multi-class Neyman-Pearson classification demonstrate the efficiency of SEPi-Prox with both subsolvers.

title: Illusion of Explainability: A Sanity Check for Spectral Band Attribution in Satellite Time-Series Crop Classification
comment: Accepted at the 4th Computer Vision for Earth Observation (CV4EO) Workshop at WACV 2027
summary: Illusion of Explainability: A Sanity Check for Spectral Band Attribution in Satellite Time-Series Crop Classification Accepted at the 4th Computer Vision for Earth Observation (CV4EO) Workshop at WACV 2027 Attribution methods are commonly validated through convergence across methods and consistency with domain knowledge, yet neither criterion establishes whether identified features are necessary for a task. This limitation is particularly relevant in multispectral remote sensing, where overlapping spectral information makes individual bands potentially substitutable. We investigate this gap in crop-type classification using GradientSHAP, Shapley sampling, and Occlusion on a U-TAE segmentation model trained on Sentinel-2 time series from the PASTIS benchmark. All three methods identify vegetation-sensitive spectral regions consistent with domain knowledge, while Shapley and Occlusion exhibit strong ordering sensitivity in deletion and insertion tests. However, these properties do not reliably predict retraining performance. Aggregate attribution consensus masks substantial per-class disagreement, with pairwise mean Spearman correlations ranging from 0.09 to 0.79. Models retrained from scratch using the five lowest-ranked bands perform comparably to or better than those using the five highest-ranked bands. Furthermore, attribution rankings from an independently trained model with identical configuration and seed identify a different top-five subset that yields better retraining performance. Analysis of all 252 five-band subsets reveals consistently low effective dimensionality (1.35 to 2.62), suggesting substantial spectral redundancy. These findings demonstrate that plausible and apparently faithful attribution rankings do not necessarily identify task-relevant bands for improved retrained performance, highlighting the limitations of band-level feature attribution in spectrally redundant input spaces.

title: Dynamic Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Networks with Nested Clustered Optimization for Multi-Asset Portfolios
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. Replication package and dataset available at this https URL
summary: Dynamic Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Networks with Nested Clustered Optimization for Multi-Asset Portfolios 10 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. Replication package and dataset available at Nested Clustered Optimization (NCO) insulates asset allocation from Markowitz covariance ill-conditioning. However, classical tree clustering relies on static pairwise Pearson correlation, failing to capture time-varying, asymmetric downside risk contagion across multi-asset markets. We propose a unified deep graph machine learning architecture: Dynamic Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Networks with Nested Clustered Optimization (ST-GAT-NCO) for multi-asset tactical allocation. The framework extracts temporal momentum and downside risk dynamics via causal dilated 1D-convolutions, then deploys a multi-head Graph Attention Network (GAT) over dynamic market topologies to learn latent spatial node representations. These learned embeddings define an angular metric distance space that guides two-stage downside NCO optimization under institutional constraints and turnover smoothing. Evaluated over a 73-month non-anticipative walk-forward out-of-sample window (January 2020 to January 2026) across 13 global asset classes net of 10 bps transaction costs, ST-GAT-NCO achieves a 5.32% CAGR and 37.06% cumulative net return, delivering an excess Sharpe ratio of 0.30 and a Sortino ratio of 0.48. This substantially outperforms classical Minimum Variance (3.68% CAGR, 0.08 Sharpe), Hierarchical Risk Parity (2.65% CAGR), and Plain Symmetric NCO (4.11% CAGR, 0.15 Sharpe), while restricting maximum drawdown to -13.07% (versus -19.44% for Equal-Weight and -16.36% for Downside NCO) under a controlled one-way turnover of 15.31%/month. Regime analysis confirms active capital preservation across the 2020 COVID-19 crash, 2022 monetary tightening, and 2023-2026 disinflation rallies.

title: CoSyDelay: Cognitive Symbolic Regression for Traffic Delay Estimation
summary: CoSyDelay: Cognitive Symbolic Regression for Traffic Delay Estimation Trustworthy estimation of traffic delays at signalized intersections is critical for modern transportation systems, as it supports proactive traffic control for congestion mitigation. Existing analytical methods often rely on idealized assumptions that limit their accuracy under complex traffic conditions, whereas data-driven methods may achieve strong estimation performance but usually lack transparent structures, which reduces confidence in their practical application. To address these limitations, we propose CoSyDelay, a cognitive symbolic regression (SR) framework for automatically deriving explicit and physically consistent empirical delay estimation expressions (DEEs). Specifically, CoSyDelay decomposes intersection-level delay estimation into turning-movement-level subproblems, thereby reducing the complexity of the symbolic search. During DEE learning, CoSyDelay constructs domain-informed symbolic inputs from traffic variables. Large language models (LLMs) are employed as symbolic search operators to iteratively generate and refine candidate expression structures, whose movement-specific coefficients are subsequently calibrated using approach-level delay labels. A composite fitness function evaluates the learned DEEs jointly in terms of estimation accuracy and compliance with specified traffic-delay principles. Experimental results on multiple signalized intersections demonstrate that the resulting expressions achieve competitive estimation performance while maintaining physical consistency, thereby supporting trustworthy delay estimation. Source code and datasets are available at .

title: Discovering Programmatic Policies from Reinforcement Learning-Based Traffic Signal Controllers
summary: Discovering Programmatic Policies from Reinforcement Learning-Based Traffic Signal Controllers Traffic signal control (TSC) is critical for mitigating urban congestion. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has achieved strong performance by learning adaptive policies from traffic observations, but learned neural controllers are often opaque, structurally complex, and difficult to generalize across scenarios. We propose PPL-TSC, a programmatic policy learning framework that distills compact and human-readable TSC policies from DRL teachers. PPL-TSC formulates policy learning as an evolutionary search over phase utility functions (PUFs), which score candidate signal phases and select the highest-utility phase for execution. Each generation consists of four steps: policy generation, policy review, policy calibration, and policy evaluation. In the generation step, a large language model (LLM) acts as a semantics-aware evolutionary operator to propose and refine candidate PUFs. Generated PUFs are screened through explicit checks for syntactic validity, mathematical soundness, and consistency with TSC principles, with invalid ones repaired through iterative feedback. Valid PUFs are then calibrated to improve behavioral fidelity to the DRL teacher, and evaluated using a joint score combining teacher fidelity and traffic-control performance to select candidates for the next generation. Extensive experiments across diverse traffic scenarios and representative DRL-based controllers show that PPL-TSC produces compact and human-readable policies, achieves competitive performance for most teacher families, improves transfer generalization, and substantially reduces computational cost. Code is available at .

title: FinVision: Multimodal AI for Visualizing Financial Narratives
summary: FinVision: Multimodal AI for Visualizing Financial Narratives Financial narratives contain rich information about firms' performance and business conditions. Conventional text analysis often summarizes this information into numerical representations, which may not fully preserve the dynamic structure described in the narrative. In this study, we develop FinVision, a domain-specific multimodal generative model that translates financial narratives into visual representations of contemporaneous market dynamics. Using 87,940 paired observations of Management Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) disclosures and stock price charts, FinVision learns the average relationship between a firm's narrative account of a fiscal year and its stock-price dynamics over the same period. Given an MD&A alone, the trained model generates a text-implied stock chart, extending financial text analysis beyond numerical representations toward text-to-visual generation. We validate FinVision in two ways. First, held-out tests show that the model generates stock-chart representations that closely resemble observed charts and outperform direct LLM prompting, general-purpose text-to-image models, and the same architecture without financial-domain adaptation. Second, we examine the economic validity of the generated representations by comparing text-implied and observed stock charts. The resulting discrepancy is systematically associated with weaker investor responses around subsequent 10-K filings and with worse subsequent market and operating outcomes. Overall, our findings show how domain-adapted multimodal generative AI can create a new visual representation of financial text and provide an additional modality for studying business communication.

title: Towards GPROF V08: A Machine-Learning Framework for Simulating Passive Microwave Observations of Precipitation
summary: Towards GPROF V08: A Machine-Learning Framework for Simulating Passive Microwave Observations of Precipitation Spatially resolved precipitation retrievals based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) can improve precipitation estimates from passive microwave (PMW) observations and will be used to implement the next operational PMW retrieval algorithm for the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission. However, the conventional radiative transfer simulations used to extend the retrieval algorithm to the various sensors of the GPM constellation do not provide the spatial coverage required to train CNN-based retrievals. To address this, we introduce a machine-learning-based simulation framework that enables the training of the CNN-based GPROF-NN 3D retrieval algorithm for the full GPM constellation. At the core of this framework is Satformer, a new neural-network architecture that can translate PMW observations between any pair of GPM sensors. The resulting synthetic observations exhibit lower errors than conventional radiative transfer simulations and lead to more accurate precipitation retrievals when used to train GPROF-NN precipitation retrievals. We further demonstrate the applicability of the framework to new instruments by developing GPROF-NN retrievals for the Microwave Imager aboard the Weather System Follow-on Microwave satellite. While GPROF-NN retrievals based on the new simulation framework achieve lower instantaneous retrieval errors and higher correlations compared to independent reference data than conventional retrievals, residual simulation errors can introduce systematic biases in the resulting retrievals. The proposed simulation framework provides a key component for extending GPROF-NN to the full GPM constellation as part of the upcoming operational GPROF V08 retrieval algorithm. The results demonstrate the potential of machine-learning-based simulations to support spatially resolved precipitation retrievals across heterogeneous satellite constellations.

title: Practice Is Not Free: Measuring the Embodied Cost of Reset-Free Robot Practice
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures. Code, data, logs and videos: this https URL
summary: Practice Is Not Free: Measuring the Embodied Cost of Reset-Free Robot Practice 16 pages, 6 figures. Code, data, logs and videos: When a robot practices without human resets, every attempt still costs wall-clock time, actuator wear, and sometimes a person's attention, yet the schedulers that decide what to practice next treat attempts as free. We present an open, low-cost testbed for measuring these costs: a self-built SO-101 arm runs two demonstration-trained ACT policies that reset each other, with a vision-based success detector and a ledger that records the time, joint travel, and human interventions of every attempt. We formulate cost-aware practice scheduling, in which task selection is rewarded by measured competence gain net of embodied cost, and specify in advance the comparison that will test it. Its first two conditions, run on hardware for 51 minutes of robot time, show that a fixed retry limit did not reduce the share of execution time lost to failures (36%, against 27% for a feasibility rule; not significant) and saved no robot time. The logs suggest why: failures showed no sign of clustering, so a retry right after a failure was as likely to succeed as any other attempt. The ledger also shows that most of the retry rule's extra human time came from cubes knocked out of reach rather than from the rule itself, and a cost-aware rule replayed on the logs recovers the sensible choice without a hand-set limit. We also report lessons from building the system, including a coverage effect in which concentrating demonstrations in a smaller workspace raised success there from 8/20 to 10/10.

title: KneeFS-Net: A Lightweight Deep Learning Model for Knee Osteoarthritis Severity Assessment with Cross-Domain External Validation
summary: KneeFS-Net: A Lightweight Deep Learning Model for Knee Osteoarthritis Severity Assessment with Cross-Domain External Validation 23 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables Knee osteoarthritis (OA) grading from radiographs using the Kellgren-Lawrence (KL) scale requires expertise that may be scarce. We present KneeFS-Net, a lightweight ordinal grader (0.8 million parameters; 0.33 GFLOPs) combining spatial, Fourier and state-space features with landmark-guided attention. On the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI) test set, KneeFS-Net achieved a quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) of 0.863, mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.325 and 97.2% within-one-grade accuracy, comparable to models with 9-35-fold more parameters. We evaluated cross-population generalization on two Bangladeshi cohorts, a single-center hospital cohort and a multi-center teleradiology cohort. Without further training or adaptation, the OAI-trained model achieved QWK 0.803, MAE 0.339 and 98.2% within-one-grade accuracy on its hospital cohort, declining to QWK 0.656 and MAE 0.522 on multi-center teleradiology images. Self-supervised pretraining on 6,092 unlabeled radiographs followed by joint fine-tuning achieved QWK 0.823, MAE 0.329 and 99.7% within-one-grade accuracy in cross-validation. These findings demonstrate accurate, efficient KL grading and potential adaptation to new populations with limited annotation.

title: The novelty exposed: ablation, reproducibility and transparency in 40 technical reports of open-weight large language models (LLMs)
comment: Empirical study with an original dataset: 40 LLM technical reports coded by two independent model coders with script-verified quotes, plus a code-level comparison of open-weight architectures in Hugging Face transformers. 20 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Data, coding protocol and scripts in the ancillary files
summary: The novelty exposed: ablation, reproducibility and transparency in 40 technical reports of open-weight large language models (LLMs) Empirical study with an original dataset: 40 LLM technical reports coded by two independent model coders with script-verified quotes, plus a code-level comparison of open-weight architectures in Hugging Face transformers. 20 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Data, coding protocol and scripts in the ancillary files In 2025 alone, 48 new large language model (LLM) architectures were added to the Hugging Face transformers library, and many of them arrive with a technical report that presents the model as new. What is actually new in these models, and is it tested? We put this question to LLM technical reports. We look at three things: what the reference code shows about how new open-weight architectures differ from earlier ones; what 40 randomly sampled technical reports claim as new and whether they support it with ablation studies; and what they disclose for reproducibility and transparency. In the library, 39 of the 48 architectures added in 2025 take at least two of their three core blocks from another model, most often Llama, although part of this reflects how the library writes code. In the reports, 19 of 73 architectural or training novelty claims come with a controlled with/without comparison; 4 of 40 reports state more than one training run; 8 rerun the models they compare against under one setup; and 1 discloses data mixture, token count, and compute together. We also looked for known components given new names: none of five candidate cases hid its origin, though we did not study model names. We propose seven reporting rules for LLM release reports and apply them to two reports. We do not judge model quality, and an untested claim may still be true.

title: Living Context Graphs: Continual Semantic Learning for Enterprise Data Reasoning
comment: 22 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Continual Learning in the Era of Foundation Models and Embodied Agents. Data splits and annotations: this https URL
summary: Living Context Graphs: Continual Semantic Learning for Enterprise Data Reasoning 22 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Continual Learning in the Era of Foundation Models and Embodied Agents. Data splits and annotations: Enterprise AI can now perform analytics, reporting, and data-driven workflows, yet the data foundations it relies on remain hard to operationalize: business meaning, relationships, metric definitions, and reporting conventions are absent from database schemas and scattered across undocumented systems and tribal knowledge. We introduce the Living Context Graph (LCG), a continually learned context layer that makes existing enterprise data operational for AI without requiring a copy or transformation of the underlying warehouse. LCG bootstraps base semantics and relationships from the data itself, builds a concept graph that indexes business context as queries are served, writes durable semantic learnings from verified outcomes, and withdraws or re-earns context when later outcomes contradict prior routes. We evaluate LCG through text-to-SQL, a core data-reasoning task, on a transfer-aware split of three BIRD databases comprising 499 questions: 353 form the learning history and 146 are held out and never used to update the context layer. Bootstrapping alone improves overall accuracy by +4.6 percentage points. Learning only from the history raises accuracy on the untouched held-out transfer set by +22.6 points (95% CI [+14.4, +30.8]), exceeding five-shot retrieval from the same history by +12.3 points. Incremental learning reaches the one-shot endpoint within observed evaluation noise on every database. Ablating the graph changes held-out accuracy by at most one question per database but increases per-query cost 2.3-3.3x and median latency 1.8-3.4x: continually learned semantics drive accuracy, while the graph makes that context efficient to serve.

title: Breaking feature collapse in self-supervised time series encoders
summary: Breaking feature collapse in self-supervised time series encoders General-purpose time series encoders promise a single backbone that generalises across tasks and domains; however, they currently do not scale. We trace this down to a critical point of failure: under the predominant masked data modelling supervision, the encoder's output tokens partially collapse. This is the natural consequence of supervising encoders only in the input space, which leaves no constraint against redundant token dimensions in the feature space. We introduce OTISv2, which suppresses the collapse by complementing the reconstruction objective in input space with two objectives in the feature space: a self-distillation loss against an exponential-moving-average teacher, and a KoLeo regulariser. Under matched training, the resulting encoder reduces the cosine similarity and lifts the effective rank of its output tokens relative to its predecessor, and it scales monotonically from 7.1 M to 116 M parameters where its predecessor declines. It matches or surpasses existing general-purpose time series encoders across 143 uni- and multi-variate datasets. To foster further research, we release our code and pre-trained weights.

title: Calpha: Toward Native Biomolecular Intelligence in a General-Purpose Language Model
summary: Calpha: Toward Native Biomolecular Intelligence in a General-Purpose Language Model Biomolecular foundation models predict the structures of proteins and their complexes accurately, and large language models (LLMs) reason in natural language, but the two remain separate: the abilities of the former are not part of a general-purpose LLM, and the reasoning of the latter does not enter a structure prediction. Calpha aims at one general model that folds proteins and complexes, understands protein sequence and structure, and lets its language reasoning influence the structures it predicts. This report covers the first step, in which an LLM outputs single-chain protein structures. Qwen3.5-9B reads a sequence enriched with ESM2 residue features. It can respond in text or emit a token that invokes a pretrained SimpleFold structure head, which receives information about the protein only through Qwen's residue states. Under a fixed folding request, the head achieves mean TM-scores of 0.808 on the FoldBench-334 development set, 0.635 on CASP16 domains and 0.900 on a CAMEO-style PDB set. We compare these predictions with a baseline in which ESM2-3B encodes the sequence and a fine-tuned SimpleFold-3B head predicts the coordinates. The two systems also differ in trainable weights, training duration and crop length. For chains of 100--299 residues, all three paired confidence intervals include zero. At 300--600 residues, the mean differences are -0.044, -0.160 and -0.025, respectively. In a separate test, four English request types triggered folding on every evaluated example. Protein training reduced accuracy on a 350-item MMLU-Pro subset from 77.4% to 70.3%. An LLM can therefore output single-chain structures from its own states, with lower long-chain scores in the current comparisons and reduced accuracy on the evaluated MMLU-Pro subset. Complex prediction, structure understanding and the effect of language reasoning on the predicted coordinates remain future work.

title: Explaining Cross-Label Decision Structure in Multi-Output Tree Ensembles
summary: Explaining Cross-Label Decision Structure in Multi-Output Tree Ensembles 53 pages, 22 figures, 11 tables A multi-output tree ensemble predicts several binary labels through decision paths that it largely shares across those labels, yet the attribution methods commonly used to explain such models treat each output in isolation. We propose multi-sink Decision Predicate Graphs (ms-DPGs), which extend decision predicate graphs with one sink per label: each leaf contributes to the sink of every label its in-bag positive count for that label. On this representation we define Shared Predicate Flow (SPF), the share of a label's decision mass that passes through conditions active for both labels of a pair, and a contracted view of the graph in which label-specific lifts indicate whether a shared condition raises the probability of both labels or of one at the expense of the other. Controlled experiments show that SPF captures shared decision conditions rather than mere feature overlap. On nine multi-label benchmarks, native multi-output forests share substantially more decision structure than Binary Relevance on eight, including five of the six on which the two are at predictive parity, even at equal hyperparameters, whereas per-label TreeSHAP rankings register the change of architecture without showing whether more is shared. Because a native forest routes every label through the same splits, SPF describes the fitted model rather than the data, and on eight of the nine benchmarks it rises when the feature-label signal is removed; a high SPF is therefore not evidence of shared predictive information. ms-DPG offers a global, predicate-level account of how a multi-output ensemble reuses decision conditions across its labels.

title: Does the Voice Matter? Evaluating Frustration Detection on Deployed Clinical Voice-Agent Calls
comment: Accepted to Ml4H 2026 Accepted to GenAI4H workshop @ Neurips 2026
summary: Does the Voice Matter? Evaluating Frustration Detection on Deployed Clinical Voice-Agent Calls Accepted to Ml4H 2026 Accepted to GenAI4H workshop @ Neurips 2026 Autonomous voice agents now conduct routine clinical follow-up calls, so some automated triage is unavoidable. A patient becoming frustrated is one thing that triage should catch. These systems typically read only the transcript the speech-to-text stage produces, not the voice, and whether that is enough is largely untested on real clinical speech. We study per-turn frustration detection on real patient calls from a deployed clinical voice agent: 150 turns from six calls labelled by three annotators, with a length-matched acted corpus as a control, and 714 turns from 30 calls. Patient turns are overwhelmingly short: across the deployed calls, roughly 59% are one or two words, against 13% in the full acted corpus, and a corpus accuracy gap remains even after the acted set is length-matched. On one-word turns, transcript-only detection does not exclude chance. Across five audio-capable language models, the transcript flags 3 or 4 of the 39 frustrated one-word turns in the 30 calls, and a classifier given only the word count reaches 57.3%. Whether audio helps depends on the model and on the instruction. Asked to attend to delivery, two Gemini 2.5 models gain 3.0 pp over the transcript across 30 calls (-1.0 to 7.5 pp). Of the turns they confidently clear, 6.9% were in fact frustrated for audio against 13.0% for the transcript, a difference of 6.1 pp (2.2 to 10.4 pp). Across the 30 calls, given one prompt identical for both inputs, no model's audio-text interval excludes zero. Under the input-specific prompts, a newer Gemini model and two smaller open models do worse with audio than with the transcript (-3.5, -8.6 and -10.6 pp). A WavLM probe trained on the clinical calls matches the best prompted model overall (71.6%) but misses every frustrated one-word turn in the 24 added calls. When a patient's turn is short, the transcript alone is not enough to rule out frustration.

title: Towards wearable-scale, transition-aware sleep staging for clinical populations
summary: Towards wearable-scale, transition-aware sleep staging for clinical populations Automatic sleep staging models are predominantly developed on healthy sleepers and generalize poorly to clinical populations with fragmented sleep. Across three cohorts (patients with stroke, isolated REM sleep behaviour disorder, and other sleep disorders), we observe 2-3x more awakenings per hour, nearly twice as much N1, and less REM sleep than in healthy sleepers. We propose a label-efficient teacher-student framework for wearable-scale sleep staging. SleepGPT (136M parameters), adapted using labels from 25% of training patients, supervises a causal CNN-GRU (31k parameters; 122 KB) that stages EEG, EOG, or both in real time. We introduce Gcv-TAD, a new black-box transition-aware distillation loss. It emphasizes uncommon stage transitions while discounting those that vary across patients, using a prior estimated from labelled patients. In patient-wise 10-fold cross-validation, Gcv-TAD improves per-patient macro F1 over supervised training on the same labels by +3.2 to +7.6 points on average. Gains are largest on N1, and performance approaches full-label training.

title: Multi-CONDOR: Learning Multistable Motion Primitives from Demonstration
summary: Multi-CONDOR: Learning Multistable Motion Primitives from Demonstration Dynamical-system-based motion policies provide a framework for learning reactive robot motions with stability and convergence properties. Many manipulation tasks, however, admit several distinct goals or a continuous set of acceptable outcomes, requiring motion primitives that preserve these alternatives. Accommodating both goal structures within a unified framework with continuous, autonomous dynamics remains an open challenge. We propose a CONDOR-based framework, multi-CONDOR, for learning motion primitives with either multiple discrete attractors or a continuous attracting goal contour. The approach combines imitation learning with losses that encourage agreement between the learned task dynamics and latent reference systems encoding the desired attraction structure. We provide a Lyapunov-based analysis of the convergence properties of the learned motion dynamics. We evaluate the framework on simulated benchmarks with discrete goals, qualitative examples with continuous goal contours, and robotic grasping experiments. In simulation, multi-CONDOR reduces trajectory RMSE by approximately 72% compared with separately learned single-goal motion primitives selected by a state machine. For tasks with two and three goals, respectively, it reduces the fraction of evaluated initial states ending outside the goal tolerance from StableNODE's 0.31% and 7.29% to 0% in both settings. Experiments with a Franka Emika robot arm demonstrate successful grasping of a container by either of its two handles using motions learned from demonstrations. Together, these results show multi-CONDOR combines motion reproduction with the flexibility to converge to alternative valid outcomes.

title: What Makes a Good Move? Learning to Act from Experience in Visual Worlds
summary: What Makes a Good Move? Learning to Act from Experience in Visual Worlds Learning visual policies requires turning interaction experience into guidance for individual decisions. Trajectory outcomes obscure action quality, while unguided exploration can revisit familiar situations. We present \textsc{LightAct}, an experience-learning framework that connects skill-guided exploration with policy internalization. Interaction segments are summarized into experience entries and consolidated into a game-specific skill that guides root collection toward broader state coverage. At each root, candidate actions are compared through short rollouts under a shared frozen policy. Environment-reported score gains are averaged across continuations and normalized into relative action rewards, producing reusable supervision for reinforcement learning. Policy training uses a compact dataset of just 1,024 decision roots collected in a single source game and paired with their action rewards. Across 170 GameWorld tasks spanning 34 games, \textsc{LightAct} improves overall progress by 23.6, 29.2, and 13.0 percentage points at the 2B, 4B, and 9B scales, respectively, with our strongest model competitive with reported proprietary-model results. Ablations show broader root-state coverage with skill guidance and consistent gains across three policy optimizers. Case studies show how rollouts distinguish actions with identical immediate gains.

title: SemiNovo: Learning Beyond Search-Identified Spectra for De Novo Peptide Sequencing
comment: 13 pages. Accepted as an oral presentation at KDD 2027, AI for Sciences Track
summary: SemiNovo: Learning Beyond Search-Identified Spectra for De Novo Peptide Sequencing 13 pages. Accepted as an oral presentation at KDD 2027, AI for Sciences Track Sensitive peptide identification is fundamental to protein characterization and novel protein discovery, for which de novo peptide sequencing (DNPS) from tandem mass spectra provides an important database-independent approach. Although deep learning has substantially advanced de novo sequencing, existing models are predominantly trained on high-confidence peptide-spectrum matches obtained through database search. This search-conditioned supervision excludes a large fraction of unidentified spectra, creating a distribution mismatch between the selectively labeled training data and the complete spectrum stream encountered at inference time, thereby limiting peptide identification performance. To address this challenge, we propose SemiNovo, a semi-supervised framework that learns jointly from identified and unlabeled spectra. SemiNovo first constructs DarkSpec, a large-scale quality-controlled corpus of unlabeled spectra collected from diverse public proteomics projects, thereby extending training beyond search-identified spectra and mitigating the resulting shift in DNPS supervision. It then combines stepwise mass-constrained autoregressive decoding with cumulative path confidence to derive reliable supervision from unlabeled spectra. Moreover, SemiNovo introduces head-wise chemical-evidence gating to improve spectral evidence aggregation under noisy and incomplete fragmentation. Experiments show that SemiNovo performs favorably against state-of-the-art methods on multiple benchmarks. Code and dataset are publicly available.

title: Think2Listen: Evidence-Centric Learning For Agentic Audio Understanding With LALMS
summary: Think2Listen: Evidence-Centric Learning For Agentic Audio Understanding With LALMS Recent advances in large audio-language models (LALMs) have broadened audio understanding across speech, sound, and music, with tool-based agents further supporting these tasks by invoking predefined audio tools. However, a persistent gap remains between perceiving acoustic content and using it as evidence for reasoning: recognizing what is audible does not ensure that a model can identify which cues resolve an uncertain decision. To bridge this gap, we propose Think2Listen, an evidence-centric learning framework for agentic audio understanding. Guided by evidence before commitment, Think2Listen couples iterative reasoning with a targeted LALM interaction to actively seek acoustic cues that distinguish competing hypotheses and revise candidate judgments based on the observations returned. It learns what to ask, how to use evidence, and when to stop, using observation-induced changes in candidate-state to inform training credit. Extensive evaluations on two benchmarks spanning seven audio categories demonstrate that Think2Listen achieves (I) enhanced multi-step audio reasoning, with gains in overall accuracy of 5.08%--17.67% over competing audio agents; and (II) improved audio understanding and reasoning across speech, sound, and music, boosting overall accuracy by 2.29%--13.10% over the corresponding baselines. The source code is available at .

title: SWE-WhatIf: Simulating Real Users of Coding Agents from Recorded Session
summary: SWE-WhatIf: Simulating Real Users of Coding Agents from Recorded Session Recorded sessions between users and coding agents offer a way to evaluate how agents complete real-world tasks and interact with users. However, these sessions cannot simply be replayed with new agents, because recorded user replies may no longer apply when an agent takes a different trajectory. We introduce SWE-WhatIf, which replays recorded sessions with new agents by modeling the user's intents, the criteria for satisfying them, and the conditions under which they arise. Using this model, a user simulator generates replies that adapt to unseen agent turns while remaining grounded in the recording. Across 89 real-world sessions, SWE-WhatIf generated the replies most similar to those of real users and matched the strongest baseline when sessions were rewritten. To test adaptation, we replay sessions with agents instructed to avoid or repeat actions that the recorded user pushed back on. SWE-WhatIf produced the highest win rate for avoiding these actions (66.3%), significantly above chance. We further demonstrate its utility by ranking five LLMs as coding agents, where the highest-ranked model depended on how users specified and developed their intents, and a study with 16 users, where replaying their own sessions changed 14 participants' rankings and informed their future agent use.

title: Searching for Autoregressive Neural Architectures from Fundamental Operations
summary: Searching for Autoregressive Neural Architectures from Fundamental Operations Expressive Neural Architecture Search (NAS) search spaces are desirable as they do not restrict the space of potential architectures to what is already established. However, few search spaces are expressive enough to represent a broad range of architecture families, and those that are have focused primarily on image classification problems. The task of autoregressive sequence modelling has become ubiquitous in modern machine learning, but no existing search space supports the construction of and search over sequence models from fundamental operations, instead imposing strong inductive biases on the structure of potential architectures. This work describes how the expressive einspace search space can be extended to yield a search space capable of representing autoregressive models using fundamental operations. We perform a series of experiments showing that the novel einspaceAR search space can find capable autoregressive sequence models from scratch--i.e., without imposing strong inductive biases. We believe that our einspaceAR search space will be a useful part of the NAS toolbox and that the techniques described in this work can serve as a blueprint for the integration of autoregressive modelling in other expressive search spaces.

title: Human-AI Co-Ideation Across Socio-Technical Configurations: An Interactional Analysis of Planar and Immersive Workspaces
summary: Human-AI Co-Ideation Across Socio-Technical Configurations: An Interactional Analysis of Planar and Immersive Workspaces Remote collaborative platforms increasingly integrate generative AI to support group ideation. These platforms are sociotechnical configurations in which spatial mediation, interaction modality, AI output format, and the mechanisms that make contributions visible to a group co-vary as properties of a deployed system. This paper examines how such configurations shape participants' collaboration and their engagement with AI during creative work. We report a comparative study of two commercially available platforms that instantiate contrasting configurations: a planar shared canvas with text-based AI integration, and an immersive virtual reality workspace with concise AI output embedded in the shared space. Fourteen all-women triads completed a structured ideation task consisting of human-only idea generation, AI-supported idea expansion, and group convergence. We analyzed collaboration patterns, selection of AI-generated ideas, perceived idea quality, workload, presence, and their lexical characteristics. The immersive configuration yielded greater spatial presence and introduced a participation paradox, in which spatial freedom enabled exploration and fragmented group coherence; it was also associated with more balanced role distribution during convergence, at the cost of higher physical demand. In both configurations, AI multiplied the idea pool, and ideas groups authored with AI available were rated above participants' own. AI output format: about 21 words per idea on the planar canvas and 3 in the immersive workspace. Tracked how participants evaluated AI-generated ideas and how often they selected them unaltered as finalists. Neither configuration made AI contributions visible or attributable to the group: participants invoked AI individually and asynchronously in both. We derive design implications for AI output format, group-visible AI invocation, and spatial support for convergence

title: Linglong Agent Service: A Runtime for Centralized Agent Reasoning and Distributed Execution
summary: Linglong Agent Service: A Runtime for Centralized Agent Reasoning and Distributed Execution LLM agents can use remote tools and cloud sandboxes, but integrating reasoning, session state, and heterogeneous execution sites remains a runtime design problem. We present Linglong Agent Service (agentsvc), a self-hosted HTTP service and embeddable Python runtime that treats execution site as a configurable dimension alongside model, tools, and context. A parent service retains inference orchestration, tool descriptions, and conversation history; each inference request selects one child environment for file, shell, terminal, and MCP operations. Direct HTTP and child-initiated WebSocket tunnels carry the same application interfaces, including portable request context and centrally managed updates. The normal core path requires no third-party Python packages, with an optional Windows pseudo-terminal dependency. We further present online_debugger as the process-scale special case of execution-site separation: an instrumented program submits exception evidence, executes session-scoped inspection tools inside the incident process, and resumes the same diagnostic session. Its default prompt requires failing-then-passing reproduction evidence for source changes, while runtime patch activation and failed-call recovery remain unimplemented. We explain the design through constrained expected-utility reasoning, compare concrete mechanisms with Hermes Agent, Pi, Codex, and Claude Code, and report implementation and regression-test evidence. The current evidence establishes executable contracts, not performance advantages, repair accuracy, or production recovery. The source code is open source under the MIT license at .

title: PlanDiv: Test-Time Scaling with Latent Plans for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: PlanDiv: Test-Time Scaling with Latent Plans for Vision-Language-Action Models 10 pages, 2 figures Test-time scaling improves vision-language-action (VLA) policies by drawing several action candidates and executing the best one. We find that its returns diminish quickly when the candidates are resampled from one decoder: they differ by noise rather than by plan, and for each of three resampling sources, going from four to eight candidates adds only 0.06-0.07 to the average number of completed tasks on CALVIN. We introduce PlanDiv, an action head that makes the candidates differ by plan: a lightweight planner proposes K latent plan hypotheses, a shared masked-diffusion executor decodes one action chunk per plan from a single backbone pass, and the policy executes the chunk that its own likelihood ranks highest. The plans are learned from demonstrations alone, without plan labels or rewards. With the backbone, data and training recipe held fixed, eight plan-conditioned candidates raise five-task chain success on CALVIN ABC$\rightarrow$D from 56.9% to 69.9%, while eight candidates from autoregressive, plan-free or same-plan resampling reach at most 64.9%. The same-plan baseline is PlanDiv's own checkpoint with the plan held fixed, so this gap comes from the plans, not from drawing more samples. On LIBERO-Long, four plans remove 40% of single-candidate failures, against at most 21% for matched resampling. On a real Franka arm the gain appears where a task admits more than one solution: PlanDiv is on par with a single-output OpenVLA-OFT+ baseline on a one-solution task and succeeds in 51 of 54 trials against 40 of 54 on two tasks with two solutions.

title: GEM-MM: Reducing VLM Hallucination with Entropy-Guided Preference Alignment
summary: GEM-MM: Reducing VLM Hallucination with Entropy-Guided Preference Alignment Vision-language models (VLMs) are routinely aligned with offline pairwise RLHF objectives, but multimodal preference data is scarce and treats every response token as equally informative. Under a small preference budget, pair construction becomes nearly irrelevant: standard DPO-style, image-conditional, and self-improvement objectives all perform within 1.1 points on MM-RLHF metrics and 0.5 points on hallucination rates, matching the SFT baseline. We call this entropy-blind preference optimization: the learning signal ignores policy uncertainty, which in chain-of-thought VLMs concentrates on specific fork tokens where visual claims are made. We introduce GEM-MM, extending entropy-guided preference modeling to VLMs. It samples on-policy candidates, rewards high-entropy reasoning forks, penalizes uncertain final answers, and updates the model via group-normalized policy gradients. On a 3000-prompt MM-RLHF budget with Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct, GEM-MM achieves the best entropy-depth preference score (61.7% vs. 57.3-58.4% baselines) and implicit-reward accuracy (41.4%). Crucially, it reduces AMBER hallucination from 23.4-24.0 to 20.6 and CHAIR from 5.0-5.1 to 4.6 at matched caption coverage. It also ranks best on all three HallusionBench granularities, with a conservative operating point raising the near-chosen rate to 62.4%. An off-the-shelf multimodal reward model ranks GEM-MM first, and two such models independently confirm our main ablations (p < 0.001). We report confidence intervals, paired significance tests, metric-reward functional overlaps, and document a collapse mode when exceeding the fair budget. Code and evaluation harness:

title: U-HamGNN: a universal model for magnetic Hamiltonians conditioned on spin and Hubbard U
summary: U-HamGNN: a universal model for magnetic Hamiltonians conditioned on spin and Hubbard U 25 pages, 5 figures The electronic structure of a magnetic crystal depends jointly on its spin configuration and the on-site Hubbard correction U, requiring a separate DFT+U calculation for each combination. We introduce U-HamGNN, an equivariant network that takes these two inputs directly and predicts spin-resolved Hamiltonians across diverse crystal chemistries.
